opus-5.5/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Single-host deployment: nginx -> gunicorn/Flask API -> Postgres + Redis.
#
# Compose restarts crashed containers and orders startup by health, but it does
# NOT restart containers that turn "unhealthy", reschedule across hosts, or do
# rolling updates. See RUNBOOK.md for the operational procedures.
#
# All credentials come from .env (copy .env.example); `${VAR:?}` makes Compose
# refuse to start if a required secret is missing instead of using a default.

name: ${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-api}

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "5"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.28-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    # The only published port. Bound to localhost by default; set
    # PROXY_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 (or a specific interface) to expose it.
    ports:
      - "${PROXY_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:${PROXY_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - edge
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health || exit 1"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 128M
    logging: *default-logging

  api:
    build:
      context: .
    image: ${API_IMAGE:-api}:${API_TAG:-local}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      APP_MODULE: ${APP_MODULE:-app:app}
      FLASK_DEBUG: "0"
      GUNICORN_WORKERS: ${GUNICORN_WORKERS:-2}
      GUNICORN_THREADS: ${GUNICORN_THREADS:-4}
      # Hostnames are compose service names on the internal "backend" network.
      # Passwords must be URL-safe (see RUNBOOK.md, "Secret handling").
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
      REDIS_URL: redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}@cache:6379/0
    # No published ports: only reachable through the proxy.
    expose:
      - "8000"
    networks:
      - edge
      - backend
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      # Liveness of the app process. Requires the app to serve GET /healthz -> 200.
      test:
        - CMD
        - python
        - -c
        - "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=3)"
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M
          pids: 256
    logging: *default-logging

  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
    volumes:
      # postgres:17 keeps data in /var/lib/postgresql/data. postgres:18+ uses
      # /var/lib/postgresql instead -- see RUNBOOK.md before a major upgrade.
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      # -h 127.0.0.1 so the check fails during first-run init, when the
      # entrypoint's temporary server only listens on the Unix socket.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$${POSTGRES_USER}\" -d \"$${POSTGRES_DB}\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 30s
    shm_size: 128m
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    stop_grace_period: 60s
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 1G
    logging: *default-logging

  cache:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}
    # Run through the image entrypoint so Redis still drops to the "redis" user.
    # Pure cache: no persistence, bounded memory with LRU eviction.
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - >-
        exec docker-entrypoint.sh redis-server
        --requirepass "$$REDIS_PASSWORD"
        --maxmemory 200mb
        --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
        --save ""
        --appendonly no
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "REDISCLI_AUTH=\"$${REDIS_PASSWORD}\" redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M
    logging: *default-logging

networks:
  # Proxy <-> API only.
  edge:
  # API <-> Postgres/Redis. internal: no route to the outside world and no
  # way to publish ports from it.
  backend:
    internal: true

volumes:
  pgdata:

opus-5.5/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
#
# Production image for the Python (Flask) API.
# - slim, pinned base (bump deliberately; pin by digest in CI for full reproducibility)
# - dependencies installed only from the pinned requirements.txt, in their own layer
# - runs as an unprivileged user under gunicorn (not the Flask dev server)

ARG PYTHON_VERSION=3.13
FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

# Fixed UID/GID so volume ownership and security policies are predictable.
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies before copying source so code changes do not bust this layer.
# requirements.txt pins exact versions; psycopg2-binary ships wheels, so no compiler is needed.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-compile -r requirements.txt

# Application code is owned by root and only readable by the app user.
# .dockerignore keeps .env, VCS data and backups out of the build context.
COPY . .

USER app:app

EXPOSE 8000

# Gunicorn settings (bind, workers, timeouts, logging, app module) live in gunicorn.conf.py
# and can be tuned through environment variables without rebuilding.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--config", "/app/gunicorn.conf.py"]

opus-5.5/03-infra-management/gunicorn.conf.py

"""Gunicorn configuration for the API container.

Every value can be overridden with an environment variable so compose/.env can
tune the service without rebuilding the image.
"""
import os

# WSGI entry point, e.g. "app:app" or "myservice.wsgi:application".
wsgi_app = os.environ.get("APP_MODULE", "app:app")

bind = os.environ.get("GUNICORN_BIND", "0.0.0.0:8000")
workers = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_WORKERS", "2"))
threads = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_THREADS", "4"))
worker_class = "gthread"

# Worker timeout sits just below nginx's proxy_read_timeout (35s) so a stuck
# request is killed by gunicorn and logged here, not silently cut by the proxy.
timeout = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_TIMEOUT", "30"))
graceful_timeout = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT", "20"))
keepalive = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_KEEPALIVE", "65"))  # > nginx upstream keepalive_timeout

# Recycle workers periodically to contain slow memory leaks.
max_requests = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_MAX_REQUESTS", "1000"))
max_requests_jitter = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_MAX_REQUESTS_JITTER", "100"))

# The container root filesystem is read-only; heartbeat files go to tmpfs.
worker_tmp_dir = "/dev/shm"

# Only the nginx container talks to gunicorn; trust X-Forwarded-Proto from the
# private compose network. Override with a narrower CIDR if you pin subnets.
forwarded_allow_ips = os.environ.get("FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS", "*")

# Log to stdout/stderr so Docker's logging driver captures everything.
accesslog = "-"
errorlog = "-"
loglevel = os.environ.get("GUNICORN_LOG_LEVEL", "info")

opus-5.5/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

# Reverse proxy for the JSON API. nginx is the edge: it terminates client
# connections and forwards to gunicorn on the private "edge" network.
# TLS is expected to be terminated here or by an upstream load balancer;
# add a 443 server block (and HSTS) when certificates are available.

user nginx;
worker_processes auto;
pid /var/run/nginx.pid;
error_log /dev/stderr warn;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
  default_type application/json;

  server_tokens off;
  sendfile on;
  tcp_nopush on;

  # Structured access log with request id and upstream timing.
  log_format json_combined escape=json
    '{"time":"$time_iso8601","request_id":"$request_id",'
    '"remote_addr":"$remote_addr","method":"$request_method",'
    '"uri":"$request_uri","status":$status,"bytes_sent":$body_bytes_sent,'
    '"request_time":$request_time,"upstream_status":"$upstream_status",'
    '"upstream_response_time":"$upstream_response_time",'
    '"user_agent":"$http_user_agent"}';
  access_log /dev/stdout json_combined;

  # Client-side limits and timeouts sized for small JSON requests.
  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_body_buffer_size 64k;
  client_header_timeout 10s;
  client_body_timeout 10s;
  send_timeout 30s;
  keepalive_timeout 30s;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json application/problem+json;
  gzip_min_length 1024;
  gzip_proxied any;
  gzip_vary on;

  # Docker's embedded DNS. Re-resolving "api" means a recreated API container
  # (new IP) is picked up without restarting nginx.
  resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;
  resolver_timeout 5s;

  upstream api_backend {
    zone api_backend 64k;
    server api:8000 resolve;
    keepalive 16;
    keepalive_timeout 60s;
  }

  server {
    listen 80 default_server;
    server_name _;

    # nginx's own liveness endpoint (used by the compose healthcheck).
    location = /nginx-health {
      access_log off;
      return 200 '{"status":"ok"}\n';
    }

    location / {
      proxy_pass http://api_backend;

      # HTTP/1.1 + empty Connection header enables upstream keepalive.
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";

      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;
      # nginx is the edge: overwrite (not append) client-supplied values so
      # X-Forwarded-For cannot be spoofed. If another proxy/LB sits in front,
      # configure ngx_http_realip_module and switch to $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for.
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $server_port;

      # Upstream timeouts. Read timeout is slightly above gunicorn's 30s
      # worker timeout so the app, not the proxy, decides when a request dies.
      proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
      proxy_send_timeout 35s;
      proxy_read_timeout 35s;

      # Do not replay requests (e.g. POSTs) against the single upstream.
      proxy_next_upstream off;

      proxy_buffering on;
      proxy_buffer_size 16k;
      proxy_buffers 8 16k;

      proxy_hide_header X-Powered-By;

      add_header X-Request-ID $request_id always;
      add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
      add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;
      add_header Referrer-Policy no-referrer always;
      add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'" always;
    }

    # Return JSON (not nginx HTML) when the API is down or times out.
    # Application-generated 5xx responses pass through unchanged.
    error_page 502 503 504 @upstream_unavailable;
    location @upstream_unavailable {
      default_type application/json;
      add_header X-Request-ID $request_id always;
      return 503 '{"error":"service_unavailable","request_id":"$request_id"}\n';
    }
  }
}

opus-5.5/03-infra-management/requirements.txt

Flask==3.1.2
gunicorn==23.0.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.10
redis==6.4.0

Evaluation 8.75 / 10 graded blind as submission Y

Good hardening and the most systematic verification (33 rendered-config assertions, healthcheck tested against loopback server). Proxy runs read-only with pid in /tmp; API read-only. Runbook is accurate and covers restore drills and per-secret rotation but is the longest in the set (~1700 words), not concise.

Strengths

  • Rendered-config assertions script; stub server healthcheck test
  • Fail-closed empty passwords
  • nginx-health restricted to 127.0.0.1
  • Explicit residual risks (outbound access, psycopg2-binary, env secrets)

Weaknesses

  • RUNBOOK far from concise
  • Redis password in args; transitive pins missing
Evidence the grader checked
  • docker compose config (dummy .env from .env.example, empty secrets filled) exit 0
  • RESPONSE lists 33 checks; my render matched ports/networks

Objective checks

Files

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

RESPONSE: Task 03, infrastructure hardening

Highest-risk problems in the original files

Ranked by risk.

  1. Postgres and Redis are published on the host. db maps 5432 and cache maps 6379 on all interfaces. Redis has no authentication. Anyone who can reach the host can connect to both.
  2. Database credentials are committed. compose.yaml contains admin:password in POSTGRES_PASSWORD and in DATABASE_URL. .env.example uses change-me, a different value that Compose never reads, so the two files disagree.
  3. Postgres data has no volume. Data lives in the container's writable layer, so docker compose down deletes the database.
  4. The API is reachable directly, bypassing nginx. Port 5000 is published, so requests skip the proxy and its headers. The process is flask run --host=0.0.0.0, the Flask development server. FLASK_ENV=development signals a debug configuration. If debug mode were enabled, the Werkzeug debugger console would be exposed on a public port.
  5. Unpinned images. nginx:latest, postgres:latest and redis:latest change without notice. A new Postgres major version would fail to start against the existing data directory.
  6. The API runs as root with default capabilities. Any compromise of the app starts with root in the container.
  7. The build is not reproducible and copies secrets. pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignores requirements.txt. It installs unpinned latest versions and drops gunicorn, which that file pins. COPY . . with no .dockerignore copies .env, .git and everything else into image layers.
  8. Startup ordering is not health-based. depends_on without conditions only orders container starts. nginx resolves api once at startup, so recreating the API later leaves the proxy pointing at a stale address until it is restarted.
  9. No restart policy, healthchecks, log rotation or resource limits. Services stay down after a reboot, unhealthy containers go unnoticed, logs grow without bound, and one container can exhaust the host's memory.
  10. The proxy config is minimal for a JSON API. It sets no Host or X-Forwarded-* headers, so the app sees nginx's address and http scheme. It relies on default timeouts. It returns nginx's HTML error pages. It has no user directive and no structured logs.

What changed

File Change
compose.yaml No host ports for db or cache. Secrets are required from .env and the stack refuses to start without them. Named volumes for Postgres and Redis. Two networks, with backend internal. Health-gated depends_on. Healthchecks on all services. Restart policy, log rotation, memory and CPU limits. Read-only root filesystems for api and proxy. Dropped capabilities and no-new-privileges. Images pinned to major versions. Fixed project name. Proxy published on 127.0.0.1 only.
Dockerfile Pinned python:3.13-slim. Installs from requirements.txt, with dependencies cached in their own layer. Runs as UID 10001. Production server is Gunicorn with explicit timeouts. Drops FLASK_ENV. Sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE.
.dockerignore (new) Keeps .env, .git, caches and deployment files out of the image.
nginx.conf Pins the user, moves the pid file to /tmp, and adds JSON access logs with request_id. Sets Host, X-Request-ID and X-Forwarded-* by overwriting client-supplied values. Sets explicit proxy timeouts. Uses a runtime-resolved upstream so the proxy survives API recreation. Returns JSON 503 for proxy-generated errors, and passes upstream responses through unchanged. Adds a container-only /nginx-health endpoint and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Caps request bodies at 1 MB.
.env.example Secrets are blank, so an unedited copy fails validation. Documents generation with openssl rand -hex 32. Adds HTTP_PORT and an optional APP_IMAGE for rollback.
.gitignore (new) Ignores .env and Python caches.
RUNBOOK.md (new) Startup, health verification, backup and restore, secret handling and rotation, rollback, maintenance, known gaps.

Behaviour changes to be aware of: the default host port is now 8080, not 80 (HTTP_PORT). The API is no longer reachable on host port 5000. Redis now requires a password, so the application's REDIS_URL must carry it (the compose file already passes it). The application's health contract is assumed, not verified (see below).

Verification performed

No containers were started, as the task required. The session has no network. Docker's daemon socket returned permission denied, so no image was built or pulled. All checks were done on copies in $TMPDIR, so no test files were written to the task directory.

  • Cross-file consistency. Service names, ports and environment variable names match across compose.yaml, nginx.conf (api:5000) and .env.example.
  • Compose validation. docker compose config -q with test-only secret values passes.
  • Fail-closed secrets. With POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD empty or unset, compose exits 1 and names the missing variable. This is the result for the unedited .env.example.
  • Rendered-config assertions (docker compose config --format json, checked by a script). 33 checks, 0 failures:
    • No host ports on api, db or cache. Proxy publishes only 127.0.0.1:8080 → 80.
    • The backend network is internal. db and cache are attached only to it.
    • api is on both networks. proxy is on the frontend network only.
    • Every service has a healthcheck, a restart policy, log rotation, a memory limit and no-new-privileges.
    • api and proxy have read-only root filesystems. api drops all capabilities.
    • api waits for db and cache to be healthy. proxy waits for api.
    • DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL are built correctly from .env values.
    • Postgres uses SIGINT for fast shutdown.
  • API healthcheck expression. Run against a loopback test server: 2xx gives exit 0, 503 gives exit 1, connection refused gives exit 1.
  • nginx.conf structure. A lint script confirmed balanced braces, terminated statements and the presence of the required directives.

Not verified

  • Runtime behaviour is untested. The Dockerfile build, the pip install, Gunicorn startup, the healthchecks in containers, and the proxy starting under its capability and read-only settings were not run. No nginx binary is available, so nginx -t was not run. No hadolint, and docker build --check needs the daemon.
  • Image tags are unchecked. python:3.13-slim, nginx:1.28-alpine, postgres:17 and redis:7-alpine were chosen without registry access. Confirm they exist when first pulled.
  • Application contract is assumed. No application code was supplied. The configuration assumes app:app, a GET /healthz that returns non-2xx when not ready, and DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL environment variables.

Residual risks

  • Transitive Python dependencies are unpinned. requirements.txt pins only top-level packages. A hash-locked file is the fix, and it needs network access to generate.
  • psycopg2-binary. The supplied package is kept. The psycopg project advises a source build for production.
  • No TLS and no rate limiting. The proxy is loopback-only HTTP. TLS must be added before any wider exposure.
  • API outbound access. The api container can reach the internet through the frontend network.
  • Secrets are environment variables. They are visible to docker inspect and to anyone with Docker access on the host.
  • Redis is treated as a cache. It has AOF persistence, but no backup. Change that if it holds state.
  • Single host. Compose is not an orchestrator.

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

RUNBOOK: API stack (nginx → API → Postgres, Redis)

Single-host Docker Compose stack. Only nginx is reachable, and only on 127.0.0.1:${HTTP_PORT} (default 8080). Postgres and Redis have no host ports and live on an internal network.

Run every command from this directory.

Assumptions about the application

The directory contains no application code. Confirm these before the first start:

  • app.py (or another importable module) exposes a WSGI object named app. The image runs gunicorn ... app:app.
  • The app reads DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL from the environment.
  • The app listens on port 5000.
  • GET /healthz returns 2xx only when the app can serve traffic (ideally after checking Postgres and Redis) and a non-2xx status otherwise. The API healthcheck and the startup ordering depend on this.
  • The app does not need schema migrations to run at startup. If it does, run them as a one-off step before the first start: docker compose run --rm api <migrate command>.

1. Startup

Prerequisites: Docker Engine with Compose v2 (docker compose version) and openssl.

cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env

Edit .env and set POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD. Generate each one with:

openssl rand -hex 32

Then validate and start:

docker compose config -q          # checks .env and interpolation; prints nothing on success
docker compose up -d --build      # builds the api image, starts services in dependency order
docker compose ps                 # wait until all four services show (healthy)

config -q fails with a message naming the missing variable if a secret is empty. Do not run docker compose config without -q in a shared terminal or log, because it prints the resolved secrets.

Startup order is db and cache, then api, then proxy. Each waits for the previous service's healthcheck to pass.

Other common commands:

docker compose logs -f --tail=100 api proxy   # proxy logs are one JSON object per request
docker compose stop                           # stop containers, keep data and containers
docker compose down                           # remove containers and network, keep volumes

Never run docker compose down -v unless you intend to delete the database. -v removes the pgdata and redisdata volumes.

2. Health verification

Run these after startup, after any change, and during an incident.

  1. Service status. Every service must show healthy in docker compose ps.

  2. End to end through the proxy. This should return 2xx and an X-Request-ID header:

    curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

  3. Proxy itself. /nginx-health only answers from inside the container. A request from the host gets 403, which is expected:

    docker compose exec proxy wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health   # prints: ok

  4. Proxy error path. Stop the API and confirm the proxy returns a JSON 503, not an HTML page. Then restart it:

    docker compose stop api
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz      # 503, body {"error":"upstream_unavailable"}
docker compose start api

  5. Database and cache answer inside the stack:

    docker compose exec db sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"'
docker compose exec cache sh -c 'redis-cli ping'           # prints PONG

  6. No unintended exposure. The PORTS column for db and cache must show no -> mapping, and proxy must show only 127.0.0.1:8080->80:

    docker compose ps --format 'table {{.Service}}\t{{.Ports}}'

  7. Hardening took effect. The API runs as UID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem:

    docker compose exec api id -u                        # prints 10001
docker compose exec api sh -c 'touch /x'             # fails: Read-only file system or Permission denied

3. Backup and restore

Postgres is the only service holding data you cannot regenerate. Redis is treated as a cache and is not backed up. If the app stores data only in Redis, add a backup step and revisit this section.

Use logical dumps. Do not copy the volume while Postgres is running.

Backup

mkdir -p backups && chmod 700 backups
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' > "backups/app-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).dump"

Confirm the archive is readable before you rely on it:

docker compose exec -T db pg_restore --list < backups/app-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.dump > /dev/null && echo "archive OK"

Backups contain all application data. Keep them out of version control and off shared storage. Keep at least one copy off the host.

Restore (replaces current data)

docker compose stop api proxy
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"' < backups/app-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.dump
docker compose up -d

To restore onto a new host, run docker compose up -d db first. Postgres creates the user and database from .env on first start. Then restore as above.

Restore drill

Test restores regularly, not only when you need one. This restores into a scratch database and drops it afterwards:

docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "CREATE DATABASE restore_check" && pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d restore_check --no-owner' < backups/app-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.dump
docker compose exec db sh -c 'psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "DROP DATABASE restore_check"'

Schedule the backup command with cron or a systemd timer, and set a retention policy.

4. Secret handling

  • Where secrets live. All secrets are in .env. The file is git-ignored (.gitignore) and excluded from the image (.dockerignore). .env.example contains no secret values.
  • Permissions. Keep .env at chmod 600.
  • Generation. Use openssl rand -hex 32. Hex output is URL-safe, which matters because DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL embed the passwords without URL-encoding. Do not use any generator that produces @ : / ? # % $ characters.
  • Who gets what. Only the containers that need a secret receive it:
    • db gets POSTGRES_PASSWORD.
    • api gets both passwords, embedded in DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL.
    • cache gets REDIS_PASSWORD in its command line and in REDISCLI_AUTH, used by its healthcheck.
    • proxy gets no secrets.
  • Limits of this approach. Anyone who can run docker inspect or read the container's environment can see these values. So can anyone with Docker access on the host. Compose has no secrets manager, so treat the host as the trust boundary.

Rotating the Postgres password

POSTGRES_PASSWORD only takes effect when the data volume is first initialized. Changing .env does not change the password of an existing database. Change it in the database first:

NEW_PW=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
docker compose exec -T -e NEW_PW="$NEW_PW" db sh -c 'psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -v pw="$NEW_PW" -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"' <<'SQL'
ALTER USER CURRENT_USER PASSWORD :'pw';
SQL

Then set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env to the same value and recreate the containers that use it:

docker compose up -d db api

Rotating the Redis password

Set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env, then recreate the two services that use it. Expect a brief API reconnect:

docker compose up -d cache api

Do not

  • Commit .env, paste it into tickets, or copy it into images.
  • Use docker compose config without -q anywhere it will be logged.

5. Rollback

Application image

Keep the current image before you rebuild:

docker tag api:local api:previous
docker compose up -d --build api          # deploy the new version

To roll back:

APP_IMAGE=api:previous docker compose up -d --no-deps api
docker compose ps                          # then run section 2 checks

To make the rollback persist across up, set APP_IMAGE=api:previous in .env, or rebuild from the previous commit of this directory.

Proxy configuration

Validate the config before you apply it:

docker compose exec proxy nginx -t

Then recreate the proxy. Recreating also works if your editor replaced the file and broke the bind mount:

docker compose up -d --force-recreate proxy

To roll back, restore the previous nginx.conf from version control and repeat.

Compose configuration

Restore the previous compose.yaml from version control, then run docker compose up -d. Services whose definitions changed are recreated.

Database

Schema migrations are often not reversible. Before any deploy that changes the schema, take a backup (section 3). To roll back data, restore that backup. Anything written after the backup is lost.

Postgres major versions

Moving postgres:17 to a newer major version is not an in-place upgrade. Dump, change the tag, start with a fresh volume, and restore. Do not change the tag on an existing pgdata volume.

6. Routine maintenance

  • Pin images by digest. Tags are mutable. After you pull and test a tag, record its digest and use image: postgres:17@sha256:... in compose.yaml:

    docker pull postgres:17
docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' postgres:17

  • Upgrade deliberately. Change one tag at a time in compose.yaml, deploy, and run section 2.

  • Resource limits in compose.yaml are starting points. Check real usage with docker stats and adjust.

  • Project name. The fixed name: api-stack keeps volume names stable if this directory is renamed or copied. Without it, a rename would silently create a new empty database volume.

7. Known gaps

  • Transitive Python dependencies are not pinned. requirements.txt pins only top-level packages. For a fully reproducible install, generate a hash-locked file with pip-compile --generate-hashes and install with pip install --require-hashes -r. This needs network access and was not done here.
  • psycopg2-binary in production. The psycopg project advises building psycopg2 from source for production. The supplied binary package was kept. Revisit if your policy requires it.
  • Base images are not digest-pinned. See section 6.
  • No TLS. The proxy serves plain HTTP on loopback only. Before exposing it beyond the host, terminate TLS at a load balancer or add a TLS listener to nginx.conf. If a load balancer sits in front, switch the proxy's X-Forwarded-For to append ($proxy_add_x_forwarded_for) and configure set_real_ip_from.
  • Client IP. Behind Docker's port publishing, the proxy sees the bridge gateway address for host clients, not their real address. X-Forwarded-For is therefore only meaningful after a real load balancer is in front.
  • API outbound access. The api container can reach the internet through the frontend network, because the proxy has to share a network with it. If the API makes no outbound calls, put proxy↔api on its own internal: true network and give the proxy a separate non-internal network.
  • No rate limiting or authentication at the proxy. Request bodies are capped at 1 MB.
  • Single host only. Compose gives no rolling updates, multi-host scheduling, or automatic failover.

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env and fill in the empty values. Never commit .env.
#   cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
# Compose refuses to start while a required value is empty.
# Generate secrets with:  openssl rand -hex 32
# Hex output is URL-safe, which the DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL built in compose.yaml require.

# Host port for the proxy. Bound to 127.0.0.1 only.
HTTP_PORT=8080

POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_DB=app

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Single-host stack for local or small-server use. This is not an orchestrator:
# no rolling updates, no multi-host scheduling. Secrets come from .env (see .env.example).

# Fixed project name, so volume names do not change if the directory is renamed or copied
name: api-stack

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.28-alpine
    ports:
      # Loopback only. Change the bind address on purpose if other hosts need access.
      - "127.0.0.1:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
      - /var/cache/nginx
    # The nginx master starts as root to bind port 80, then drops to the nginx user for workers
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    cap_add: [CHOWN, SETGID, SETUID, NET_BIND_SERVICE]
    security_opt:
      - "no-new-privileges:true"
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging

  api:
    build: .
    image: "${APP_IMAGE:-api:local}"
    # Not published to the host. Only the proxy reaches it, over the frontend network.
    expose:
      - "5000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}@cache:6379/0"
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      # Expects GET /healthz to return 2xx only when the app can serve (see RUNBOOK.md)
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/healthz', timeout=3)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt:
      - "no-new-privileges:true"
    pids_limit: 256
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 1.0
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: "${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}"
      POSTGRES_DB: "${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}"
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    # Not published to the host. Reachable only from api, on the internal backend network.
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", 'pg_isready -U "$$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$$POSTGRES_DB"']
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
      start_period: 10s
    # SIGINT is Postgres's fast shutdown. SIGTERM waits for clients to disconnect and usually runs into the grace period.
    stop_signal: SIGINT
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    security_opt:
      - "no-new-privileges:true"
    pids_limit: 256
    mem_limit: 1g
    cpus: 1.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    # Password required. AOF persistence goes to the redisdata volume.
    # Treated as a cache: capped at 256 MB with LRU eviction. If Redis becomes a queue or session store, revisit the eviction policy.
    command:
      - redis-server
      - --appendonly
      - "yes"
      - --requirepass
      - "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}"
      - --maxmemory
      - 256mb
      - --maxmemory-policy
      - allkeys-lru
    environment:
      # Lets redis-cli in the healthcheck authenticate without putting the password on its command line
      REDISCLI_AUTH: "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}"
    volumes:
      - redisdata:/data
    # Not published to the host. Reachable only from api, on the internal backend network.
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
    security_opt:
      - "no-new-privileges:true"
    pids_limit: 256
    mem_limit: 384m
    cpus: 0.5
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging

networks:
  frontend:
  backend:
    # No route outside the host. db and cache are unreachable from outside the stack.
    internal: true

volumes:
  pgdata:
  redisdata:

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
    WEB_CONCURRENCY=2

WORKDIR /app

# Unprivileged runtime user with a fixed UID so file ownership is predictable
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

# Install pinned dependencies before copying code so code edits reuse this layer
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

# Code is root-owned, so the runtime user can read but not modify it.
# .dockerignore keeps .env and other local files out of the image.
COPY . .

USER app
EXPOSE 5000

# Production WSGI server instead of `flask run`. Assumes app.py defines a Flask object named `app`.
# The port is not published by compose, so only the proxy can reach it and trusting its X-Forwarded-* headers is safe.
CMD ["gunicorn", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", \
     "--timeout", "30", \
     "--graceful-timeout", "30", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--forwarded-allow-ips", "*", \
     "app:app"]

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

# Edge proxy for the JSON API. Mounted over /etc/nginx/nginx.conf in nginx:1.28-alpine.
user nginx;
worker_processes auto;

# /var/run is not writable on the read-only root filesystem
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;

error_log /dev/stderr warn;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  server_tokens off;

  # No query string: it can carry tokens, and this log is shipped to stdout
  log_format api_json escape=json
    '{"time":"$time_iso8601","remote_addr":"$remote_addr","request_id":"$request_id",'
    '"method":"$request_method","path":"$uri","status":$status,'
    '"bytes_sent":$body_bytes_sent,"request_time":$request_time,'
    '"upstream_time":"$upstream_response_time"}';
  access_log /dev/stdout api_json;

  # Docker's embedded DNS. Resolving at request time keeps the proxy working when the api
  # container is recreated and gets a new IP, which a startup-time upstream would not survive.
  resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;

  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_header_timeout 10s;
  client_body_timeout 10s;
  send_timeout 30s;
  keepalive_timeout 30s;

  add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
  add_header X-Request-ID $request_id always;

  server {
    listen 80 default_server;
    server_name _;

    # Container healthcheck only. Requests from outside the container get 403.
    location = /nginx-health {
      access_log off;
      allow 127.0.0.1;
      deny all;
      return 200 "ok\n";
    }

    location / {
      set $api_upstream http://api:5000;
      proxy_pass $api_upstream;

      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";

      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;

      # nginx is the public edge, so it overwrites client-supplied forwarding headers rather than appending to them
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;

      # Gunicorn's sync workers are killed after 30s (see Dockerfile), so nginx waits a little longer and clients see the app's own failure, not a proxy timeout
      proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
      proxy_send_timeout 60s;
      proxy_read_timeout 60s;

      # Proxy-generated errors get a JSON body. Upstream responses pass through unchanged
      # because proxy_intercept_errors is off (the default), so an app 503 keeps its body.
      error_page 502 503 504 = @upstream_unavailable;
    }

    location @upstream_unavailable {
      internal;
      default_type application/json;
      return 503 '{"error":"upstream_unavailable"}\n';
    }
  }
}

haiku-5.5/03-infra-management/requirements.txt

Flask==3.1.2
gunicorn==23.0.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.10
redis==6.4.0

Evaluation 8.75 / 10 graded blind as submission W

Thorough hardening: Redis writes its requirepass into a tmpfs config file (no password in args) and runs as the redis user, read-only; nginx runs as uid 101 with all temp paths in /tmp; API read_only with cap_drop. Runbook is concise and correct on rotation and tag rollback.

Strengths

  • Redis config generated in /tmp with umask 077, no password on the command line
  • Proxy loopback 127.0.0.1:80 -> 8080, user 101, read_only
  • pids limits on every service
  • Rotation updates role first then recreates

Weaknesses

  • Top-level Python pins only
  • nginx-health is proxy-local only (end-to-end via /health documented)
Evidence the grader checked
  • docker compose config (dummy .env from .env.example, empty secrets filled) exit 0
  • rendered cache cmd writes /tmp/redis.conf then exec redis-server

Objective checks

Files

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Hardening Summary and Verification

Highest-Risk Original Problems

  1. Hardcoded credentials and unauthenticated Redis (compose.yaml, .env.example)

    • compose.yaml embedded POSTGRES_USER: admin, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password, and DATABASE_URL: postgres://admin:password@db:5432/app directly in version-controlled config, ignoring .env.example.
    • cache (Redis) had no authentication (REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379) and no memory cap/eviction policy, exposing an unauthenticated in-memory store to arbitrary commands and unbounded RAM growth.
    • Fix: Removed all embedded credentials; required POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, and REDIS_PASSWORD via Compose ${VAR:?...} interpolation from .env (documented in .env.example); enabled Redis requirepass (written to a 0600 tmpfs config rather than exposed on argv) with maxmemory 128mb and allkeys-lru.

  2. Publicly exposed database, cache, and backend API ports (compose.yaml)

    • db (5432:5432), cache (6379:6379), and api (5000:5000) were all published on 0.0.0.0, exposing Postgres, unauthenticated Redis, and the Flask app directly on the host network and bypassing nginx.
    • All four services shared a single implicit default bridge network.
    • Fix: Removed host ports from db, cache, and api (using internal expose only); bound proxy to ${PROXY_BIND_IP:-127.0.0.1}:${PROXY_PORT:-80}:8080; segmented traffic into edge (proxy <-> api) and internal: true (api <-> db, cache) networks.

  3. Root container execution, dev server in production, and unpinned dependencies (Dockerfile)

    • Dockerfile ran as root, set ENV FLASK_ENV=development, and used Werkzeug's single-process development server (flask run --host=0.0.0.0) instead of a production WSGI server.
    • It ignored the pinned requirements.txt (running pip install flask psycopg2 redis after COPY . .), breaking layer caching and reproducibility, and had no .dockerignore (risking .env and repo metadata leaking into the image).
    • Fix: Switched to python:3.13-slim-bookworm, added .dockerignore, installed pinned packages from requirements.txt before COPY, set FLASK_DEBUG=0, created dedicated UID/GID 10001:10001 (app) with read-only /app permissions, and configured gunicorn (2 workers, 4 threads, --worker-tmp-dir /dev/shm, stdout/stderr logs).

  4. No Postgres data persistence and floating :latest tags (compose.yaml, Dockerfile)

    • db had no volume mount for /var/lib/postgresql/data, so container recreation wiped all database data.
    • nginx:latest, postgres:latest, redis:latest, and python:3.13 risked unannounced major-version breaks (including Postgres on-disk format mismatches).
    • Fix: Added named volume postgres_data mounted to /var/lib/postgresql/data and pinned images to nginx:1.27-alpine, postgres:17-bookworm, redis:7.4-alpine, and python:3.13-slim-bookworm.

  5. No health checks, race-prone startup ordering, or operational guardrails (compose.yaml)

    • depends_on waited only for container start (service_started), letting api crash-loop before Postgres/Redis finished initializing and letting proxy serve 502s before api was ready.
    • Missing restart, bounded logging (risking disk exhaustion), stop_grace_period, read_only rootfs/capability drops, and deploy.resources limits.
    • Fix: Added meaningful health checks (pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1, REDISCLI_AUTH redis-cli ping, Python urllib.request on api /health, BusyBox wget on proxy /nginx-health), health-gated depends_on (condition: service_healthy), unless-stopped restarts, json-file log rotation (10m x 5), CPU/memory/PID resource bounds, and non-root read_only + cap_drop: [ALL] on proxy, api, and cache (plus no-new-privileges:true across all services).

  6. Minimal nginx.conf unsuitable for a JSON API

    • Missing forwarding headers (Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Request-ID), explicit client/proxy timeouts, body size cap, security headers, structured upstream timing logs, and dynamic DNS re-resolution (causing stale IP 502s after api recreations).
    • Fix: Hardened nginx.conf to run unprivileged on port 8080 with /tmp temp/pid paths, JSON-API timeouts (5s connect, 30s send, 60s read, 1m max body), standard proxy/security headers, JSON gateway error responses (502/503/504), loopback-only /nginx-health, and resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off.

Verification Performed

All checks were run offline inside 03-infra-management after final configuration edits, without starting containers or using the network:

  • Compose schema and interpolation validation (with .env.example):
    • docker compose --env-file .env.example config -q -> exited 0 (compose config -q: OK).
    • docker compose --env-file .env.example config -> verified rendered services (api, cache, db, proxy), volumes (postgres_data), networks (edge, internal: true), healthchecks, resource limits, and that only proxy publishes a host port (127.0.0.1:80->8080).
  • Fail-closed secret validation (without .env):
    • docker compose config -q -> exited 1 with explicit missing-variable errors for POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, and REDIS_PASSWORD.
  • YAML and file structure verification:
    • python3 -c "import yaml; ..." -> parsed compose.yaml via yaml.safe_load cleanly (services: ['api', 'cache', 'db', 'proxy'], volumes: ['postgres_data'], networks: {'edge': {'driver': 'bridge'}, 'internal': {'driver': 'bridge', 'internal': True}}).
    • python3 static assertions on nginx.conf and Dockerfile -> verified balanced braces (12 pairs), required proxy/timeout/resolver directives in nginx.conf, pinned base image, requirements.txt, USER 10001:10001, gunicorn, FLASK_DEBUG=0, and absence of FLASK_ENV=development in Dockerfile.
    • ls -la -> verified readable file permissions (0644) for mounted nginx.conf and confirmed no .env file with live credentials exists in the workspace.

Not run in this environment: Container image builds, container runtime startup/healthcheck execution (docker compose up), and nginx -t / hadolint / yamllint (container startup and network access are prohibited by task constraints, and nginx, hadolint, and yamllint binaries are not installed on this host).

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Deployment Runbook

Operational guide for the hardened proxy (nginx) -> api (Flask/Gunicorn) -> db (PostgreSQL) + cache (Redis) stack.

1. Startup

  1. Create a local environment file from the template and set unique URL-safe secrets:
    cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
# Generate values for POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD:
openssl rand -hex 24
    Edit .env to replace both placeholder passwords (hex avoids URL-encoding issues in DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL). Adjust PROXY_PORT=8080 if port 80 is unavailable or running rootless Docker.
  2. Validate the Compose configuration before starting:
    docker compose config -q
    Compose refuses to start if required variables (POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, REDIS_PASSWORD) are missing or empty.
  3. Build and start the stack:
    docker compose up -d --build
    Health-gated depends_on enforces startup order: db and cache become healthy first, then api, then proxy. Application expectation: the Python service exposes WSGI entrypoint app:app (override api.command if different) and GET /health returning HTTP 200.

2. Health Verification

  1. Confirm all four services report healthy and only proxy publishes a host port:
    docker compose ps
    Expected port binding: 127.0.0.1:${PROXY_PORT:-80}->8080/tcp on proxy only (api, db, and cache must show no published host ports).
  2. Verify nginx edge liveness and end-to-end API health through the proxy:
    docker compose exec proxy wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/nginx-health
curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${PROXY_PORT:-80}/health"
  3. Inspect logs or detailed healthcheck output if a service fails to go healthy:
    docker compose logs --tail=100 proxy api db cache
docker inspect --format='{{json .State.Health}}' "$(docker compose ps -q api)"

3. Backup and Restore (PostgreSQL)

Postgres data persists in the named postgres_data volume. Redis (cache) is configured as an ephemeral LRU cache (128mb limit, persistence disabled); Postgres is the system of record.

Never run docker compose down -v in an environment where data must be kept — -v deletes postgres_data.

Backup

Stream a consistent custom-format dump to the host:

set -a && . ./.env && set +a
mkdir -p backups && chmod 700 backups
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc > "backups/db_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).dump"

Store backups off-host (encrypted) and periodically test restores against a scratch volume.

Restore

Stop api so no connections or writes race with the restore, restore the dump, then restart api:

set -a && . ./.env && set +a
docker compose stop api
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  --clean --if-exists --no-owner < backups/db_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.dump
docker compose start api

Re-run the health checks in Section 2 afterward.

4. Secret Handling

  • Local files: Keep .env untracked (.gitignore / .dockerignore) with 0600 permissions. Never bake .env or credentials into images or compose.yaml.
  • DSN safety: Use alphanumeric/hex secrets (e.g., openssl rand -hex 24) so special characters do not break DATABASE_URL or REDIS_URL.
  • Rotation:
    1. Update POSTGRES_PASSWORD and/or REDIS_PASSWORD in .env.
    2. For Postgres (which only applies POSTGRES_PASSWORD on initial initdb), update the existing DB role first:
      set -a && . ./.env && set +a
docker compose exec -T db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "ALTER USER \"$POSTGRES_USER\" WITH PASSWORD '$POSTGRES_PASSWORD';"
    3. Recreate containers so api and cache pick up the new credentials:
      docker compose up -d --force-recreate cache api
  • Production hardening: Beyond single-host Compose, replace .env secrets with mounted secret files (e.g., /run/secrets/* with POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE and a secret manager) and terminate TLS before proxy (or add TLS server blocks in nginx.conf).

5. Rollback

Tag releases explicitly before deploying (IMAGE_TAG=v1.2.3 docker compose build api) so the prior image remains available.

  1. Application image rollback (no rebuild required):
    IMAGE_TAG=<previous-tag> docker compose up -d --no-deps --no-build api
    Wait for api to become healthy and verify curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${PROXY_PORT:-80}/health". (nginx.conf re-resolves api via 127.0.0.11 every 10s, so proxy picks up the new api container IP automatically.)
  2. Database schema rollback: If the failed release applied a destructive or backward-incompatible migration, restore the pre-deploy backup (Section 3) before starting the previous IMAGE_TAG.
  3. Configuration rollback: Restore compose.yaml, nginx.conf, or Dockerfile from the last known-good commit, run docker compose config -q, and apply with docker compose up -d.

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env (`cp .env.example .env`) and replace placeholder secrets before starting.
# Generate URL-safe random secrets (hex avoids URL-encoding issues in DSNs):
#   openssl rand -hex 24

# PostgreSQL
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-generate-with-openssl-rand-hex-24
POSTGRES_DB=app

# Redis
REDIS_PASSWORD=change-me-generate-with-openssl-rand-hex-24

# Nginx proxy host binding (loopback by default; use PROXY_PORT=8080 for rootless Docker)
PROXY_BIND_IP=127.0.0.1
PROXY_PORT=80

# API image naming for tagged deploys and rollbacks
API_IMAGE=app-api
IMAGE_TAG=local

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "5"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    user: "101:101"
    command: ["nginx", "-e", "stderr", "-g", "daemon off;"]
    ports:
      - "${PROXY_BIND_IP:-127.0.0.1}:${PROXY_PORT:-80}:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - edge
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-T", "3", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/nginx-health"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m,uid=101,gid=101
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 128M
          pids: 64
        reservations:
          cpus: "0.10"
          memory: 32M

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    image: ${API_IMAGE:-app-api}:${IMAGE_TAG:-local}
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?Set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
      REDIS_URL: redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?Set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}@cache:6379/0
      FLASK_DEBUG: "0"
    expose:
      - "5000"
    networks:
      - edge
      - internal
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    stop_grace_period: 35s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m,uid=10001,gid=10001
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M
          pids: 128
        reservations:
          cpus: "0.25"
          memory: 128M

  db:
    image: postgres:17-bookworm
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER in .env}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:?Set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
    expose:
      - "5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - internal
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 20s
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M
          pids: 128
        reservations:
          cpus: "0.25"
          memory: 128M

  cache:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    user: redis
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - umask 077 && printf 'requirepass "%s"\nsave ""\nappendonly no\nmaxmemory 128mb\nmaxmemory-policy allkeys-lru\ndir /tmp\n' "$$REDIS_PASSWORD" > /tmp/redis.conf && exec redis-server /tmp/redis.conf
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:?Set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}
    expose:
      - "6379"
    networks:
      - internal
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "REDISCLI_AUTH=\"$$REDIS_PASSWORD\" redis-cli ping | grep -qx PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=32m,mode=1777
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M
          pids: 64
        reservations:
          cpus: "0.10"
          memory: 64M

volumes:
  postgres_data:

networks:
  edge:
    driver: bridge
  internal:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
    FLASK_DEBUG=0

WORKDIR /app

# Create a dedicated non-root user and group with fixed IDs matching compose tmpfs mounts.
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
    && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

# Install pinned dependencies separately so code edits reuse the dependency layer.
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application files owned by root:app and keep /app read-only to the app user.
COPY --chown=root:app . .
RUN chmod -R a+rX,go-w /app

USER 10001:10001

EXPOSE 5000

# Override app:app via Compose command if the WSGI callable lives in another module.
CMD ["gunicorn", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", \
     "--workers", "2", \
     "--threads", "4", \
     "--timeout", "60", \
     "--graceful-timeout", "30", \
     "--keep-alive", "5", \
     "--worker-tmp-dir", "/dev/shm", \
     "--forwarded-allow-ips", "*", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-", \
     "app:app"]

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

worker_processes auto;
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;
error_log /dev/stderr warn;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
  default_type application/json;

  server_tokens off;
  sendfile on;
  tcp_nopush on;
  tcp_nodelay on;

  # Store temp buffers in /tmp so the container root filesystem can remain read-only.
  client_body_temp_path /tmp/client_temp;
  proxy_temp_path /tmp/proxy_temp;
  fastcgi_temp_path /tmp/fastcgi_temp;
  uwsgi_temp_path /tmp/uwsgi_temp;
  scgi_temp_path /tmp/scgi_temp;

  log_format json_api '$remote_addr - $request_id "$request" $status $body_bytes_sent '
                      'rt=$request_time uct="$upstream_connect_time" urt="$upstream_response_time" '
                      'xff="$http_x_forwarded_for"';
  access_log /dev/stdout json_api;

  # Keep payloads and client wait times bounded for a small JSON API.
  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_header_timeout 10s;
  client_body_timeout 15s;
  send_timeout 30s;
  keepalive_timeout 65s;

  gzip on;
  gzip_comp_level 5;
  gzip_min_length 1024;
  gzip_vary on;
  gzip_types application/json application/problem+json text/plain;

  server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name _;

    add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
    add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
    add_header Referrer-Policy "no-referrer" always;

    # Re-resolve Docker Compose service DNS so API container replacements do not leave stale IPs.
    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;

    # Return JSON rather than nginx HTML on gateway failures; API 4xx/5xx bodies pass through untouched.
    error_page 502 @err_502;
    error_page 503 @err_503;
    error_page 504 @err_504;

    location = /nginx-health {
      access_log off;
      allow 127.0.0.1;
      deny all;
      default_type application/json;
      return 200 '{"status":"ok"}';
    }

    location / {
      set $api_upstream http://api:5000;
      proxy_pass $api_upstream;
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_redirect off;

      proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $http_host;
      proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";

      proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
      proxy_send_timeout 30s;
      proxy_read_timeout 60s;

      proxy_buffering on;
      proxy_buffers 8 16k;
      proxy_buffer_size 16k;
    }

    location @err_502 {
      default_type application/json;
      return 502 '{"error":"bad_gateway"}';
    }

    location @err_503 {
      default_type application/json;
      return 503 '{"error":"service_unavailable"}';
    }

    location @err_504 {
      default_type application/json;
      return 504 '{"error":"gateway_timeout"}';
    }
  }
}

gemini-hydrogen/03-infra-management/requirements.txt

Flask==3.1.2
gunicorn==23.0.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.10
redis==6.4.0

Evaluation 8.75 / 10 graded blind as submission S

Well-hardened stack with fail-closed secrets, read-only API, loopback publish, Redis auth and cache-only settings, gunicorn config file; healthcheck command tested against a stub server. Runbook is good and adds a section on migrating data from the old compose project, which shows judgment.

Strengths

  • Healthcheck path parameterised; tested for 200/404/500/refused
  • Restore drops/recreates DB then pg_restore --exit-on-error
  • Explicit section on moving from the previous compose file/project
  • nginx -t via compose run before restart

Weaknesses

  • Redis password visible in command args
  • Proxy not read-only
  • RUNBOOK ~975 words
Evidence the grader checked
  • docker compose config (dummy .env from .env.example, empty secrets filled) exit 0
  • rendered cache command includes requirepass value

Objective checks

Files

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Response — Task 03: hardening the deployment

The configuration is rewritten and passes every offline check available here. Nothing was built or started, so it has not run end to end. Two settings depend on application code that is not in this directory and need confirming before first start:

  • WSGI entry point: gunicorn loads app:app (override with WSGI_APP in .env).
  • Health endpoint: the API must answer GET /healthz with 200 (override with API_HEALTHCHECK_PATH in .env). If it does not, the API is marked unhealthy and the proxy will not start.

Highest-risk original problems

  1. Postgres published on 0.0.0.0:5432 with admin / password committed in compose.yaml. Anyone who could reach the host had the database.
  2. Redis published on 0.0.0.0:6379 with no authentication.
  3. API published on 0.0.0.0:5000, bypassing nginx, served by the Flask development server as root. The dev server is not meant for production load or exposure, and a compromise of the process was root in the container.
  4. Postgres data had no named volume. It sat in an anonymous volume that a docker compose down / up cycle leaves behind, so the database came back empty. With postgres:latest, a pull could also change the major version under existing data.
  5. Non-reproducible image. pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignored the pinned requirements.txt (so gunicorn was never installed), every image was latest, and COPY . . without a .dockerignore would bake a local .env into the image.
  6. No health checks, health-based ordering, restart policy, log rotation or resource limits. depends_on only ordered container creation, so the API could start before Postgres accepted connections; a crash stayed down; logs grew without bound.
  7. nginx passed no client information and used defaults unsuited to an API. The app saw Host: api:5000 and the proxy's IP, timeouts were 60s, errors were HTML, and the config was mounted writable.

What changed

File Change
compose.yaml Only nginx is published (loopback :8080 by default). Credentials are required from .env. Two networks: frontend (proxy, api) and backend (api, db, cache; internal). Health checks on all four services and depends_on: service_healthy. Named pgdata volume. Pinned image tags, restart: unless-stopped, rotated json-file logs, CPU / memory / PID limits, no-new-privileges. API runs read-only with all capabilities dropped. Redis requires a password and is bounded as an LRU cache.
Dockerfile python:3.13-slim-bookworm, dependencies from requirements.txt in a cached layer, fixed non-root UID 10001, root-owned code, gunicorn as the server.
gunicorn.conf.py (new) Bind, workers/threads, timeouts, worker recycling, logging; all overridable by env.
nginx.conf Forwarded headers (Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For/-Proto/-Host, X-Request-ID), 3s connect / 35s read timeouts, 1 MB body limit, JSON access log, JSON body on 502/503/504, own /nginx-health, re-resolves the API address so a recreated API container is picked up.
.env.example Passwords left empty on purpose (Compose refuses to start until set), plus bind address, port, image tag, health path.
.dockerignore, .gitignore (new) Keep .env and backups/ out of images and git.
RUNBOOK.md (new) Startup, health verification, backup/restore, secrets, deploy/rollback, migration from the old file.

Verification performed

All offline, without contacting the Docker daemon:

  • docker compose config -q (Compose v5.6.1):
    • no .env → exits 1, naming each missing variable;
    • .env.example unmodified → exits 1 on the two empty passwords;
    • both passwords filled in → exits 0.
  • Read the resolved output: the only published port is 127.0.0.1:8080→80; backend is internal: true; the pgdata volume, limits, logging, health checks and service_healthy conditions appear on the intended services.
  • Ran the API health-check command, taken from the resolved Compose output, against a local stub HTTP server: exit 0 on 200 (default path and an overridden one); exit 1 on 404, on 500, and on connection refused.
  • Executed gunicorn.conf.py with plain Python: defaults and the env overrides (WSGI_APP, WEB_CONCURRENCY, PORT) resolve as intended.
  • nginx.conf: structural check only (balanced blocks, terminated statements), plus a manual read of every directive.

Not verified

  • No image was built and no container started (per the task), so the Dockerfile, container health checks, Redis/Postgres flags and the runbook commands are untested against a live stack.
  • nginx -t was not run; there is no nginx binary here. docker compose run --rm --no-deps proxy nginx -t does it on first use.
  • gunicorn is not installed locally, so its own config check was not run.
  • Image tags were written from memory with no registry access: python:3.13-slim-bookworm, nginx:1.28-alpine, postgres:17-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine. Confirm they pull, and move to newer patch lines if available.

Assumptions and behaviour changes to confirm

  • Redis is a cache: no persistence, allkeys-lru at 256 MB. Wrong if the app keeps sessions or queues there.
  • The API does not write to its own filesystem outside /tmp (read_only).
  • nginx now listens on 127.0.0.1:8080, not 0.0.0.0:80; set HTTP_BIND / HTTP_PORT in .env for a public deployment.
  • The project name is fixed to api-stack and Postgres to major 17. Data in the old stack's anonymous volume is not carried over (RUNBOOK section 6).
  • FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=* makes gunicorn trust forwarded headers. That holds only while the API port stays unpublished.

Remaining gaps, deliberately left

  • No TLS. nginx serves plain HTTP; terminate TLS in front of it or add certificates before exposing it publicly. If a TLS terminator is added in front, X-Forwarded-Proto must be passed through instead of $scheme.
  • Dependencies are pinned at the top level only. Transitive packages (Werkzeug, Jinja2, …) still float, and base images are pinned by tag, not digest. A hash-locked file (pip-compile --generate-hashes, installed with --require-hashes) and image digests need network access to produce.
  • Secrets are environment variables, and the Redis password a process argument: readable by anyone with Docker access on the host.
  • Backups are manual; scheduling and off-host copies are the operator's.
  • Compose restarts crashed containers but does not restart ones that are merely unhealthy, and there is no rolling update: a deploy or rollback briefly interrupts the API.

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook — API stack (nginx → API → Postgres + Redis)

Single host, Docker Compose. Run every command from this directory. Only nginx is reachable from the host; the API, Postgres and Redis have no published ports.

1. Startup

First time on a host:

cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
# Fill in POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD, each from:
openssl rand -hex 24

Start (or apply any change to .env / compose.yaml):

docker compose config -q          # fails with a clear message if a value is missing
docker compose up -d --build --wait

--wait returns once every service reports healthy. Order is enforced by health: db and cache → api → proxy.

If it ends with dependency failed to start: container ... is unhealthy, read docker compose logs api. The two usual causes are settings that depend on the application:

Setting Default Where
WSGI entry point (module:callable) app:app WSGI_APP in .env
Health endpoint (must return 200) /healthz API_HEALTHCHECK_PATH in .env

Stop without losing data: docker compose down. Never add -v unless you intend to delete the database volume.

2. Health verification

docker compose ps                                   # all four services "healthy"
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/nginx-health        # proxy alone → ok
curl -fsS -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz          # proxy → API → 200
docker compose exec db sh -c 'pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"'
docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping            # PONG

Adjust host and port if HTTP_BIND / HTTP_PORT differ from the defaults.

Confirm nothing but the proxy is exposed (expect no output):

ss -ltn | grep -E ':(5000|5432|6379)\b'

Logs: docker compose logs -f --tail=100 <service>. nginx writes one JSON line per request; its request_id is sent to the API as X-Request-ID and returned to the client. Logs rotate at 5 × 10 MB per service, so ship them elsewhere if you need history.

3. Backup and restore

Postgres is the only durable state (volume api-stack_pgdata). Redis is configured as a cache and is not backed up.

Backup (safe while the stack is running):

mkdir -p backups && chmod 700 backups
f=backups/app-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --format=custom' > "$f"
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore --list < "$f" | head     # readable archive?

Nothing schedules this for you: run it from host cron and copy the files off the host. backups/ is ignored by git and excluded from the image.

Restore (replaces the whole database; take a fresh backup first if the current data has any value):

docker compose stop proxy api
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'dropdb -U "$POSTGRES_USER" --if-exists --force "$POSTGRES_DB" && createdb -U "$POSTGRES_USER" "$POSTGRES_DB"'
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --no-owner --exit-on-error' < backups/<file>.dump
docker compose up -d --wait

A backup is only proven by restoring it. Periodically restore the latest dump into a scratch database (createdb restore_test, pg_restore -d restore_test, check a few tables, dropdb restore_test).

4. Secret handling

  • Secrets live only in .env on the host (mode 600, ignored by git, excluded from the image by .dockerignore). compose.yaml holds none and refuses to start if one is missing.
  • Use hex or alphanumeric values: they are embedded in connection URLs.
  • They reach containers as environment variables, and the Redis password also as a process argument, so anyone with Docker access on the host can read them. Treat membership of the docker group as access to the secrets.
  • Keep docker compose config output out of tickets and chat; it prints the resolved values.

Rotate the Postgres password (POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env is only applied when the volume is first initialised, so change it in the database first):

docker compose exec db sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "\password"'
# put the same value in .env, then:
docker compose up -d --wait

Rotate the Redis password: change REDIS_PASSWORD in .env, then docker compose up -d --wait. The cache restarts empty.

5. Deploy and rollback

Deploy a new API version. Note the current API_TAG first — that is the rollback target.

grep '^API_TAG=' .env                 # write this down
# set API_TAG=<new release id, e.g. git short SHA> in .env
docker compose up -d --build --wait

Roll back the API:

# set API_TAG=<previous value> in .env
docker image ls api-stack/api         # the previous tag must still be present
docker compose up -d --no-build --wait

Do not prune images until a release has proven itself; with no registry, a pruned tag can only be recovered by rebuilding from the old commit.

Roll back configuration (compose.yaml, nginx.conf): restore the previous version of the file from git, then

docker compose config -q
docker compose run --rm --no-deps proxy nginx -t    # only if nginx.conf changed
docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose restart proxy                        # only if nginx.conf changed

Compose does not notice edits to the mounted nginx.conf; the restart is what loads it.

Database: rolling back the image does not undo schema or data changes. Take a backup (section 3) before any deploy that migrates the schema, and restore it if the old code cannot run against the new schema. Changing the Postgres major version (the postgres:17-alpine tag) is a dump-and-restore migration, not a tag edit, in either direction.

6. Moving from the previous compose file

The old file ran under a different project name, published 80/5000/5432/6379 and kept Postgres data in an anonymous volume as user admin. Before first start of this version: dump the old database if it holds anything worth keeping (pg_dump as in section 3, with -U admin), run docker compose down with the old file, then start this stack and restore.

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env, fill in the two passwords, and keep .env out of git:
#   cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
# Compose refuses to start while any required value below is empty.

POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_DB=app

# Generate each with:  openssl rand -hex 24
# Use hex/alphanumeric values only: these are placed inside connection URLs,
# and "$" is special to Compose.
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=
REDIS_PASSWORD=

# Where nginx listens on the host. The defaults are local-only; for a public
# deployment use HTTP_BIND=0.0.0.0 and HTTP_PORT=80, behind TLS.
HTTP_BIND=127.0.0.1
HTTP_PORT=8080

# Image tag of the API to run. Set to a release id (e.g. git short SHA) when
# deploying; the previous value is what you roll back to.
API_TAG=local

# Application-specific: the WSGI entry point ("module:callable") gunicorn
# loads, and a path the API answers with HTTP 200 when it can serve requests.
WSGI_APP=app:app
API_HEALTHCHECK_PATH=/healthz
