fable-5.2/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Single-host deployment: nginx -> API -> Postgres + Redis.
# All credentials come from .env (see .env.example); nothing secret lives here.

# Fixed project name, so the pgdata volume keeps its name if this directory moves.
name: api-stack

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "5"

x-hardening: &default-hardening
  restart: unless-stopped
  logging: *default-logging
  security_opt:
    - no-new-privileges:true

services:
  proxy:
    <<: *default-hardening
    image: nginx:1.28-alpine
    # The only published port in the stack. Loopback by default; set
    # HTTP_BIND=0.0.0.0 in .env to accept outside traffic.
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s
    cpus: 0.5
    mem_limit: 128m
    pids_limit: 128

  api:
    <<: *default-hardening
    build: .
    # Tagged per release so a rollback is "point API_TAG at the previous image".
    image: "${API_IMAGE:-api-stack/api}:${API_TAG:-local}"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "postgres://${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}@cache:6379"
      # Both depend on the application; see RUNBOOK.md section 1.
      WSGI_APP: "${WSGI_APP:-app:app}"
      HEALTHCHECK_PATH: "${API_HEALTHCHECK_PATH:-/healthz}"
      # Trust X-Forwarded-* from the proxy. Safe because the API port is not
      # published and nginx is the only other container on the frontend network.
      FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS: "*"
    expose:
      - "5000"
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      # A real HTTP request through gunicorn and the app; any status >= 400,
      # a timeout or a refused connection counts as unhealthy.
      test:
        - CMD
        - python
        - -c
        - "import os, urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000' + os.environ.get('HEALTHCHECK_PATH', '/healthz'), timeout=3)"
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    # Slightly longer than gunicorn's 30s graceful timeout.
    stop_grace_period: 35s
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cpus: 1.0
    mem_limit: 512m
    pids_limit: 256

  db:
    <<: *default-hardening
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: "${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}"
      POSTGRES_DB: "${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}"
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    expose:
      - "5432"
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      # Over TCP on purpose: during first-run initialisation Postgres listens
      # only on its unix socket, and must not be reported ready at that point.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 30s
    # Time for a clean shutdown checkpoint before Docker sends SIGKILL.
    stop_grace_period: 1m
    shm_size: 128m
    cpus: 1.0
    mem_limit: 1g
    pids_limit: 256

  cache:
    <<: *default-hardening
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    # Used as a cache: bounded memory, LRU eviction, nothing written to disk.
    # If the application keeps durable data in Redis, change this policy and
    # add a volume before relying on it.
    command:
      - redis-server
      - --requirepass
      - "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}"
      - --maxmemory
      - 256mb
      - --maxmemory-policy
      - allkeys-lru
      - --save
      - ""
      - --appendonly
      - "no"
    environment:
      # Read by redis-cli in the health check below.
      REDISCLI_AUTH: "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}"
    expose:
      - "6379"
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    cpus: 0.5
    mem_limit: 384m
    pids_limit: 128

networks:
  # proxy <-> api. Also gives the API outbound access if it calls external services.
  frontend:
  # api <-> db/cache. Internal: no route to or from the outside world.
  backend:
    internal: true

volumes:
  pgdata:

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# Pinned to a Python minor and Debian release. For byte-for-byte rebuilds, pin
# the digest too:  --build-arg PYTHON_IMAGE=python:3.13-slim-bookworm@sha256:...
ARG PYTHON_IMAGE=python:3.13-slim-bookworm
FROM ${PYTHON_IMAGE}

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
    PIP_ROOT_USER_ACTION=ignore

# Fixed UID/GID so file ownership is predictable across rebuilds and hosts.
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --home-dir /app \
      --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies first: this layer is rebuilt only when requirements.txt changes.
# Versions come from the pinned requirements.txt, never from "latest on PyPI".
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Application code stays root-owned, so the runtime user cannot modify it.
# .dockerignore keeps .env, backups and deployment files out of the image.
COPY . .

USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 5000

# Production WSGI server; bind, workers and timeouts live in gunicorn.conf.py.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--config", "/app/gunicorn.conf.py"]

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/gunicorn.conf.py

"""Gunicorn settings for the API container. Every value can be overridden by env."""

import os

# WSGI entry point as "module:callable". "app:app" is what `flask run` picked up
# by default in the old image; change WSGI_APP if the application lives elsewhere.
wsgi_app = os.environ.get("WSGI_APP", "app:app")

bind = "0.0.0.0:" + os.environ.get("PORT", "5000")

# Sized for the 1 CPU / 512 MiB limit in compose.yaml. Threads suit an
# I/O-bound JSON API; raise workers together with the CPU limit.
workers = int(os.environ.get("WEB_CONCURRENCY", "2"))
threads = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_THREADS", "4"))

# Kept just under nginx's proxy_read_timeout (35s) so a stuck request is
# ended by gunicorn, which logs it, rather than by the proxy.
timeout = int(os.environ.get("GUNICORN_TIMEOUT", "30"))
graceful_timeout = 30
keepalive = 5

# Recycle workers periodically so a slow leak cannot grow into the memory limit.
max_requests = 2000
max_requests_jitter = 200

# The root filesystem is read-only; worker heartbeat files go to tmpfs.
worker_tmp_dir = "/dev/shm"

# Errors to stderr for `docker compose logs`. Access logging is done once, by nginx.
errorlog = "-"
loglevel = os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "info")

fable-5.2/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

user nginx;
worker_processes 2;
error_log /dev/stderr warn;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  server_tokens off;

  # One JSON object per request; request_id ties a proxy line to an API log line.
  log_format json_combined escape=json
    '{"time":"$time_iso8601","remote_addr":"$remote_addr",'
    '"request_id":"$request_id","method":"$request_method",'
    '"uri":"$request_uri","status":$status,"bytes_sent":$body_bytes_sent,'
    '"request_time":$request_time,"upstream_time":"$upstream_response_time",'
    '"user_agent":"$http_user_agent"}';
  access_log /dev/stdout json_combined;

  # Docker's embedded DNS. Together with the variable in proxy_pass below, the
  # API address is re-resolved, so recreating the api container (deploy,
  # rollback) does not leave nginx pointing at a dead IP.
  resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;

  # Client side: JSON bodies are small, and slow clients should not hold workers.
  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_header_timeout 15s;
  client_body_timeout 15s;
  send_timeout 30s;
  keepalive_timeout 65s;

  server {
    listen 80 default_server;
    server_name _;

    add_header X-Request-ID $request_id always;
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;

    # Answers from nginx itself, so the proxy's health is independent of the API.
    location = /nginx-health {
      access_log off;
      default_type text/plain;
      return 200 "ok\n";
    }

    location / {
      set $api_upstream http://api:5000;
      proxy_pass $api_upstream;

      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";

      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;

      # Fail fast if the API is down; allow slightly longer than gunicorn's
      # 30s request timeout so the API, not the proxy, ends a slow request.
      proxy_connect_timeout 3s;
      proxy_send_timeout 30s;
      proxy_read_timeout 35s;
    }

    # When the API is unreachable or times out, clients still get JSON rather
    # than nginx's HTML error page. The original 502/503/504 status is kept.
    error_page 502 503 504 @upstream_error;
    location @upstream_error {
      default_type application/json;
      return 503 '{"error":"upstream_unavailable"}\n';
    }
  }
}

Runbook covers tag-based rollback and correctly notes nginx must be reloaded because the upstream is resolved at startup.

Strengths

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Hardening Review and Verification Summary

Highest-Risk Original Problems

  1. Hardcoded credentials and unauthenticated Redis (compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: POSTGRES_USER: admin, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password, and DATABASE_URL: postgres://admin:password@db:5432/app were committed in plaintext, and Redis ran with no password (requirepass).
    • Fix: Removed all embedded credentials; required POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, and REDIS_PASSWORD via fail-fast ${VAR:?...} interpolation; enforced scram-sha-256 host authentication on Postgres; enabled --requirepass on Redis with REDISCLI_AUTH for CLI health checks; updated .env.example for straightforward local setup.

  2. Public exposure of database, cache, and raw API ports (compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: Postgres (5432), Redis (6379), and the raw Flask API (5000) were published on all host interfaces (0.0.0.0), exposing data stores directly and letting clients bypass nginx. All four services also shared a single implicit default network, allowing proxy to reach db and cache.
    • Fix: Removed all host port bindings from db, cache, and api; bound proxy to ${HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}:8080; segmented traffic into explicit frontend (proxy <-> api) and backend (internal: true, api <-> db, cache) networks.

  3. Root execution, development server, and debug mode in production (Dockerfile)

    • Original risk: The API container ran as root, set ENV FLASK_ENV=development, and launched Werkzeug's single-threaded development server (flask run --host=0.0.0.0).
    • Fix: Switched to a multi-stage python:3.13-slim-bookworm build with a dedicated non-root user (app, UID/GID 10001), read-only application file permissions (root:app, u=rwX,g=rX,o=), and exec-form gunicorn (gunicorn==23.0.0) logging to stdout/stderr. Added read_only: true, tmpfs, cap_drop: [ALL] (with minimal required caps added back only on db for initdb/privilege drop), and no-new-privileges:true across services; ran proxy as non-root nginx on port 8080 and cache as non-root redis.

  4. Non-reproducible dependency builds, unpinned :latest images, and .env image-leak risk (Dockerfile, compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: Dockerfile ran COPY . . before pip install flask psycopg2 redis (ignoring the pinned requirements.txt, breaking layer caching, and building unpinned dependencies). There was no .dockerignore, risking copying a local .env into the image. compose.yaml used floating :latest tags for nginx, postgres, and redis.
    • Fix: Installed dependencies strictly from requirements.txt inside a dedicated builder virtualenv layer before copying app source; added .dockerignore excluding .env*, infra files, docs, and dumps; pinned images to python:3.13-slim-bookworm, nginx:1.27-alpine, postgres:17-alpine, and redis:7.4-alpine.

  5. No Postgres persistence (compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: db stored data only in the container's writable layer; recreating the container caused total data loss.
    • Fix: Added named volume postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data, shm_size: 128m, and stop_grace_period: 30s for clean checkpoints on shutdown. Explicitly configured Redis as a bounded volatile LRU cache (--maxmemory 128mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru --save "" --appendonly no).

  6. Missing health checks, readiness ordering, resource limits, and log rotation (compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: Plain depends_on started api before Postgres/Redis were ready and left proxy unordered; containers had no restart policy, unbounded log growth (disk-exhaustion risk), and no CPU/memory/PID caps.
    • Fix: Added health checks on all four services (pg_isready with configured user/DB, redis-cli ping, Python stdlib probe to http://127.0.0.1:5000/health, and local-only /nginx-health probe), depends_on with condition: service_healthy, restart: unless-stopped, json-file log rotation (10m x 3, compressed), and modest CPU/memory/PID limits appropriate for single-host Compose.

  7. Minimal, unhardened reverse proxy configuration (nginx.conf, compose.yaml)

    • Original risk: nginx.conf was bind-mounted read-write, disclosed the nginx version (server_tokens on by default), omitted forwarding/security headers and HTTP/1.1 keepalive, had no request body limits or API-appropriate timeouts, and returned HTML error pages for gateway errors.
    • Fix: Mounted nginx.conf read-only (:ro), disabled server_tokens, added HTTP/1.1 upstream keepalive (api_backend), forwarded Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host, and X-Request-ID, aligned connect/send/read timeouts (5s/30s/30s) with Gunicorn (--timeout 30), set client_max_body_size 1m, enabled JSON gzip and structured JSON access logs, added API security headers, restricted /nginx-health to 127.0.0.1, and returned JSON bodies for 413/502/503/504 errors.

Files Delivered

  • Dockerfile — hardened multi-stage Python 3.13 slim image with non-root app user, pinned requirements.txt install, Gunicorn, and health check.
  • .dockerignore — excludes .env*, infra manifests, docs, caches, and backups from the build context.
  • compose.yaml — hardened Compose configuration with fail-fast env vars, explicit frontend/backend networks, Postgres persistence, health checks and health-gated dependencies, restart/logging/resource settings, and container privilege drops.
  • nginx.conf — non-root JSON API reverse proxy config with proxy/security headers, timeouts, keepalive, structured logging, JSON error responses, and local-only /nginx-health.
  • .env.example — complete local configuration template matching compose.yaml.
  • RUNBOOK.md — concise operational guide covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback.

Verification Performed

All verification was performed offline without starting containers, per task constraints:

  1. Compose schema and variable interpolation (docker compose config with .env.example):
    • Ran docker compose -f compose.yaml --env-file .env.example config (Docker Compose v5.6.1).
    • Result: Exit code 0; verified rendered service definitions, network topology (frontend bridge, backend internal bridge), postgres_data volume, :ro bind mount on nginx.conf, health checks, service_healthy dependencies, resource limits, logging options, and absence of published ports on api, db, and cache.
  2. Fail-fast missing-secret check (docker compose config without env file):
    • Ran docker compose -f compose.yaml config with no .env present.
    • Result: Exited non-zero (EXIT=1) with explicit interpolation errors for every missing required variable (POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, REDIS_PASSWORD).
  3. Static syntax and hygiene checks (Python script):
    • Parsed the Python HEALTHCHECK one-liner with ast.parse and verified it matches both Dockerfile and compose.yaml.
    • Checked nginx.conf brace nesting and quote balance across all lines.
    • Verified no :latest image tags or original hardcoded credentials (admin:password, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password) remain in Dockerfile or compose.yaml.

Limitations Not Verified Offline

  • Because container execution and network access were disallowed, image builds (docker compose build), runtime nginx -t inside nginx:1.27-alpine, live container startup/health transitions, and pg_dump/pg_restore against a running Postgres container were not executed.

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Operations Runbook

This runbook covers single-host Docker Compose operation for the hardened proxy (nginx) -> api (Flask/Gunicorn) -> db (PostgreSQL) + cache (Redis) stack.

Operational scope: Docker Compose is a single-host runner, not a multi-node orchestrator. Container recreates incur brief downtime, and there is no automatic cross-host failover. For production internet traffic, place this stack behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer (enabling HTTPS, HSTS, and set_real_ip_from / trusted X-Forwarded-Proto forwarding).

Architecture Summary

  • Exposed port: Only proxy publishes a host port (${HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080} -> container 8080). api, db, and cache publish no host ports.
  • Networks:
    • frontend: connects proxy and api only (proxy cannot reach db or cache).
    • backend (internal: true): connects api, db, and cache with no external routing.
  • State: PostgreSQL persists data in the named volume postgres_data. Redis runs as a bounded, volatile LRU cache (128mb, persistence disabled).
  • Application expectations: The API image serves WSGI entrypoint app:app via Gunicorn on port 5000 and exposes GET /health returning HTTP 200 when ready.

1. Startup

  1. Create .env from .env.example and restrict its permissions:
    cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
  2. Generate strong, URL-safe secrets (alphanumeric plus -_.~, because POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD are interpolated into connection URIs) and set them in .env:
    openssl rand -base64 24 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '='
  3. Validate Compose configuration and variable interpolation before starting:
    docker compose config --quiet
    Compose refuses to start if POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, or REDIS_PASSWORD is unset or empty.
  4. Build and start the stack:
    docker compose up -d --build
    Startup order is enforced by health checks: db and cache must become healthy before api starts, and api must become healthy before proxy starts.

2. Health Verification

  1. Confirm all four services are running and report (healthy):
    docker compose ps
  2. If a service is unhealthy or still starting, inspect its health check output and recent logs:
    docker compose logs --tail=50 proxy api db cache
docker inspect --format='{{json .State.Health}}' "$(docker compose ps -q api)"
  3. Verify end-to-end routing and response headers through proxy:
    curl -fsSi "http://${HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}/health"
    Confirm HTTP 200, X-Request-ID, security headers (X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY), and no nginx version in the Server header.
  4. Confirm internal-only services have no published host ports:
    docker compose ps --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
    Only proxy should list a host port mapping.

3. Backup and Restore (PostgreSQL)

PostgreSQL (postgres_data) is the persistent store. Redis is a volatile cache and does not require backup.

Backup

Stream a compressed custom-format dump to a private host directory (store encrypted copies off-host and never commit dumps to git):

mkdir -p backups && chmod 700 backups
set -a && source .env && set +a
BACKUP_FILE="backups/pg_${POSTGRES_DB}_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump"

(umask 077 && docker compose exec -T db pg_dump \
  -U "$POSTGRES_USER" \
  -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -Fc \
  --no-owner \
  --no-privileges > "$BACKUP_FILE")

Verify the backup archive is readable and non-empty:

docker compose exec -T db pg_restore --list < "$BACKUP_FILE" | head -n 20

Restore

  1. Stop api to halt application writes (keep db running):
    docker compose stop api
  2. Take a safety backup of the current database state (using the Backup command above) before overwriting.
  3. Restore the target dump into db:
    set -a && source .env && set +a
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore \
  -U "$POSTGRES_USER" \
  -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  --clean \
  --if-exists \
  --no-owner \
  --no-privileges \
  --single-transaction < "$BACKUP_FILE"
  4. Flush Redis so stale cached entries cannot contradict restored database rows:
    docker compose exec cache redis-cli FLUSHALL
  5. Restart api and verify stack health:
    docker compose start api
docker compose ps

Test restores periodically into a separate scratch database to verify backup usability.

4. Secret Handling

  • Local files: Keep .env untracked in git and mode 600. .dockerignore excludes .env* so secrets are never baked into the API image.
  • Production secrets: On a production host, avoid long-lived plaintext .env files where possible—inject credentials from a secret manager into the deployment environment or switch to file-based Docker secrets (POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE and mounted read-only secret files).
  • Avoid leaking secrets in logs/history: Never pass passwords on CLI flags (e.g., redis-cli -a ...); cache uses REDISCLI_AUTH from container environment instead.
  • Rotating the PostgreSQL password: POSTGRES_PASSWORD is only read by Postgres during initial volume creation (initdb). To rotate an existing database:
    1. Update the role password inside Postgres first:
      set -a && source .env && set +a
docker compose exec -T db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -v new_pw="'<NEW_URL_SAFE_PASSWORD>'" \
  -c "ALTER ROLE \"$POSTGRES_USER\" WITH PASSWORD :new_pw;"
    2. Update POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env.
    3. Recreate api and db so container environments match:
      docker compose up -d db api
  • Rotating the Redis password: Update REDIS_PASSWORD in .env, then recreate cache and api:
    docker compose up -d cache api

5. Deployment and Rollback

Tagging Releases

Build and tag each release with an immutable version or git SHA so prior images remain available for rollback:

API_TAG="$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" docker compose build api

Update API_TAG in .env (or pass it in the environment), take a pre-deploy Postgres backup before any schema migration, and deploy:

docker compose up -d --no-build api
docker compose exec proxy nginx -s reload
docker compose ps

(Reloading proxy refreshes nginx's upstream DNS cache if api received a new bridge IP on recreate.)

Rolling Back the API Image

  1. Set API_TAG in .env to the last known-good tag (check available local images with docker images "${API_IMAGE:-app-api}").
  2. Recreate api without rebuilding and reload proxy:
    docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate api
docker compose exec proxy nginx -s reload
  3. Verify health (docker compose ps and curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health).

Rolling Back Configuration (compose.yaml / nginx.conf)

  1. Restore the previous known-good revision from git:
    git checkout <good-commit> -- compose.yaml nginx.conf
  2. Validate and re-apply:
    docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up -d

Database Migration Rollback

Prefer backward-compatible (expand/contract) schema changes so rolling back the API does not require downgrading the database. If an irreversible migration must be undone, follow the Restore procedure above using the pre-deploy backup.

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env and replace all placeholder secrets before starting:
#   cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
# Never commit .env to version control.
# Use URL-safe characters (alphanumeric and -_.~) for passwords interpolated into URIs.

# Reverse proxy host binding (bind to 127.0.0.1 locally; place behind TLS in production)
HTTP_BIND=127.0.0.1
HTTP_PORT=8080

# API image tag (pin to release tag or commit SHA for controlled deploys/rollbacks) and concurrency
API_IMAGE=app-api
API_TAG=local
WEB_CONCURRENCY=2

# PostgreSQL credentials (required; Compose fails fast if unset or empty)
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=replace-with-strong-postgres-password
POSTGRES_DB=app

# Redis password (required; Compose fails fast if unset or empty)
REDIS_PASSWORD=replace-with-strong-redis-password

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"
    compress: "true"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    user: "nginx"
    entrypoint: ["nginx", "-e", "/dev/stderr", "-g", "daemon off;"]
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=16m
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    networks:
      - frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q -T 3 --spider http://127.0.0.1:8080/nginx-health || exit 1"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s
    stop_grace_period: 15s
    cpus: 0.5
    mem_limit: 128m
    pids_limit: 64
    logging: *default-logging

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    image: "${API_IMAGE:-app-api}:${API_TAG:-local}"
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?POSTGRES_USER is required}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?POSTGRES_DB is required}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?REDIS_PASSWORD is required}@cache:6379/0"
      WEB_CONCURRENCY: "${WEB_CONCURRENCY:-2}"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import sys, urllib.request; r = urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3); sys.exit(0 if r.status == 200 else 1)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    cpus: 1.0
    mem_limit: 512m
    pids_limit: 128
    logging: *default-logging

  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: "${POSTGRES_USER:?POSTGRES_USER is required}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required}"
      POSTGRES_DB: "${POSTGRES_DB:?POSTGRES_DB is required}"
      POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS: "--auth-host=scram-sha-256"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m
      - /var/run/postgresql:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=16m
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cap_add:
      - CHOWN
      - DAC_OVERRIDE
      - FOWNER
      - SETGID
      - SETUID
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    shm_size: 128m
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 15s
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    cpus: 1.0
    mem_limit: 512m
    pids_limit: 128
    logging: *default-logging

  cache:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    user: "redis"
    entrypoint: ["sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - 'exec redis-server --save "" --appendonly no --maxmemory 128mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru --requirepass "$$REDIS_PASSWORD"'
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?REDIS_PASSWORD is required}"
      REDISCLI_AUTH: "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?REDIS_PASSWORD is required}"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=16m
      - /data:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=16m
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli ping | grep -qx PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s
    stop_grace_period: 15s
    cpus: 0.5
    mem_limit: 256m
    pids_limit: 64
    logging: *default-logging

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

volumes:
  postgres_data:

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm AS builder

ENV PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /build

RUN python -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm AS runtime

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    WEB_CONCURRENCY=2

RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
    && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --home-dir /nonexistent --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

WORKDIR /app

COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY . .

RUN chown -R root:app /app \
    && chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /app

USER app

EXPOSE 5000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
    CMD ["python", "-c", "import sys, urllib.request; r = urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3); sys.exit(0 if r.status == 200 else 1)"]

CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "--threads", "2", "--timeout", "30", "--graceful-timeout", "30", "--worker-tmp-dir", "/tmp", "--access-logfile", "-", "--error-logfile", "-", "app:app"]

gemini-neon/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

worker_processes auto;
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
    include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type application/json;

    # Keep temporary buffers under /tmp so the container root filesystem can stay read-only
    client_body_temp_path /tmp/client_temp;
    proxy_temp_path /tmp/proxy_temp;
    fastcgi_temp_path /tmp/fastcgi_temp;
    uwsgi_temp_path /tmp/uwsgi_temp;
    scgi_temp_path /tmp/scgi_temp;

    server_tokens off;
    sendfile on;
    tcp_nopush on;
    tcp_nodelay on;
    reset_timedout_connection on;

    # Client timeouts and payload limit suitable for a JSON API
    keepalive_timeout 65s;
    client_header_timeout 10s;
    client_body_timeout 15s;
    send_timeout 15s;
    client_max_body_size 1m;

    # Structured JSON access logs to stdout; warnings/errors to stderr
    log_format json_api escape=json
        '{"time":"$time_iso8601",'
        '"request_id":"$request_id",'
        '"remote_addr":"$remote_addr",'
        '"method":"$request_method",'
        '"uri":"$request_uri",'
        '"status":$status,'
        '"body_bytes_sent":$body_bytes_sent,'
        '"request_time":$request_time,'
        '"upstream_response_time":"$upstream_response_time",'
        '"upstream_addr":"$upstream_addr"}';

    access_log /dev/stdout json_api;
    error_log /dev/stderr warn;

    # Compress JSON responses
    gzip on;
    gzip_comp_level 5;
    gzip_min_length 256;
    gzip_vary on;
    gzip_proxied any;
    gzip_types application/json application/problem+json text/plain;

    upstream api_backend {
        server api:5000;
        keepalive 16;
    }

    server {
        listen 8080;
        server_name _;

        # Security headers appropriate for a JSON API
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
        add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
        add_header Referrer-Policy "no-referrer" always;
        add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'" always;
        add_header X-Request-ID $request_id always;

        # Local-only liveness endpoint for the proxy container healthcheck
        location = /nginx-health {
            allow 127.0.0.1;
            deny all;
            access_log off;
            default_type application/json;
            return 200 '{"status":"ok"}';
        }

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://api_backend;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;

            # Preserve upstream keepalive and pass client/request metadata
            proxy_set_header Connection "";
            proxy_set_header Host $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;

            # Timeouts aligned with Gunicorn (--timeout 30)
            proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
            proxy_send_timeout 30s;
            proxy_read_timeout 30s;

            # Buffer responses so slow clients do not tie up Gunicorn workers
            proxy_buffering on;
            proxy_buffer_size 8k;
            proxy_buffers 8 16k;
            proxy_busy_buffers_size 32k;

            # Avoid retrying non-idempotent API requests on upstream errors
            proxy_next_upstream off;
            proxy_redirect off;
            proxy_hide_header X-Powered-By;
        }

        # Return JSON error bodies instead of default HTML pages
        error_page 413 = @error_413;
        error_page 502 = @error_502;
        error_page 503 = @error_503;
        error_page 504 = @error_504;

        location @error_413 {
            default_type application/json;
            return 413 '{"error":"payload_too_large"}';
        }

        location @error_502 {
            default_type application/json;
            return 502 '{"error":"bad_gateway"}';
        }

        location @error_503 {
            default_type application/json;
            return 503 '{"error":"service_unavailable"}';
        }

        location @error_504 {
            default_type application/json;
            return 504 '{"error":"gateway_timeout"}';
        }
    }
}

Evaluation 8.75 / 10 graded blind as submission I

Strong config with gunicorn.conf.py, multi-stage venv, read-only API and unprivileged read-only proxy on 8080, Redis auth, explicit networks. Verification table is specific and matches what I rendered. Runbook is excellent (tagged releases with retag-based rollback, TCP-verified rotation, honest list of what Compose does not do). Redis ends up running as root because the command starts with sh -c.

Strengths

  • Proxy user 101, read_only, tmpfs for cache/run/tmp, listens 8080
  • Rotation verifies new password over TCP from the api container
  • Clear 'Compose does not restart unhealthy containers' limits section
  • JSON 503 with Retry-After from nginx when upstream down

Weaknesses

  • cache command ['sh','-c','exec redis-server ...'] bypasses the image entrypoint's privilege drop, so redis runs as root
  • Default HTTP_BIND=0.0.0.0 publishes 80 on all interfaces
  • RUNBOOK ~1470 words
Evidence the grader checked
  • docker compose config (dummy .env from .env.example, empty secrets filled) exit 0
  • rendered cache cmd=['sh','-c','exec redis-server --requirepass "$$REDIS_PASSWORD" ...']

Objective checks

Files

deepseek-v4.1-flash/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

RESPONSE — review of the original deployment

Scope: Dockerfile, compose.yaml, nginx.conf, .env.example. No application code, no extra services, no Kubernetes. Containers were not started.

Highest-risk original problems

  1. Postgres and Redis were published on the host, with the DB password in the compose file. ports: 5432:5432 / 6379:6379 plus postgres://admin:password@db exposed the database to anything that could reach the host, using a credential that was both weak and world-readable in the repo. Redis had no requirepass at all: an unauthenticated cache on a public interface is a data-exposure and denial-of-service risk, and a well-known route to remote code execution once persistence or module loading is reachable, not just a cache leak. Fixed: no published port for api, db or cache; db/cache live on an internal: true network with no route off the host; Redis requires a password; every credential is a required ${VAR:?} interpolation from .env. Verified from the rendered compose model (see below).

  2. The API ran as root, with the Flask development server, and installed floating dependencies. FROM python:3.13 + pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignored requirements.txt, so two builds of the same commit could ship different library versions; flask run is a development server with no worker recycling, no graceful drain, no request limits and no timeout handling, and the default user is root. FLASK_ENV=development advertised development behaviour. Fixed: multi-stage build with a pinned requirements.txt installed into a venv; runtime python:3.13-slim-bookworm; uid/gid 10001; gunicorn with gthread, timeouts, max_requests recycling and /dev/shm heartbeats; read_only rootfs, cap_drop: ALL, no-new-privileges, init: true.

  3. No healthchecks and no health-based startup ordering. depends_on: [db, cache] only waits for container start: the API came up before Postgres finished initdb, crashed on the first connection, and only survived if something restarted it — which nothing did. Fixed: pg_isready against the TCP listener the API uses, authenticated redis-cli ping, an API liveness check against /healthz, and a proxied /healthz on nginx; depends_on now waits for service_healthy on cache→api→proxy.

  4. Postgres had no volume. Every docker compose down, up after an image change, or container removal destroyed the database. There was also no backup procedure. Fixed: named volume pgdata with PGDATA in a subdirectory, and a backup/restore section in RUNBOOK.md (logical pg_dump -Fc, restore procedure, volume snapshot, restore drill).

  5. Silent data-format upgrades from floating image tags. postgres:latest can jump a major version under an existing data directory and refuse to start (or worse); nginx:latest/redis:latest made deployments unreproducible. Fixed: pinned minor tags (nginx:1.27-alpine, postgres:17-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine, python:3.13-slim-bookworm); the runbook calls out that a Postgres major upgrade needs pg_dump/ pg_upgrade, not a tag bump.

  6. nginx was a bare pass-through. No X-Forwarded-*/X-Real-IP (the app saw nginx's IP and http), no upstream keepalive, no timeouts (default 60 s proxy_read_timeout holds connections on a hung API), no body limit, no server_tokens off, and no JSON error response. It also exposed the API directly on 5000, bypassing the proxy entirely, and mounted nginx.conf read-write. Fixed: rewritten nginx.conf — server_tokens off, edge-authoritative X-Forwarded-For (overwritten, not appended, so clients cannot spoof it), X-Forwarded-Proto/Host, X-Real-IP, X-Request-ID, upstream keepalive 32, 5 s connect / 30 s read/write timeouts, 2 MB body cap, gzip for JSON, security headers, JSON 503 with Retry-After, dotfile deny, and a /healthz passthrough. The API port is no longer published at all.

  7. No restart policy, no log bound, no resource bound. json-file logs grow without limit until the disk fills (which stops Postgres); a single runaway worker can starve the host; a crash stays down. Fixed: restart: unless-stopped, json-file capped at 10 MB × 3, CPU/memory limits per service, shm_size for Postgres, and stop_grace_period long enough for a clean Postgres checkpoint and gunicorn drain.

  8. COPY . . put secrets and VCS data in the image. With a .env on disk, the whole build context — including credentials — landed in a layer, and every source edit invalidated the dependency layer. Fixed: .dockerignore excludes .env* (except the example), .git, backups and docs; dependencies are installed before the source copy; the runtime user cannot write to the app directory.

Verification performed

Check Command Result
Compose model is valid docker compose config --quiet (dummy env) exit 0
Missing secret fails fast same command with env unset exits non-zero, names POSTGRES_USER/REDIS_PASSWORD
Only the proxy publishes a port parse of docker compose config --format json api, db, cache → ports: []; proxy → 80:8080
Healthchecks + ordering wired same parse all four have healthchecks; api depends on db+cache healthy; proxy on api healthy
Backend isolated same parse networks.backend.internal == true
Persistence same parse named volume app_pgdata mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data
No literal credentials left grep -rniE 'admin:|password@|change-me|:latest|flask run|FLASK_ENV' over the deliverables no matches (only a doc sentence warning against :latest)
gunicorn.conf.py syntax python3 -m py_compile OK
nginx.conf structure brace/directive balance + cross-check of upstream name, listen port, /healthz balanced; upstream api matches the compose service; listen 8080 matches 80:8080; /healthz matches the healthcheck path
Ports agree across files manual cross-check gunicorn binds 0.0.0.0:8000, nginx proxy_pass http://api + upstream api { server api:8000 }, API expose: 8000, proxy listen 8080 mapped 80:8080

Not verified, and why:

  • nginx -t — no nginx binary in this environment and no network to fetch one; the config was checked structurally instead. Run docker compose exec proxy nginx -t before the first real start.
  • docker build / docker compose up — the Docker daemon is not running here, and the task forbids starting containers.
  • TLS — out of scope; nginx here speaks HTTP only and expects a terminator in front (documented in the config header and runbook).
  • Application behaviour — the app itself is not in this task's files.

Assumptions and residual risks

  • The app exposes GET /healthz (liveness) and GET /readyz (Postgres + Redis readiness) and imports as app:app (override with APP_MODULE). Without these endpoints the healthchecks fail: they are the one contract this configuration adds.
  • psycopg2-binary is kept from the supplied requirements.txt. It is fine for this size of deployment; building against libpq (source psycopg2 plus libpq5 in the runtime stage) is the stricter option.
  • .env secrets are visible to root and to anyone who can run docker inspect on the host. Docker Compose secrets: or an external secret manager is the next step; this is documented rather than pretended away.
  • deploy.resources.limits are honoured by Compose, reservations are not; restart does not act on an unhealthy-but-running container. Both are stated plainly in RUNBOOK.md — Compose is not an orchestrator.
  • Adding hash-pinned dependencies (pip-compile --generate-hashes) would make installs resistant to a compromised index; exact versions are pinned now, hashes were not generated because it requires network access.

deepseek-v4.1-flash/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

RUNBOOK — app deployment (nginx + API + Postgres + Redis)

Four containers on one host:

service reachable from published host port
proxy (nginx 1.27) the internet / your LB ${HTTP_PORT} (default 80)
api (gunicorn, uid 10001) proxy only none
db (Postgres 17) api only none
cache (Redis 7) api only none

backend is an internal: true network, so Postgres and Redis have no route off the host. frontend carries proxy↔api traffic and gives the API egress if it calls external services. Only proxy publishes a port.

Application contract assumed by this configuration (the app code is not part of this task):

  • GET /healthz — cheap liveness check, no dependency calls, 200 when the process can serve. Used by the container healthcheck.
  • GET /readyz — readiness check that pings Postgres and Redis and returns 503 when either is unavailable. Used by operators and by a load balancer, not by the container healthcheck (a dependency outage should not mark the API container itself unhealthy).

1. First start

cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
# fill in POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD; use different values:
#   openssl rand -hex 24
$EDITOR .env

docker compose config          # renders the resolved config; fails loudly if a
                               # required variable is missing
docker compose build
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps              # wait for "healthy" on db, cache, api, proxy

Postgres initialises from POSTGRES_* only on first start with an empty pgdata volume. Changing those values later does not change the database password — see §4.

docker compose down stops everything but keeps the pgdata volume. docker compose down -v deletes the database volume; take a backup first.

2. Health verification

# Edge, end to end (also proves nginx can reach the API):
curl -fsS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/healthz

# Readiness incl. Postgres and Redis:
curl -fsS http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/readyz

# Container-level state and health-check history:
docker compose ps
docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.State.Health.Status}}' \
  $(docker compose ps -q)
docker compose exec proxy nginx -t    # config syntax inside the running proxy

# Direct service probes (no published ports needed):
docker compose exec db    sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"'
docker compose exec cache sh -c 'REDISCLI_AUTH="$REDIS_PASSWORD" redis-cli --no-auth-warning ping'
docker compose exec api   python -c 'import urllib.request;print(urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8000/readyz").status)'

# Recent errors only:
docker compose logs --since 10m --no-log-prefix api proxy | grep -iE 'error|critical|traceback' || true

Expected: healthy for all four; /healthz and /readyz return 200; Redis returns PONG.

If api is healthy but proxy is not, nginx cannot resolve/reach api — check name resolution and connectivity from inside the proxy:

docker compose exec proxy wget -q -O - http://api:8000/healthz

3. Backups and restore

Logical backup (safe while running; -Fc is compressed and restore-selective):

mkdir -p backups
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' \
  > "backups/app-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump"

Verify a dump before trusting it:

docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_restore --list' < backups/app-<ts>.dump | head

Restore (stop writers first; --clean drops and recreates objects):

docker compose stop api
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists --no-owner --single-transaction' \
  < backups/app-<ts>.dump
docker compose start api

Full-volume backup (host-level snapshot, for disaster recovery only; requires a brief stop so the files are consistent):

docker compose stop db
docker run --rm -v app_pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data:ro -v "$PWD/backups:/backup" \
  alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).tar.gz -C /var/lib/postgresql/data .
docker compose start db

Restore the volume only into an empty pgdata (docker compose down -v first) and never while db is running. Keep backups off the host; a pgdata volume only survives failures of the container, not of the disk.

Schedule pg_dump from cron/systemd with the same command; retention is your policy (e.g. daily × 14, weekly × 8). Redis is a cache with persistence disabled — losing it is expected and requires no backup.

4. Secrets

  • All credentials live in .env (mode 0600, owner root or the deploy user, listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore). Nothing is baked into the image or in compose.yaml.
  • .env values are visible to anyone who can run docker inspect on the host, and to root. That is the trade-off for a single-host deployment. For stronger isolation use Docker Compose/Swarm secrets: (files mounted at /run/secrets/*, POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE) or an external secret manager, and read them the same way from the API.
  • Never pass secrets on the command line (they land in shell history and ps); never put them in nginx.conf or image ENV/ARG.
  • Rotate on a schedule and after any suspected exposure.

Rotating the database password (the container's POSTGRES_PASSWORD is ignored once the volume is initialised). The generated hex value has no SQL metacharacters, so it can be interpolated safely:

set -a; . ./.env; set +a          # load POSTGRES_USER/POSTGRES_DB for the CLI
NEW=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
docker compose exec -T db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "ALTER ROLE \"$POSTGRES_USER\" WITH PASSWORD '$NEW';"

sed -i "s/^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*/POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$NEW/" .env
docker compose up -d --no-deps --force-recreate api

# Verify over TCP with the real DSN (a local `psql` inside db uses socket auth
# and would not prove the password works):
docker compose exec -T api python -c \
  'import os, psycopg2; psycopg2.connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]).close(); print("db auth ok")'

Rotating the Redis password: update REDIS_PASSWORD in .env, then docker compose up -d --no-deps --force-recreate cache api (Redis applies requirepass only at start; the cache is flushed).

If .env is ever committed or leaks, treat every value in it as compromised and rotate all of them.

5. Deploy and rollback

Never deploy a mutable :latest. Tag every build with the commit it came from and keep the previous tags on the host (or push them to a registry):

TAG=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
docker compose build                            # builds app-api:local
docker image tag app-api:local "app-api:$TAG"   # archive this build

# deploy (and rollback): choose which archived build runs
docker image tag "app-api:$TAG" app-api:local
docker compose up -d --no-deps --force-recreate api
curl -fsS http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/readyz

compose.yaml names the image app-api:local; the retag step is what selects which build runs. For a registry flow, push app-api:$TAG and change the image: field (or set it via an override file) to that reference, then docker compose pull api && docker compose up -d --no-deps api.

Rollback is a redeploy of the previous tag — the exact same commands with $TAG replaced by the previous one:

docker image tag "app-api:$PREVIOUS_TAG" app-api:local
docker compose up -d --no-deps --force-recreate api
curl -fsS http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/readyz
docker compose ps

This is a recreate, not a rolling update: expect a few seconds of 503 from nginx while the API restarts (nginx returns {"error":"service_unavailable"} with Retry-After: 5). Database migrations are the hard part — make them forward-compatible (expand/contract) so the previous API version can still run against the newer schema; otherwise roll back the data as well:

docker compose stop api
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists --no-owner --single-transaction' \
  < backups/app-<ts>.dump
docker compose start api

If the host itself is lost: install Docker, restore this directory, restore .env from your secret store, recreate the pgdata volume from the last dump, docker compose up -d.

6. What Compose does and does not do here

It does: restart crashed containers (unless-stopped, with Docker's exponential backoff), order startup on health (depends_on + condition: service_healthy), cap CPU/memory, rotate logs at 10 MB × 3, and keep data services off the public network.

It does not:

  • restart or replace a container that is running but unhealthy — health status is reported, nothing acts on it. Alert on it; do not expect self-healing.
  • reschedule onto another host, drain a node, or roll back a failed deploy.
  • give zero-downtime updates, or restart dependents when a dependency dies.
  • enforce deploy.resources.reservations (limits are applied by Compose, reservations are only meaningful in Swarm).
  • isolate the host from a compromised container beyond the controls above — read_only, cap_drop: ALL, no-new-privileges and the internal network reduce blast radius, they are not a sandbox.

If you outgrow those limits, the next step is an orchestrator, not more Compose features.

7. Routine checks

  • docker compose ps — all four healthy.
  • Disk: docker system df, du -sh backups — a full disk stops Postgres.
  • Logs: JSON driver, rotated; ship them if you need history beyond 3 files.
  • Base images are pinned to minor tags on purpose. Bump them deliberately (Renovate/Dependabot PR, changelog review), not by switching back to latest; a Postgres major bump on an existing pgdata volume needs pg_dump/pg_upgrade.

deepseek-v4.1-flash/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env and fill in real values:  cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
#
# .env is read by Docker Compose for ${VAR} interpolation. It must never be
# committed (it is in .gitignore / .dockerignore) and never baked into an
# image. Generate each secret separately -- do not reuse passwords:
#
#   openssl rand -hex 24
#
# Hex keeps the value URL-safe: DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL are assembled from
# these values, so characters like @ : / # ? would need percent-encoding.

# --- Postgres ---------------------------------------------------------------
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=
POSTGRES_DB=app

# --- Redis ------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cache requires AUTH even though it has no published port.
REDIS_PASSWORD=

# --- API runtime ------------------------------------------------------------
# Module gunicorn imports, as <module>:<callable>.
APP_MODULE=app:app

# 2 x CPU cores is a good starting point; raise if requests are I/O bound.
GUNICORN_WORKERS=2
GUNICORN_THREADS=4
LOG_LEVEL=info
ENVIRONMENT=production

# --- Edge proxy -------------------------------------------------------------
# Host port published by the proxy. 80 needs no extra privileges for the
# Docker daemon; use 8080 when running rootless or behind another proxy.
HTTP_PORT=80
# Set to 127.0.0.1 to expose the proxy on loopback only (e.g. behind a cloud
# load balancer that terminates TLS on the same host).
HTTP_BIND=0.0.0.0
