  • rendered cache command includes requirepass

Objective checks

Files

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Response — highest-risk original problems and verification

Highest-risk problems in the supplied configuration

  1. Weak hardcoded credentials on a published database port. compose.yaml set POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password (user admin), inlined the same secret in the api's DATABASE_URL, and published 5432:5432 to the host — anyone who could reach the host could log in to Postgres with a password that was also sitting in the repo. Redis (6379:6379) was likewise published with no authentication at all, which is effectively remote code execution on the cache host.
  2. API exposed around the proxy, running as root on the dev server. The api published 5000:5000, bypassing nginx entirely, and the Dockerfile ran flask run (single-threaded development server, not built for untrusted traffic) as root with FLASK_ENV=development — one app bug away from a root shell in the container.
  3. Nothing pinned, dependencies not reproducible. python:3.13, nginx:latest, postgres:latest, redis:latest, and pip install flask psycopg2 redis (no versions, ignoring the pinned requirements.txt that was already present, and choosing source-built psycopg2 over the shipped binary). Any rebuild could silently change every layer, including major database upgrades against an existing data directory.
  4. No Postgres persistence. No volume for /var/lib/postgresql/data, so recreating the db container destroyed the database.
  5. Startup raced dependency readiness. List-form depends_on only waits for containers to start, and there were no healthchecks anywhere; the api could crash-loop against a Postgres that was still initialising, and "is it up?" had no machine-readable answer.
  6. Proxy passed no client context and had no bounds. nginx.conf set no Host/X-Real-IP/X-Forwarded-* headers (the app could not see real client IPs or scheme, breaking logging, rate decisions, and secure cookies), and set no timeouts or body-size limit, so slow or oversized requests could tie up API workers indefinitely. It also resolved api once at startup, so a recreated api container left nginx proxying to a dead IP.
  7. Build context leaked into the image. COPY . . with no .dockerignore baked whatever sat beside the Dockerfile — including a real .env — into the image, and copying source before installing dependencies invalidated the dependency layer on every code change.
  8. No operational guard-rails. No restart policy, unbounded container logs (a chatty service could fill the disk), no CPU/memory limits, one implicit flat network (the proxy could reach Postgres directly), and .env.example disagreed with compose.yaml (user app/change-me in the example vs hardcoded admin/password actually used).

What changed (summary)

  • Dockerfile: pinned slim base, deps installed from requirements.txt with --no-cache-dir before source copy, dedicated non-root app user, gunicorn instead of flask run, stdlib HEALTHCHECK on /health, dev-mode env removed. Added .dockerignore (notably excludes .env).
  • compose.yaml: secrets only via .env interpolation with :? fail-fast; no published ports for api/db/cache; Redis requires a password; pinned images; named volumes for Postgres (and Redis AOF); explicit edge/backend networks with backend internal; healthgated depends_on (service_healthy); per-service healthchecks; restart: unless-stopped, bounded json-file logging, CPU/memory limits; read-only root filesystems + tmpfs for proxy/api, cap_drop: ALL and no-new-privileges for the api; APP_VERSION image tagging for rollback. .env.example now matches the variables actually used and ships empty passwords with generation instructions; .gitignore covers .env.
  • nginx.conf: forwarding headers, runtime re-resolution of api via Docker DNS (resolver 127.0.0.11 + variable proxy_pass), connect/send/ read timeouts aligned with gunicorn, client_max_body_size 1m, gzip for JSON, server_tokens off, baseline security headers, and a proxy-local /healthz for its own healthcheck.
  • RUNBOOK.md: startup, health verification, pg_dump/pg_restore backup/restore, secret generation/rotation, tag-based rollback, and the limits of single-host Compose (plus the /health and app:app entrypoint assumptions).

Verification performed

Per the task constraints, no containers were started and no network was used; verification was static only:

  • Read all five supplied files in full and audited them line by line against the task goals before editing.
  • Parsed the rewritten compose.yaml with Python/PyYAML to confirm valid YAML. (See repository session for command output.)
  • Ran docker compose config (client-side render/validation only — pulls and starts nothing) with throwaway POSTGRES_PASSWORD/REDIS_PASSWORD values supplied via the shell environment (no .env file created), and inspected the rendered config to confirm: only the proxy publishes a port; db/cache have none; healthchecks and service_healthy conditions render as intended; both networks and both named volumes are wired to the right services; interpolated DATABASE_URL/REDIS_URL contain no committed secret.
  • Repeated docker compose config without the passwords to confirm Compose fails fast with the :? error instead of rendering empty credentials.
  • Grepped the final files for regression markers: latest, password as a literal value, FLASK_ENV, flask run, published 5432/6379 mappings, and USER/root usage — confirming the original defects are gone and that Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf agree on the api port (5000) and service name (api).
  • requirements.txt already pinned gunicorn==23.0.0 and psycopg2-binary, which the new Dockerfile now actually installs; no dependency changes were needed.

Not verified (out of scope / impossible under the constraints): actually building or booting the stack, runtime behaviour of the healthchecks against the real application (there is no app source in this directory — GET /health and the app:app entrypoint are documented assumptions in RUNBOOK.md), nginx -t against the nginx binary (none installed locally; config was checked by inspection), and that the pinned image tags resolve in a registry (no network). These need a live docker compose up smoke test on a host with registry access before production use.

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook — Python API behind nginx (Compose, single host)

Topology: proxy (nginx, the only published port) → api (gunicorn, port 5000 on internal networks only) → db (Postgres) and cache (Redis). Two networks keep traffic separated: edge (proxy ↔ api) and backend (api ↔ db/cache, no route outside). The proxy cannot reach the database or cache. Postgres data lives in the named volume db-data; Redis AOF in cache-data.

This is a single-host Compose deployment, not an orchestrator: no HA, no scheduling, no zero-downtime upgrades. Host loss = downtime. Restarts (unless-stopped), log rotation, and CPU/memory limits in compose.yaml are local guard-rails, not a substitute for monitoring or a second host.

Prerequisites and assumptions

  • Docker Engine with Compose v2 (docker compose version).
  • The application exposes GET /health returning HTTP 200 when it can serve (used by the api healthchecks; make it check DB/Redis connectivity with short timeouts so "healthy" is meaningful).
  • The app entrypoint is app.py exposing app (the gunicorn target in the Dockerfile). If yours differs, change the final app:app argument.
  • The app honours DATABASE_URL / REDIS_URL and trusts X-Forwarded-* only from this proxy (e.g. Werkzeug ProxyFix with x_for=1, x_proto=1) — safe because the api port is never published.
  • The api and proxy containers run with read-only filesystems. If the app must write files (uploads, local caches), add a named volume for that path instead of removing read_only.

Configure

cp .env.example .env
# Fill in POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD, e.g. with: openssl rand -hex 32
chmod 600 .env

Passwords must be URL-safe (hex output is) because Compose embeds them in DATABASE_URL / REDIS_URL. Compose refuses to start if either password is empty — that failure is intentional.

Startup

docker compose config        # validate + show interpolated config (check for surprises)
docker compose build api
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps            # wait until db/cache/api/proxy show "(healthy)"

Startup order is health-gated: api starts only after pg_isready and the authenticated Redis PING pass; the proxy starts only after api /health passes. First boot is slower while Postgres initialises the volume.

Health verification

docker compose ps                          # STATUS column shows health
curl -fsS http://localhost/healthz         # nginx itself: "ok"
curl -fsS http://localhost/health          # through proxy to the API
docker compose logs --tail=100 api db cache proxy
docker compose exec db pg_isready
docker compose exec cache redis-cli --no-auth-warning -a "$REDIS_PASSWORD" ping   # paste value from .env

If a service is unhealthy, read its logs first, then the failing check:

docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' app-api-1   # adjust container name

Also confirm nothing except the proxy is reachable from the host: docker compose ps should show a published port only for proxy (0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp by default). db/cache/api must show no host ports.

Backup and restore (Postgres)

Back up with a logical dump (safe while running), and store dumps off the host — a backup that only exists next to the volume is not a backup.

# Backup (.env values apply inside the container)
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U app -d app -Fc > backup-$(date +%F).dump
sha256sum backup-*.dump

# Restore into a running stack (app stopped to avoid writes mid-restore)
docker compose stop api proxy
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U app -d app --clean --if-exists < backup-YYYY-MM-DD.dump
docker compose up -d

Rehearse a restore before you need one (e.g. into a scratch docker compose -p restore-test project) and verify the API passes its health checks against the restored data. Never run docker compose down -v on the real project unless data loss is intended — it deletes db-data.

Secret handling

  • .env is the only place secrets live: mode 600, listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore, never pasted into images, tickets, or chat. .env.example ships with empty password fields on purpose.
  • Anyone with Docker/host access can read container env and command lines (docker inspect, ps), including the Redis password. Treat host and Docker-socket access as root-equivalent and restrict it accordingly.
  • Rotation: generate a new value, update .env, then docker compose up -d db cache api to recreate the affected containers. For Postgres, change the password inside the database too (ALTER USER app PASSWORD '...') — POSTGRES_PASSWORD only sets it on first volume initialisation; rotate DB first, then .env, then restart api. Redis picks up the new password on recreate; restart api after it.
  • If a secret ever lands in git or an image, rotate it — deleting the commit/file is not enough.
  • For anything beyond this single-host setup, move secrets to the platform's secret store instead of a file on disk.

Release and rollback

Releases are image tags. Set APP_VERSION in .env per release:

# Release
sed -i 's/^APP_VERSION=.*/APP_VERSION=1.4.0/' .env   # or edit by hand
docker compose build api          # builds app-api:1.4.0
docker compose up -d api proxy    # proxy waits for the new api to be healthy
docker compose ps && curl -fsS http://localhost/health

# Rollback (no rebuild needed while the old image is still on the host)
sed -i 's/^APP_VERSION=.*/APP_VERSION=1.3.2/' .env
docker compose up -d api proxy

Keep the last few app-api:* images on the host; prune only after a release has baked. Database migrations constrain rollback: only roll the app back across backward-compatible migrations; otherwise restore the database from backup (above) and accept the downtime — Compose gives you no rolling deploys, so expect a brief outage while api recreates.

Updating base images

Base images are patch/minor-pinned (python:3.13.7-slim-bookworm, postgres:17.6-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine, nginx:1.27.5-alpine). Bump them deliberately: edit the tag, docker compose build/pull, redeploy, watch health and logs. For stricter reproducibility, pin by digest (image: postgres:17.6-alpine@sha256:... from docker compose images / the registry) once a tested build exists. Similarly, requirements.txt pins exact versions; add hashes (pip install --require-hashes, generated e.g. via pip-tools) if the supply-chain bar rises.

TLS

This stack serves plain HTTP on HTTP_PORT. For real users, terminate TLS in front (host reverse proxy or load balancer) or add certificates to nginx.conf (and then enable HSTS). X-Forwarded-Proto already reflects the scheme nginx saw, so app-level secure-cookie/redirect logic keeps working either way.

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env, fill in the secrets, then: chmod 600 .env
# Never commit .env (it is listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore).
#
# Generate each password with a URL-safe alphabet, because the values are
# embedded into DATABASE_URL / REDIS_URL by compose.yaml:
#   openssl rand -hex 32

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=
POSTGRES_DB=app

REDIS_PASSWORD=

# Host port the proxy publishes. Keep 80 unless something else owns it.
HTTP_PORT=80

# Tag for the locally built API image (app-api:<APP_VERSION>). Bump on each

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/.gitignore

.env

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Small single-host deployment: nginx -> Python API -> Postgres / Redis.
#
# All secrets come from a local .env file (cp .env.example .env, then fill
# it in and `chmod 600 .env`). Values marked `:?` make Compose fail fast
# with a clear error instead of silently starting with an empty password.
# Nothing credential-shaped is committed in this file.
#
# Compose is a single-host process manager here, not an orchestrator: no
# scheduling, no HA, no zero-downtime deploys. restart/log/limit settings
# below are local guard-rails only (see RUNBOOK.md).

name: app

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27.5-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    # The only published port in the stack. Terminate TLS in front of this
    # (host reverse proxy / load balancer) for real production traffic, or
    # extend nginx.conf with certificates -- do not serve users over plain
    # HTTP on the open internet.
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - edge
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /var/cache/nginx
      - /var/run
      - /tmp
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    healthcheck:
      # /healthz is answered by nginx itself (see nginx.conf); busybox wget
      # ships in the Alpine image.
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://127.0.0.1/healthz"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 5s
      retries: 3
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 128M

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    # Tagging the built image makes rollback a version change, not a rebuild
    # (APP_VERSION in .env, bumped per release; see RUNBOOK.md).
    image: app-api:${APP_VERSION:-dev}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      # Built from .env values; passwords must be URL-safe (see .env.example).
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-app}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-app}
      REDIS_URL: redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}@cache:6379/0
    # Internal visibility only: reachable from proxy via the edge network,
    # never published to the host.
    expose:
      - "5000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - edge
      - backend
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    healthcheck:
      # Mirrors the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK; drives proxy startup ordering.
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 20s
      retries: 3
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M

  db:
    image: postgres:17.6-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-app}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-app}
    # No ports: only the api can reach Postgres, over the backend network.
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - backend
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER:-app} -d $${POSTGRES_DB:-app}"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 10s
      retries: 5
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M

  cache:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Password auth as defence in depth on top of network isolation.
    # (Compose interpolation means the value is visible via `docker inspect`
    # to anyone with Docker access on the host -- treat host/Docker access
    # as privileged; see RUNBOOK.md.)
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--requirepass", "${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}"]
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:?set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}
    # No ports: only the api can reach Redis, over the backend network.
    volumes:
      - cache-data:/data
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli --no-auth-warning -a \"$${REDIS_PASSWORD}\" ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 5s
      retries: 5
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M

# Two explicit networks: proxy <-> api (edge) and api <-> db/cache
# (backend, internal = no route to the outside world). The proxy cannot
# reach the database or cache at all, even if it is compromised.
networks:
  edge:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

volumes:
  # Survives `docker compose down`; only `down -v` destroys data (see the
  # backup/restore section of RUNBOOK.md before ever running that).
  db-data:
    driver: local
  # Redis AOF. If Redis is ever reduced to a pure throwaway cache this
  # volume (and --appendonly) can be dropped.
  cache-data:
    driver: local

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# Pin the patch version and slim variant: reproducible base, small surface.
# Bump deliberately after testing; do not use floating tags such as `python:3.13`.
FROM python:3.13.7-slim-bookworm

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /app

# Dedicated non-root user/group to run the application.
RUN groupadd --system app \
    && useradd --system --gid app --no-create-home app

# Install dependencies before copying source so this layer is cached until
# requirements.txt changes. Exact versions come from the pinned
# requirements.txt (Flask, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary, redis) -- never from a
# floating `pip install flask ...` line.
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application source. .dockerignore keeps .env and other local files
# out of the image.
COPY --chown=app:app . .

USER app

EXPOSE 5000

# The application must expose GET /health returning HTTP 200 when it can
# serve traffic (see RUNBOOK.md). Uses only the Python standard library so
# no curl/wget has to be installed into the slim image.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=15s --retries=3 \
    CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3)"

# Production WSGI server (never `flask run`). Assumes the app module is
# `app.py` exposing `app` -- adjust the final argument (e.g. `wsgi:app`)
# if the project uses a different entrypoint. Tune workers/threads to the
# host (roughly 2 x vCPU workers is a common starting point).
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "--workers", "2", "--threads", "4", \
     "--timeout", "30", "--graceful-timeout", "30", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", "--error-logfile", "-", "app:app"]

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

# Reverse proxy for the JSON API: proxy -> api:5000 (Compose `edge` network).

user nginx;
worker_processes auto;
error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log warn;
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
    include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type application/octet-stream;

    # Logs go to the container's stdout/stderr (the image symlinks these
    # paths), where Compose's bounded json-file logging captures them.
    access_log /var/log/nginx/access.log combined;

    server_tokens off;
    sendfile on;
    keepalive_timeout 65s;

    # Temp paths under tmpfs mounts so the container can run read-only.
    client_body_temp_path /tmp/client_body;
    proxy_temp_path /tmp/proxy;
    fastcgi_temp_path /tmp/fastcgi;
    uwsgi_temp_path /tmp/uwsgi;
    scgi_temp_path /tmp/scgi;

    # JSON compresses well; only bother above 1 KiB.
    gzip on;
    gzip_types application/json;
    gzip_min_length 1024;

    # Reject oversized JSON payloads before they reach the API. Raise this
    # only for specific endpoints that legitimately need larger bodies.
    client_max_body_size 1m;
    client_body_timeout 10s;
    client_header_timeout 10s;
    send_timeout 30s;

    # Docker's embedded DNS. Combined with the variable in proxy_pass below
    # this makes nginx re-resolve `api` at runtime, so a recreated api
    # container (new IP) does not require an nginx restart and a stale IP
    # cannot black-hole traffic.
    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=30s ipv6=off;
    resolver_timeout 5s;

    server {
        listen 80;
        server_name _;

        # Conservative headers for an API (clients are programs, not
        # browsers rendering pages; HSTS only makes sense once TLS is on).
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
        add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
        add_header Referrer-Policy "no-referrer" always;

        # Liveness of nginx itself, used by the Compose healthcheck.
        location = /healthz {
            access_log off;
            default_type text/plain;
            return 200 "ok\n";
        }

        location / {
            # Variable (not a literal host) so the resolver above is used
            # per-request instead of resolving once at startup.
            set $api_upstream api;
            proxy_pass http://$api_upstream:5000;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;

            # Tell the API who the real client is. The app must only trust
            # these headers because the api port is not published (only
            # this proxy can reach it). Enable the framework's proxy-fix
            # handling (e.g. Werkzeug ProxyFix, x_for=1, x_proto=1).
            proxy_set_header Host $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";

            # Fail fast instead of stacking up hung requests: connect
            # quickly, and give the API at most one gunicorn worker-cycle
            # (its --timeout is 30s) plus margin to answer.
            proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
            proxy_send_timeout 30s;
            proxy_read_timeout 60s;
        }
    }
}

muse-wonder-full/03-infra-management/requirements.txt

Flask==3.1.2
gunicorn==23.0.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.10
redis==6.4.0

Evaluation 8 / 10 graded blind as submission AG

Very careful design (hex-validated Redis password written to a private config, Redis/proxy/API all read-only with cap_drop ALL, transitive pins, authenticated DB healthcheck, excellent runbook). But nginx runs as uid 101 on a read-only root with only client_body/proxy temp paths moved; fastcgi/uwsgi/scgi temp dirs still default to /var/cache/nginx with no tmpfs, which nginx creates at startup, so the proxy very likely fails to start.

Strengths

  • Redis password never on command line; validated length/charset
  • Atomic dump, destructive restore guarded by && chain
  • Rotation and rollback procedures precise

Weaknesses

  • nginx.conf sets only client_body_temp_path and proxy_temp_path; read_only proxy has tmpfs only on /tmp -> likely 'mkdir() /var/cache/nginx/fastcgi_temp failed (Read-only file system)'
  • No end-to-end confirmation possible offline
Evidence the grader checked
  • docker compose config (dummy .env from .env.example, empty secrets filled) exit 0
  • grep AG/nginx.conf temp paths: only lines 15-16
  • rendered proxy tmpfs=['/tmp:size=32m,mode=1777'], read_only=True, user=101:101

Objective checks

Files

gpt-6.1-sol/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Infrastructure hardening response

All requested deliverables are present: corrected Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf; updated .env.example; and RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secrets, and rollback. Added the minimal app.py because no application module was supplied, pinned the complete Python runtime dependency set, and added Git/build exclusions for secrets and backups. No unrelated services were added.

Highest-risk original problems

  1. Public data services and embedded credentials. Postgres and Redis published host ports; Postgres used admin/password, and Redis had no authentication. The API's public port bypassed nginx. Only nginx now publishes a port, bound to loopback by default. Postgres/Redis share an internal backend network, both require externally supplied passwords, and Redis checks password format.
  2. Unsafe and non-repeatable API runtime. The Dockerfile ran as root using Flask's development server, ignored requirements.txt, installed unpinned packages, and copied the entire directory into the image. It now runs Gunicorn as uid 10001, copies only required files, installs exact direct and transitive versions with --no-deps, and checks dependency consistency at build time. No actual application source had been supplied initially.
  3. Data loss and uncontrolled version changes. No explicit named Postgres volume existed; image recreation could orphan an implicit anonymous volume. latest could also introduce incompatible database major versions. Data now uses a named volume and images specify patch tags, with digest overrides and database upgrade limitations documented.
  4. Startup races and no operational bounds. Ordering alone did not verify dependency readiness. Authenticated database/cache probes now gate API startup, and API readiness gates nginx. Each service has restart policy, rotating logs, CPU/memory/PID limits, and a shutdown grace period. Compose's limitations after startup are documented explicitly.
  5. Incomplete proxy behavior. nginx lacked client/protocol forwarding policy and explicit timeouts. It now overwrites untrusted forwarding headers, bounds request sizes and timeouts, avoids automatic upstream retries, logs to the container streams, and refreshes Docker DNS after API replacement. Its config is mounted read-only and it runs without root.

Verification performed

  • Docker Compose v5.1.4 parsed and rendered the configuration offline using .env.example plus dummy password fixtures. Assertions checked the exact four services, sole loopback proxy publication, network membership/internal flag, named data volume, health-based dependencies, read-only mounts, capability drops, restart/logging settings, and CPU/memory/PID limits.
  • Independently emptied each password fixture; Compose rejected both missing password cases with the expected variable named in its error.
  • Parsed/compiled app.py without generating bytecode and checked all 11 runtime packages have exact version pins. Reviewed the non-root Gunicorn command, Dockerfile readiness probe, explicit copies, and build exclusions.
  • Executed the actual readiness/liveness functions with stubbed Flask and mocked database/cache clients: healthy dependencies succeed; database errors, Redis errors, false PING, unexpected SQL results, invalid port configuration, and missing configuration return 503. Checked resource cleanup, bounded timeouts, disabled Redis retries, and responses containing no exception/secret details. These are logic checks, not real Flask/driver integration tests.
  • Parsed Redis startup and database/cache healthcheck shell scripts with sh -n. Executed only Redis password validation/config generation, replacing its final server launch with an exit: two valid hexadecimal fixtures passed, four invalid fixtures failed, and the generated config had mode 0600. Temporary files were created and removed inside this directory.
  • Parsed all eight runbook shell blocks with sh -n and checked nginx's block structure, forwarding directives, DNS resolver, writable paths, and timeouts. Confirmed no real .env file was created.

No network access, package downloads, image pulls/builds, container starts, HTTP requests, or live database/cache probes were performed. A host nginx executable is unavailable, so nginx -t was not run. Image availability, actual wheel installation, current vulnerabilities, and runtime integration remain unverified; the runbook supplies the deployment checks. Patch tags are not immutable digests, environment secrets remain visible to Docker administrators, and the example's bootstrap database role is a superuser; these limits and their production follow-ups are documented.

gpt-6.1-sol/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Small API operations

Run all commands from this directory. Use Docker Engine with the Docker Compose v2 plugin (2.20+ or compatible newer versions), not legacy docker-compose or Swarm. This is one host with four services; it provides neither high availability nor automatic rolling deployment. No containers were started during this task.

Startup

umask 077
cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))'
python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))'

Put the independently generated values in POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD in .env. Redis requires at least 32 hexadecimal characters. Blank passwords cause configuration validation to fail. The API uses separate connection fields, so database passwords do not require URL escaping. Set API_IMAGE to a new release tag, such as small-api:release-001, before building.

docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up --detach --build --wait --wait-timeout 120

The supplied app.py makes this otherwise source-less example runnable: / returns JSON, /health/live checks the application process, and /health/ready performs an authenticated SELECT 1 and Redis PING with bounded timeouts and no retries. Extend this module for the real API and retain these health routes. Gunicorn runs as uid 10001. nginx and Redis also run without root or capabilities; their writable temporary files live on tmpfs. Postgres uses its official entrypoint to initialize volume ownership and drop privileges.

Only nginx publishes a host port, at 127.0.0.1:8080 by default. The API reaches db:5432 and cache:6379 by Docker DNS on an internal backend network. Redis is an authenticated, disposable cache with a 128 MiB limit and LRU eviction; recreation loses its contents. Do not use it for durable jobs or primary data. Postgres data lives in the named small-api_postgres_data volume. Keep the Compose project name stable. docker compose down preserves that volume; do not use down --volumes or prune it when data must survive.

These defaults serve HTTP locally. Before public exposure, provide HTTPS at the existing ingress and deliberately configure the bind address and firewall. nginx overwrites incoming forwarding headers because it is the direct edge. If another proxy is introduced, configure explicit trusted proxy addresses and scheme handling before relying on forwarded client information.

Health verification and diagnosis

docker compose ps
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/live
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready
docker compose exec -T proxy nginx -t
docker compose exec -T api id
docker compose logs --tail 100 proxy api db cache

Both HTTP checks should return {"status":"ok"}. Readiness returns HTTP 503 when either dependency fails; nginx's healthcheck exercises that same route through the proxy. If HTTP_PORT changed, adjust the URLs. docker compose ps should show only the proxy port published, all services healthy, and id should show uid 10001. To inspect a particular probe failure locally:

docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' "$(docker compose ps --quiet api)"

API startup waits for healthy Postgres and Redis; proxy startup waits for a healthy API. These conditions apply during startup. A later unhealthy status does not restart a container or stop its dependants. unless-stopped restarts exited processes, not merely unhealthy processes. Investigate logs, credentials, memory limits, and dependencies, then recreate/restart the affected service. DNS is re-resolved by nginx after API replacement. Logs rotate at 10 MiB with three files per service; CPU, memory, and PID limits are starting budgets to tune against real load, not capacity guarantees.

Backup and restore

Back up before upgrades or migrations. These commands authenticate inside the database container without printing the password; never copy a live data directory as a logical backup.

umask 077
mkdir -p backups
backup="backups/app-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump"
docker compose exec -T db sh -ec 'PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" exec pg_dump --host=127.0.0.1 --username="$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname="$POSTGRES_DB" --no-password --format=custom' > "$backup.tmp" && mv "$backup.tmp" "$backup"
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore --list < "$backup"

Only a successful dump is renamed to .dump; remove a failed .tmp and retry. Archive listing is a preliminary integrity check. Copy successful backups to encrypted storage outside this host, apply a retention policy, and periodically test a restore to a separate database before trusting them. The dump contains the database, not cluster roles or .env; retain those settings securely too.

The following restore destroys the current application database. Select and verify the intended backup, take a fresh pre-restore backup, and stop all writers (including external clients). Use the recorded compatible Postgres image.

backup=backups/app-REPLACE_WITH_TIMESTAMP.dump
test -s "$backup" && \
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore --list < "$backup" && \
docker compose stop proxy api cache && \
docker compose exec -T db sh -ec 'export PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD"; dropdb --host=127.0.0.1 --username="$POSTGRES_USER" --no-password --if-exists --force "$POSTGRES_DB"; createdb --host=127.0.0.1 --username="$POSTGRES_USER" --no-password --owner="$POSTGRES_USER" --template=template0 "$POSTGRES_DB"' && \
docker compose exec -T db sh -ec 'PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" exec pg_restore --host=127.0.0.1 --username="$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname="$POSTGRES_DB" --no-password --exit-on-error --single-transaction --no-owner --no-privileges' < "$backup"

The && chain stops on failure, including a missing or unreadable archive. Proceed only if every restore command succeeds. Stopping Redis clears stale cached data. Dropping/recreating the database also removes objects absent from the backup. On failure keep writers stopped, investigate, and repeat the restore. On success:

docker compose up --detach --no-build --wait --wait-timeout 120
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready

Secrets and versions

.env is a local convenience, not a secret manager. It and backups/ are ignored by Git, and the build context admits only the Dockerfile, requirements, and API source. Do not commit real secrets, paste resolved Compose output into tickets, or expose container inspection output: environment secrets are visible to Docker administrators. Redis's private startup config avoids passwords in process arguments. Use a managed secret source or mounted secret files for a production deployment and adapt the clients accordingly.

Postgres initialization variables apply only when the data volume is empty. Changing .env alone does not rotate an existing database password. Use an interactive psql session (docker compose exec db psql -U app -d app, adjusting the names) and \password app; then update .env and recreate db and api so their probes and clients use the new value. Expect downtime and do not delete the volume. To rotate Redis's password, update .env and recreate cache and api; its cache contents will be lost. Re-run health verification afterward.

The official image makes POSTGRES_USER the bootstrap superuser. This minimal example uses that role for its read-only readiness query; provision a separate least-privilege application role before adding business database operations.

All Python runtime dependencies, including transitive dependencies, have exact versions. Installation uses binary wheels with --no-deps and pip check. Image tags specify patch versions but tags can be republished. For immutable releases, replace the image variables with approved repository@sha256:... references and retain built API images, dependency wheels/hashes, and config snapshots. Artifact availability and current vulnerability status have not been checked offline; review and update the pinned baseline before deployment.

Rollback

Before each release, retain the previous API image under a distinct tag/digest, record all image references, save compose.yaml and nginx.conf securely in backups/, and take a database backup. Never overwrite or prune the sole copy of the previous image. Expect a brief interruption while Compose replaces services.

Restore the previous Compose/nginx files and set the image variables in .env to the recorded versions while retaining current valid secrets. Then:

docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up --detach --no-build --pull never --wait --wait-timeout 120
curl --fail --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready

--no-build --pull never reuses the retained release instead of rebuilding or fetching a different image. Prefer backward-compatible schema changes. If a migration prevents application rollback, keep writers stopped and use the pre-release restore procedure; that loses writes since the backup. Never run an older Postgres major version against a newer major's data directory. Major database upgrades require a separate upgrade/restore plan, not a tag rollback.

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

"""Minimal runnable JSON API; replace/extend routes with the real application."""

import os

import psycopg2
import redis
from flask import Flask, jsonify
from redis.backoff import NoBackoff
from redis.retry import Retry


app = Flask(__name__)
app.config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 1024 * 1024


@app.get("/")
def index():
    return jsonify(service="small-api")


@app.get("/health/live")
def live():
    return jsonify(status="ok")


@app.get("/health/ready")
def ready():
    """Verify authenticated access without writing application data."""
    connection = None
    cache = None
    try:
        connection = psycopg2.connect(
            host=os.environ["POSTGRES_HOST"],
            port=int(os.environ.get("POSTGRES_PORT", "5432")),
            user=os.environ["POSTGRES_USER"],
            password=os.environ["POSTGRES_PASSWORD"],
            dbname=os.environ["POSTGRES_DB"],
            connect_timeout=2,
            options="-c statement_timeout=2000",
        )
        with connection.cursor() as cursor:
            cursor.execute("SELECT 1")
            if cursor.fetchone() != (1,):
                raise RuntimeError("Unexpected database health result")
        cache = redis.Redis(
            host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"],
            port=int(os.environ.get("REDIS_PORT", "6379")),
            password=os.environ["REDIS_PASSWORD"],
            socket_connect_timeout=1,
            socket_timeout=1,
            retry=Retry(NoBackoff(), 0),
        )
        if not cache.ping():
            raise RuntimeError("Unexpected cache health result")
    except (psycopg2.Error, redis.exceptions.RedisError, KeyError, ValueError, RuntimeError):
        # Do not expose connection strings, credentials, or exception messages.
        return jsonify(status="unavailable"), 503
    finally:
        if connection is not None:
            connection.close()
        if cache is not None:
            cache.close()
    return jsonify(status="ok")

gpt-6.1-sol/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

name: small-api

x-service-defaults: &service-defaults
  restart: unless-stopped
  init: true
  security_opt:
    - no-new-privileges:true
  logging:
    driver: json-file
    options:
      max-size: "10m"
      max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    <<: *service-defaults
    image: ${NGINX_IMAGE:-nginx:1.28.0-alpine}
    user: "101:101"
    ports:
      - "${PROXY_BIND:-127.0.0.1}:${HTTP_PORT:-8080}:8080"
    volumes:
      - type: bind
        source: ./nginx.conf
        target: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        read_only: true
        bind:
          create_host_path: false
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=32m,mode=1777
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - frontend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 8s
      start_period: 10s
      retries: 3
    cpus: "0.50"
    mem_limit: 64m
    pids_limit: 64
    stop_grace_period: 35s

  api:
    <<: *service-defaults
    image: ${API_IMAGE:-small-api:local}
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        PYTHON_IMAGE: ${PYTHON_IMAGE:-python:3.13.7-slim-bookworm}
    environment:
      POSTGRES_HOST: db
      POSTGRES_PORT: "5432"
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-app}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-app}
      REDIS_HOST: cache
      REDIS_PORT: "6379"
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:?Set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}
    expose:
      - "5000"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=32m,mode=1777
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    # The readiness healthcheck is defined in the Dockerfile.
    cpus: "1.0"
    mem_limit: 256m
    pids_limit: 128
    stop_grace_period: 35s

  db:
    <<: *service-defaults
    image: ${POSTGRES_IMAGE:-postgres:17.6-bookworm}
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-app}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-app}
      POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS: --auth-host=scram-sha-256
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      # TCP plus an authenticated query verifies initialization and credentials.
      test:
        - CMD-SHELL
        - 'PGPASSWORD="$$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" PGCONNECT_TIMEOUT=2 PGOPTIONS="-c statement_timeout=2000" psql --host=127.0.0.1 --username="$$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname="$$POSTGRES_DB" --no-password --no-psqlrc --set=ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --tuples-only --command="SELECT 1" >/dev/null'
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 30s
      retries: 5
    cpus: "1.0"
    mem_limit: 512m
    pids_limit: 256
    shm_size: 128m
    stop_grace_period: 60s

  cache:
    <<: *service-defaults
    image: ${REDIS_IMAGE:-redis:7.4.5-bookworm}
    user: "999:999"
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:?Set REDIS_PASSWORD in .env}
    # Generate a private config instead of putting the password in argv.
    # Hex secrets avoid Redis config quoting ambiguity.
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-ec"]
    command:
      - |
        case "$$REDIS_PASSWORD" in
          *[!0-9a-fA-F]*) echo 'REDIS_PASSWORD must be hexadecimal' >&2; exit 1 ;;
        esac
        if [ "$${#REDIS_PASSWORD}" -lt 32 ]; then
          echo 'REDIS_PASSWORD must contain at least 32 hexadecimal characters' >&2
          exit 1
        fi
        umask 077
        printf 'requirepass %s\n' "$$REDIS_PASSWORD" > /tmp/redis-auth.conf
        exec redis-server /tmp/redis-auth.conf --bind 0.0.0.0 --protected-mode yes --save '' --appendonly no --maxmemory 128mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=8m,uid=999,gid=999,mode=0700
      - /data:size=8m,uid=999,gid=999,mode=0700
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", 'test "$$(REDISCLI_AUTH="$$REDIS_PASSWORD" redis-cli --host 127.0.0.1 --no-auth-warning ping)" = PONG']
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 5s
      retries: 3
    cpus: "0.50"
    mem_limit: 192m
    pids_limit: 64
    stop_grace_period: 15s

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

volumes:
  postgres_data:

ARG PYTHON_IMAGE=python:3.13.7-slim-bookworm
FROM ${PYTHON_IMAGE}

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /app

# Every runtime dependency, including transitive dependencies, is pinned.
# --no-deps prevents the installer from silently adding unlocked packages.
COPY requirements.txt ./requirements.txt
RUN python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --only-binary=:all: --no-deps -r requirements.txt \
    && python -m pip check \
    && groupadd --gid 10001 app \
    && useradd --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

COPY --chown=10001:10001 app.py ./app.py
USER 10001:10001

EXPOSE 5000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=8s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
    CMD ["python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health/ready', timeout=6).close()"]

CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind=0.0.0.0:5000", "--workers=2", "--worker-class=gthread", "--threads=4", "--timeout=30", "--graceful-timeout=30", "--keep-alive=5", "--worker-tmp-dir=/tmp", "--access-logfile=-", "--error-logfile=-", "app:app"]

gpt-6.1-sol/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

# The image runs as uid 101 and listens on an unprivileged port.
worker_processes 1;
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;
error_log /dev/stderr warn;

events {
    worker_connections 512;
}

http {
    default_type application/json;
    server_tokens off;
    access_log /dev/stdout;

    client_body_temp_path /tmp/client_body;
    proxy_temp_path /tmp/proxy;
    client_max_body_size 1m;
    client_header_timeout 10s;
    client_body_timeout 10s;
    send_timeout 30s;
    keepalive_timeout 15s;

    # Docker's DNS: re-resolve after an API container is replaced.
    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s ipv6=off;
    resolver_timeout 3s;

    server {
        listen 8080;
        server_name _;

        location / {
            set $api_upstream api:5000;
            proxy_pass http://$api_upstream;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";
            proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
            # nginx is the directly exposed edge; discard untrusted client headers.
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $http_host;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port "";
            proxy_set_header Forwarded "";

            proxy_connect_timeout 3s;
            proxy_send_timeout 30s;
            proxy_read_timeout 30s;
            proxy_request_buffering on;
            proxy_buffering on;
            proxy_next_upstream off;
        }
    }
}

qwen3.8-max/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

RESPONSE — review of the original deployment configs

Highest-risk problems in the original files (ranked)

  1. Postgres and Redis published on host ports with hardcoded credentials (compose.yaml: admin:password inline, 5432:5432, 6379:6379, plus 5000:5000 for the API). On any host with a public interface this exposes the database to the internet behind a guessable password — direct data breach / ransom risk. Redis was exposed with no auth at all. Fix: all credentials now come from .env (${VAR:?err} interpolation, fails loudly when missing); db/cache publish no ports and sit on an internal: true network; the API is reachable only via nginx; the single published port is the proxy's.

  2. Development Flask server as PID 1, as root (Dockerfile: FLASK_ENV=development, CMD flask run). The Werkzeug dev server is single-threaded, not hardened, and in debug mode exposes an interactive Python console on error pages — remote code execution if reachable; any exploit also lands as root in the container. Fix: gunicorn (already pinned in requirements.txt) with bounded workers/threads/timeouts, and a dedicated non-root user (app, UID/GID 10001); compose adds no-new-privileges, read_only rootfs + /tmp tmpfs, and init.

  3. No Postgres volume — the database lived in the container's writable layer, so any recreate (up -d, image update, OOM kill) destroyed all data. Fix: named volume pgdata (plus redisdata for Redis AOF) and a documented backup/restore procedure in RUNBOOK.md.

  4. Non-reproducible builds (FROM python:3.13 full image, pip install flask psycopg2 redis unpinned, ignoring the pinned requirements.txt; nginx/postgres/redis:latest in compose). Deploys drifted silently and pulled in unvetted versions (supply-chain + "works on Tuesday" risk); plain psycopg2 also implies an unnecessary compiler in the image. Fix: python:3.13-slim, install strictly from requirements.txt (copied first for layer caching), base images pinned to minor versions (nginx:1.28-alpine, postgres:17-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine).

  5. No health checks, depends_on without conditions — containers started in name-only order, so the API raced Postgres/Redis at boot and nginx happily 502'd; failures were silent. Fix: health checks on all four services (app /healthz, /nginx-health, pg_isready, redis-cli ping) and depends_on: condition: service_healthy chaining proxy -> api -> db/cache.

  6. nginx proxy missing forwarding headers and timeouts — the app saw the proxy's IP as client IP, wrong scheme, and a hung backend could pin connections forever; the hostname api was resolved once at boot, so recreating the API container left nginx pointing at a dead IP until manual restart. Fix: X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host, X-Real-IP, proxy_http_version 1.1, connect/send/read timeouts (5s/30s/30s), client_max_body_size 1m, gzip for JSON, server_tokens off, and runtime re-resolution via Docker DNS (resolver 127.0.0.11 + variable proxy_pass).

  7. COPY . . with no .dockerignore — a local .env, git history, and caches would be baked into image layers (secret leakage via image sharing) and invalidate the dependency layer on every code change. Fix: .dockerignore added; requirements copied/installed before code.

  8. No restart policy, log rotation, or resource limits — a crashed service stayed dead, json logs grew unbounded (disk exhaustion), and one runaway container could starve the host. Fix: restart: unless-stopped, json-file logs capped at 3x10 MB per service, per-service CPU/memory limits via deploy.resources.limits — explicitly as guardrails, with RUNBOOK notes that Compose offers no orchestration beyond this.

Verification performed (no containers started, no network used)

  • docker compose config (Compose v5.5.0) with dummy env vars: passes; rendered output confirms only proxy publishes a port (80), health checks and depends_on: service_healthy conditions survive rendering, resource limits/log options/internal network are present, and DATABASE_URL interpolates correctly from the environment.
  • docker compose config without env vars: fails fast with clear "required variable ... is missing" errors — confirms no silent default credentials.
  • Python checks over the rendered/final files: YAML parses; db, cache, and api define no ports:; backend network is internal: true; pgdata/redisdata volumes declared; no admin:password-style literals remain in any committed file.
  • Static lint of nginx.conf: balanced braces/quotes; forwarding headers, timeouts, resolver, variable-based proxy_pass, server_tokens off, and both health locations present. nginx -t could not be run (would require pulling/starting a container, which the task forbids); the config uses the variable-upstream pattern that also passes nginx -t outside Docker because no name is resolved at config-load time.
  • Static lint of Dockerfile: slim base, dependency layer before code copy, non-root USER before CMD/HEALTHCHECK, no FLASK_ENV, gunicorn exec- form CMD, exec-form health check.
  • Image build (docker build) was not run: it requires network access to pull bases/packages, which is out of scope per the task constraints.

Assumptions and residual risks

  • The app source is not in this directory. Dockerfile assumes WSGI entry point wsgi:app and a GET /healthz endpoint (should verify DB/Redis); adjust the CMD if the module differs. requirements.txt was already pinned and was kept as-is.
  • Internal API port changed 5000 -> 8000 (gunicorn convention); only nginx talks to it, nothing external changes.
  • No TLS: nginx listens on 80 and expects an upstream terminator (or added certs) before real internet exposure.
  • Minor-version pins, not digests; for full reproducibility pin digests and add --require-hashes to requirements in CI.
  • read_only: true on api assumes the app writes only to /tmp.

qwen3.8-max/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

RUNBOOK — small-api (nginx + Flask API + Postgres + Redis)

Single-host Docker Compose deployment. Not Kubernetes, not multi-node.

Architecture

internet -> host:${HTTP_PORT:-80} -> proxy (nginx, "frontend" net)
                                       -> api (gunicorn :8000, frontend+backend)
                                            -> db    (postgres:17, backend only, internal)
                                            -> cache (redis:7.4,   backend only, internal)
  • The only published port is the proxy's HTTP port. api, db, and cache have no host ports; db/cache sit on an internal: true network.
  • Data volumes: pgdata (Postgres), redisdata (Redis AOF). Redis is configured as a cache (allkeys-lru, 256 MB); Postgres is the source of truth and the only thing that must be backed up.
  • The API image expects a WSGI entry point wsgi:app (adjust the CMD in Dockerfile if yours is e.g. app:app) and a GET /healthz endpoint returning 200 (it should verify DB/Redis connectivity).

Prerequisites

  • Docker Engine 24+ with Compose v2 (docker compose version).
  • Free port 80 on the host (or set HTTP_PORT in .env).

Startup

cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
# edit .env: real POSTGRES_PASSWORD (openssl rand -hex 32), etc.

docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps          # wait until all services show "healthy"

Startup order is enforced by health-gated depends_on: db/cache healthy -> api healthy -> proxy starts. Compose exits with a clear error if .env is missing required variables.

Health verification

docker compose ps                                   # HEALTH column = healthy
curl -fsS http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/healthz # end-to-end (nginx -> api -> deps)
curl -fsS http://localhost:${HTTP_PORT:-80}/nginx-health  # proxy alone

docker compose exec db    pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"
docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping            # -> PONG

# Inspect raw health probe history for a service:
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' \
  $(docker compose ps -q api) | python3 -m json.tool

Unhealthy services are auto-restarted (restart: unless-stopped); check docker compose logs -f <svc> and docker inspect ... .State.Health for the failing probe output.

Backup / restore (Postgres)

Logical dump — safe while running; take before every deploy and on a cron (e.g. nightly, keep 14 days off-host):

mkdir -p backups
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' \
  > "backups/app-$(date +%F-%H%M).dump"

# verify the dump is readable:
pg_restore --list "backups/app-YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM.dump" | head

Restore (destructive — drops and recreates objects):

docker compose up -d db                 # ensure db is healthy first
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists' \
  < backups/app-YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM.dump
docker compose restart api              # clear stale connections/pools

Cold volume backup (rare; full-fidelity, requires downtime):

docker compose stop db
docker run --rm -v small-api_pgdata:/data -v "$PWD/backups":/out alpine \
  tar czf /out/pgdata-$(date +%F).tgz -C /data .
docker compose start db

Redis holds cache only: do not back it up; it repopulates on its own.

Secret handling

  • All secrets live in .env (mode 600, git-ignored, never in images or compose.yaml). .env.example contains placeholders only.
  • Generate: openssl rand -hex 32. Keep POSTGRES_PASSWORD alphanumeric or URL-encode it — it is interpolated into DATABASE_URL.
  • Rotate the DB password:
    1. docker compose exec db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "ALTER USER \"$POSTGRES_USER\" PASSWORD 'NEW-PASSWORD';"
    2. Update .env, then docker compose up -d api (recreates api with the new URL).
  • If .env is ever leaked or committed, treat all values as compromised: rotate immediately and scrub git history.
  • Scaling up: move to Docker secrets / an external secret manager and mount secrets as files instead of env vars; env vars are visible via docker inspect to anyone with docker access.

Rollback

Every deploy should tag the built API image so you can step back:

# at deploy time (release v1.4.0):
docker compose build api
docker tag small-api:local small-api:v1.4.0
IMAGE_TAG=v1.4.0 docker compose up -d        # runs the tagged image

Roll back the application:

IMAGE_TAG=v1.3.0 docker compose up -d --no-build api   # previous known-good tag
docker compose ps && curl -fsS http://localhost/healthz

Roll back configuration (compose.yaml / nginx.conf / Dockerfile): revert the commit in git, then docker compose up -d (nginx-only changes: docker compose exec proxy nginx -s reload after re-rendering, or docker compose restart proxy).

Database: schema migrations are not auto-reversible. If a deploy included migrations, roll the data back by restoring the pre-deploy dump (above) — take that dump before deploying. Prefer backward-compatible migrations (expand/contract) so old app versions run against the new schema.

Never run docker compose down -v on a live host — it deletes pgdata.

Routine operations

docker compose logs -f api          # logs are json-file, rotated 3x10 MB
docker compose restart api          # gunicorn graceful reload
docker compose down                 # stop (volumes survive)
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d   # patch base images (test first)

Resource limits (CPU/memory per service) are set in compose.yaml under deploy.resources.limits — tune to the host, they are guardrails, not autoscaling. Compose gives you no leader election, no zero-downtime rolling updates, and no self-healing beyond container restarts; plan a maintenance window for deploys and keep an eye on df -h for the docker data root.

Known caveats / assumptions

  • TLS terminates upstream (cloud LB, reverse proxy, or add 443 + certs to nginx). Port 80 is plain HTTP; do not expose this directly to the internet without TLS in front.
  • api runs with read_only: true and a writable /tmp tmpfs; if the app must write elsewhere, add a named volume for that path.
  • Image tags are pinned to minor versions (nginx 1.28, postgres 17, redis 7.4, python 3.13-slim); for full reproducibility pin digests in CI and add hashes to requirements.txt (pip-compile --generate-hashes).

# Generate strong secrets, e.g.:  openssl rand -hex 32
# Keep POSTGRES_PASSWORD alphanumeric (or URL-encode it): it is

# --- Postgres -----------------------------------------------------------

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me
POSTGRES_DB=app

# --- Publishing ---------------------------------------------------------

qwen3.8-max/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Small single-host deployment: nginx -> Flask/gunicorn API -> Postgres + Redis.
# Secrets come from .env (see .env.example); nothing sensitive is committed.
# Compose is NOT an orchestrator: pin versions, back up Postgres, and put a
# real LB/TLS terminator + secret manager in front before serious production
# use (see RUNBOOK.md).

name: small-api

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  # Only service with a published port.
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.28-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      # busybox wget from the alpine base; checks the proxy only.
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "--spider", "http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s
    logging: *default-logging
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 128M

  api:
    build:
      context: .
    image: small-api:${IMAGE_TAG:-local}
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    environment:
      # Interpolated from .env at deploy time - no credentials in this file.
      # Keep POSTGRES_PASSWORD alphanumeric or URL-encode special characters.
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
    # No host port: reachable only from the frontend network via nginx.
    expose:
      - "8000"
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    logging: *default-logging
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M

  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    # No published port; backend network is internal-only.
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$${POSTGRES_USER}\" -d \"$${POSTGRES_DB}\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 15s
    logging: *default-logging
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 1G

  cache:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Treat Redis as a cache: bounded memory, LRU eviction, AOF so warm data
    # survives restarts. If Redis ever holds queues/sessions (data you cannot
    # afford to lose), switch maxmemory-policy to noeviction and revisit.
    command:
      - redis-server
      - --appendonly
      - "yes"
      - --maxmemory
      - 256mb
      - --maxmemory-policy
      - allkeys-lru
    volumes:
      - redisdata:/data
    # No published port; backend network is internal-only.
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    logging: *default-logging
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 512M

networks:
  # proxy <-> api
  frontend:
  # api <-> db/cache; internal: no route to/from outside the compose project
  backend:
    internal: true

volumes:
  pgdata:
  redisdata:

qwen3.8-max/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /app

# Dedicated non-root user with a fixed UID/GID
RUN groupadd --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd --uid 10001 --gid app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --create-home app

# Install pinned dependencies FIRST (layer cache + reproducible installs).
# requirements.txt is the single source of truth; psycopg2-binary needs no
# compiler toolchain, keeping the image slim.
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Application code last; owned by the runtime user, not root.
COPY --chown=app:app . .

USER app

EXPOSE 8000

# Image-level health check (compose.yaml also defines one; identical command).
# Expects the app to serve GET /healthz returning 200.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]

# Production WSGI server (NOT `flask run`). Adjust "wsgi:app" if the entry
# point differs (e.g. "app:app"). Logs go to stdout/stderr for `docker logs`.
CMD ["gunicorn", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "2", \
     "--threads", "4", \
     "--timeout", "30", \
     "--graceful-timeout", "15", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-", \
     "wsgi:app"]

qwen3.8-max/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;

error_log  /var/log/nginx/error.log  warn;
pid        /var/run/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections  1024;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/octet-stream;

    log_format  main  '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" '
                      '$status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" '
                      '"$http_user_agent" "$http_x_forwarded_for" '
                      'rt=$request_time urt=$upstream_response_time';

    access_log  /var/log/nginx/access.log  main;

    sendfile           on;
    tcp_nopush         on;
    keepalive_timeout  65;
    server_tokens      off;

    # Docker's embedded DNS. The upstream is referenced through a variable in
    # proxy_pass so nginx re-resolves "api" at runtime (TTL-aware) instead of
    # caching one container IP at boot. This survives `compose up -d api`
    # recreations and avoids nginx failing to start while api is still down.
    resolver  127.0.0.11  valid=10s  ipv6=off;

    # JSON API: reject oversized uploads early.
    client_max_body_size  1m;

    gzip             on;
    gzip_min_length  1024;
    gzip_proxied     any;
    gzip_types       application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

    server {
        listen      80;
        server_name _;

        add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
        add_header X-Frame-Options        DENY    always;

        # Liveness of the proxy itself (used by the compose healthcheck).
        location = /nginx-health {
            access_log   off;
            default_type text/plain;
            return 200 "ok\n";
        }

        # Everything else (including the app's /healthz, for end-to-end
        # checks) is proxied to the API.
        location / {
            set $api_upstream http://api:8000;

            proxy_pass         $api_upstream;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;

            # Trustworthy client identity / scheme for the app behind us.
            proxy_set_header Host              $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host  $host;
            proxy_set_header Connection        "";

            # Timeouts sized for a JSON API: fast connect, bounded read/send
            # so a hung worker can't pin a connection indefinitely.
            proxy_connect_timeout  5s;
            proxy_send_timeout     30s;
            proxy_read_timeout     30s;
        }
    }
}

gpt-6-luna/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Review response

Highest-risk original problems

  • The database password was hard-coded as admin:password, and Postgres, Redis, and the API were all published directly on host ports. That exposed data services and bypassed nginx.
  • The API ran Flask's development server as root, despite gunicorn already being listed as a dependency. The Docker build ignored requirements.txt and installed unpinned package names; all service images also used mutable latest tags.
  • There were no health checks, readiness-based startup dependencies, or persistent Postgres volume. A simple start order could leave the API connecting before its dependencies were ready, and database data could be lost when the container was replaced.
  • nginx forwarded requests without client/protocol headers or explicit connection and response timeouts.

Changes and verification

The API now runs Gunicorn as UID/GID 10001 with an exact, fully pinned Python dependency set. Compose keeps only nginx host-published, separates edge and internal data networks, persists Postgres in pgdata, and defines health checks, health-based startup dependencies, restart policies, bounded logs, resource limits, and graceful stop periods. nginx forwards the client and scheme headers and sets bounded proxy timeouts. .env.example, local ignore rules, RUNBOOK.md, and this review record cover local secrets and operations.

Static review confirmed that Compose contains no published API, Postgres, or Redis ports, no embedded database password, and no latest image tags. The configuration was checked with docker compose --env-file .env.example config --quiet; this validates Compose parsing without starting containers. No containers were started. Runtime behavior could not be checked because this directory contains no API implementation; the default Gunicorn target is app:app, and its readiness check requires GET /healthz to return HTTP 200.

gpt-6-luna/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook

Start and verify

The API image expects a Flask WSGI target in APP_MODULE (default app:app) and a fast GET /healthz route that returns HTTP 200 when the API is ready. The supplied directory has no API source, so provide that module and route in the application before expecting the API container to become healthy.

  1. Copy .env.example to .env. Replace POSTGRES_PASSWORD with the output of openssl rand -hex 32; hexadecimal keeps the value safe inside the generated DATABASE_URL. Keep the other settings appropriate for the deployment.
  2. Start the stack with docker compose up -d --build.
  3. Check docker compose ps for healthy services, then verify nginx and the proxied API with curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/_nginx_health and curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz. If HTTP_PORT was changed, use that port. Inspect failures with docker compose logs --tail=100 api db cache proxy.

Only nginx is published to the host. The API is reachable by nginx over the edge network, while Postgres and Redis are reachable by the API over the internal backend network. Redis is a volatile cache and is not backed up. Compose health checks gate startup order; they do not provide orchestration, traffic failover, or automatic recovery from application-level failures.

Backup and restore

Make and protect a custom-format Postgres backup before upgrades or data changes. Store backups outside the project directory and encrypt them when they leave the host:

umask 077
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' > /secure/backups/backup-$(date +%F).dump

To restore, stop API writes, then restore the selected dump into the configured database. This replaces objects present in the archive; confirm the target and retain a separate pre-restore backup first.

docker compose stop api
docker compose exec -T db sh -c 'pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"' < /secure/backups/backup-YYYY-MM-DD.dump
docker compose up -d api proxy
docker compose ps

The named pgdata volume survives docker compose down; docker compose down -v removes it and must not be used when the database should be retained.

Secrets

Keep .env local and out of version control. It is excluded from this directory's Git and Docker build contexts; commit only .env.example. Do not put real values in Compose files or logs. Compose passes the database password as a container environment variable, which is visible to administrators of the Docker host. For production, source it from an approved secret manager and adapt the API to consume mounted secrets if the deployment requires them. Changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env does not rotate the role password in an already-initialized data volume; rotate the database role and API secret together.

Rollback

Keep the last known-good application and configuration revision plus a pre-deployment database dump. To roll back, check out that revision and run docker compose up -d --build, then verify the health checks and API. Do not remove the Postgres volume. If a schema change is incompatible with the old application, stop writes and restore the pre-deployment dump before bringing the old API back up. Compose restart policies restart failed containers but do not roll out versions or undo schema changes.
