RESPONSE — Task 03 hardening review

Highest-risk problems in the original configuration

  1. Plaintext, guessable credentials committed in compose.yaml. The DATABASE_URL contained admin:password and POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password directly in version-controlled config — secrets in git history, trivial to guess, and inconsistent with .env.example (app/change-me). Anyone with repo read access had the database password.

  2. Database and cache published to the host with no authentication. db mapped 5432:5432 and cache mapped 6379:6379, and Redis had no requirepass. An open, unauthenticated Redis plus a weak-password Postgres reachable on all host interfaces is the single most dangerous issue: it exposes data exfiltration and known Redis-based remote-code-execution paths to anything that can reach the host. The api also published 5000:5000, letting callers bypass nginx entirely (and reach the dev server directly).

  3. API ran as root on the Flask development server with FLASK_ENV=development. flask run is single-process and explicitly not a production server; if the dev/debug mode is reachable it risks the Werkzeug debugger (RCE). Running as root compounds any container escape. The image never referenced the already-pinned requirements.txt.

  4. Non-reproducible, secret-leaking build. FROM python:3.13 + pip install flask psycopg2 redis installed unpinned packages at build time, ignored requirements.txt, would drift between builds, and COPY . . pulled .env, .git and any local secrets into the image layers. All three service images used floating :latest tags, so a rebuild could silently pull a new major Postgres/Redis/nginx.

  5. No persistence and no real readiness gating. Postgres had no named volume — docker compose down or any container recreation destroyed all data. depends_on only waited for containers to start, not to be ready, so the API could connect before Postgres/Redis accepted connections and crash. There were no healthchecks anywhere.

  6. Reverse proxy unfit for a JSON API. The minimal nginx.conf set no X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host headers (the app saw the proxy as the client and would generate wrong URLs/schemes), had no timeouts or body-size limits, used the default text/html type, no access/error logging, and HTTP/1.0 to the upstream (no keepalive).

  7. Operational gaps: no restart policy, unbounded json-file logs (disk fill), no resource limits, no explicit networks (everything on one flat default bridge, db/cache reachable from the proxy tier), and .env.example was incomplete (no Redis password, no proxy-port setting) and did not match the hardcoded values.

What I changed

  • Secrets: all credentials now come from a git-ignored .env via ${...} interpolation; compose.yaml/Dockerfile contain zero credential literals. .env.example documents every variable with placeholders. Redis now requires AUTH (--requirepass + REDISCLI_AUTH), so no passwordless cache exists. .gitignore and .dockerignore keep secrets out of git and the image.
  • Exposure: only proxy publishes a host port (configurable PROXY_PORT, default 80). api, db, cache have no ports:. Two explicit networks: backend is internal: true (no egress/gateway, hosts db+cache), frontend carries proxy↔api. Internal communication is explicit and segmented.
  • Runtime: python:3.13-slim, deps installed from pinned requirements.txt before source copy (layer caching), dedicated unprivileged app user, production gunicorn (2 workers/2 threads, 30s timeout, logs to stdout), PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE/PYTHONUNBUFFERED/no pip cache. No FLASK_ENV=development.
  • Reliability: healthchecks on all four services (pg_isready, redis-cli ping, app GET /health, proxy /healthz); depends_on uses condition: service_healthy so startup is gated on real readiness. Named volumes pgdata/cache_data persist data (Redis AOF on). Pinned image major tags. Per-service restart: unless-stopped, bounded json-file logging (10m × 3), and mem_limit/cpus/pids_limit.
  • Proxy: Host/X-Real-IP/X-Forwarded-For/X-Forwarded-Proto/ X-Forwarded-Host/X-Request-ID, HTTP/1.1 + keepalive upstream, JSON default type and JSON-structured logs, connect/send/read/body/header timeouts, 1m body cap, server_tokens off, a dependency-free /healthz, and no blind retries of non-idempotent methods.
  • Kept scope: still a single-host Compose stack. No replicas, rolling updates, placement, or secret manager were added — the RUNBOOK states plainly that Compose is not an orchestrator and that HA is out of scope.

Verification performed (static only — no containers started, no network used)

  • docker compose config with inline env values: the file parses, interpolates all ${...} variables correctly, and the rendered config shows no exposed 5432/6379/5000 host ports and no credential literals. Passed.
  • python3 + PyYAML: compose.yaml parses as valid YAML; health-based depends_on, named volumes, networks and the YAML logging anchor all resolve. Passed.
  • nginx.conf could not be binary-validated (nginx is not installed locally, and starting a container / pulling an image is out of scope). It was checked structurally (balanced braces, directives, proxy_*/header set, timeouts). Verify with docker compose run --rm proxy nginx -t before production use.
  • Static scans: no admin/password literals, no :latest tags, no ports: on api/db/cache, USER app present, requirements.txt fully pinned. Passed.
  • Not run (intentionally, per task constraints): building the image, starting any container, live healthchecks, backup/restore exercises, and nginx -t. All curl/pg_dump/pg_restore commands in RUNBOOK.md are documented procedures, not executed here.

Deliverables

  • Dockerfile, compose.yaml, nginx.conf, .env.example — corrected config
  • .gitignore, .dockerignore — secret hygiene (new)
  • RUNBOOK.md — startup, health, backup/restore, secrets, rollback
  • RESPONSE.md — this file

hy4/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

RUNBOOK — small-api stack

Single-host Docker Compose deployment: nginx (proxy) → gunicorn/Flask (api) → db (Postgres 17) and cache (Redis 7). All commands run from this directory. This is a single-node setup, not a cluster; it has no automatic failover, no rolling deploys and no built-in secret store.

1. Startup

Prerequisites: Docker with the Compose v2 plugin; ports PROXY_PORT free.

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env: set strong POSTGRES_PASSWORD and REDIS_PASSWORD (see §4).
# e.g. python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(24))"

docker compose config          # review the fully rendered config (secrets masked in output)
docker compose build           # reproducible: pinned requirements.txt, slim base
docker compose up -d           # starts in dependency/health order

Startup order is enforced by health-based depends_on: db and cache must report healthy before api starts, and api must be healthy before proxy. start_period gives a slow first boot (Postgres init, gunicorn workers) time to settle. Compose does not wait for the application to be "ready" beyond its healthcheck — if your app needs DB migrations, run them explicitly (below) after up.

The application must provide app.py exposing a Flask app with a GET /health route returning 200. /health should check what the app actually needs (a trivial DB SELECT 1 and/or Redis PING); keep it cheap because it runs every 15s.

# Example one-off migration/initialisation (adapt to your app):
docker compose run --rm api flask --app app db upgrade

2. Health verification

docker compose ps                         # STATUS should show (healthy) for db, cache, api, proxy
docker compose logs --tail=50 api         # gunicorn access/errors go to stdout
curl -fsS http://localhost:${PROXY_PORT:-80}/healthz   # proxy liveness, no upstream needed
curl -fsS http://localhost:${PROXY_PORT:-80}/health    # app health through the proxy

Direct dependency checks (run from inside the network, no host ports needed):

# Use sh -c with escaped $$ so the variables expand INSIDE the container,
# not in the host shell (where .env is not sourced).
docker compose exec db sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$$POSTGRES_DB"'
docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping          # REDISCLI_AUTH is set in the service

If a service is unhealthy, inspect docker compose logs <svc> and docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' <container> for the failing probe. Only proxy publishes a host port; api, db, cache are reachable solely over the internal networks.

3. Backup and restore

Postgres data lives in the named volume pgdata; Redis AOF in cache_data. Back up while the stack is running is fine for pg_dump (logical, consistent).

Backup (logical, portable):

# sh -c with escaped $$ expands the vars inside the container. PGPASSWORD /
# .pgpass may also be needed depending on the image's pg_hba; the db image
# trusts local socket connections from its own user by default.
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_dump -U "$$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' \
  > backup_$(date +%F_%H%M).dump

Store dumps off-host and encrypted. The Redis volume is a cache (AOF, LRU eviction) — it is rebuildable and normally not backed up; re-warm after a restore. If you must snapshot volumes, stop the stack first for a consistent copy:

docker compose down            # stops containers, KEEPS volumes
docker run --rm -v small-api_pgdata:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/pgdata_$(date +%F).tgz -C /data .
docker compose up -d

Restore (destroys current DB contents — confirm first):

docker compose up -d db                                  # ensure db is healthy
docker compose exec -T db sh -c \
  'pg_restore -U "$$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists' \
  < backup_YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM.dump
docker compose restart api                               # reconnect pools

docker compose down -v DELETES both named volumes permanently. Never use -v unless you intend to wipe data. There are no automatic backups; schedule the pg_dump command (cron/systemd timer) on the host.

4. Secret handling

  • The only place real credentials go is .env, which is git-ignored (.gitignore) and excluded from the image (.dockerignore). compose.yaml and Dockerfile contain no credential literals — they interpolate ${POSTGRES_USER}, ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, ${POSTGRES_DB}, ${REDIS_PASSWORD}.
  • .env.example documents every required variable with placeholder values; it is safe to commit and is the template operators copy.
  • db receives only the three POSTGRES_* vars via an explicit environment: list; api gets DATABASE_URL / REDIS_URL built from the same variables. Using explicit lists (rather than env_file: .env) keeps the Redis password and proxy port out of containers that don't need them. Redis requires AUTH; no passwordless cache is reachable (and no port is published).
  • Rotation: change the value in .env, then docker compose up -d to recreate affected services. Rotating POSTGRES_PASSWORD on an existing volume does not re-init the DB — also ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD inside db, or restore from a dump into a fresh volume. Rotate REDIS_PASSWORD similarly (the command flag is read on restart).
  • For anything beyond a single host, move to a real secret manager (Docker secrets / Vault / cloud KMS). Compose .env is file-based, not a secrets backend; do not treat it as one.
  • Never pass secrets on the CLI (-e, redis-cli -a) where they leak into process lists and shell history; the REDISCLI_AUTH env var avoids -a.

5. Rollback

Config/code changes are rolled back by reverting and recreating:

git revert <commit>            # or git checkout <previous> -- Dockerfile compose.yaml nginx.conf
docker compose up -d --build   # re-resolve config and rebuild the api image

Pinning matters: images use explicit major tags (postgres:17-alpine, redis:7-alpine, nginx:1.27-alpine) and the base is python:3.13-slim, not latest, so a rebuild is reproducible. requirements.txt is fully pinned.

  • To roll back only the image while keeping data: docker compose build api && docker compose up -d --no-deps api.
  • A bad deploy that corrupted data: docker compose down (keep volumes), restore the dump from §3, then up -d. Volumes are never removed by down alone, which is what makes this safe.
  • Keep the previous known-good image tag/commit hash handy. Because this is a single node, any rollback is briefly disruptive (no rolling update) — plan a maintenance window. Compose provides no built-in canary/blue-green; that is an orchestrator concern, deliberately out of scope.

6. Shutdown / troubleshooting

docker compose down            # stop, keep volumes (normal)
docker compose down -v         # DESTRUCTIVE: also deletes pgdata + cache_data
docker compose logs -f         # tail all services
docker compose restart <svc>   # recreate one service

Logs are json-file with max-size: 10m / max-file: 3 per service so a chatty API cannot fill the disk. Resource limits (mem_limit, cpus, pids_limit) and restart: unless-stopped keep a single runaway container from taking down the host — but these are per-container guards, not cluster-wide QOS.

hy4/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

# Copy to .env and fill in real values BEFORE `docker compose up --build`.
#   cp .env.example .env
# .env is git-ignored (see .gitignore) and is excluded from the image (see
# .dockerignore). NEVER commit .env and never put real secrets in this file.

# Postgres credentials (consumed by `db` via env_file and by `api` via the
# interpolated DATABASE_URL in compose.yaml). Generate a strong password, e.g.:
#   python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(24))"
POSTGRES_USER=app
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me
POSTGRES_DB=app

# Redis AUTH password. Redis 7 without a password is a common open-cache leak;
# this is required and must be the same value used in REDIS_URL.
REDIS_PASSWORD=change-me-too

# Host port for the single public entrypoint (the reverse proxy only).
# db, cache and api publish NO host ports.
PROXY_PORT=8080

hy4/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Single-host Compose stack. This is intentionally NOT an orchestrator: no
# replicas, rolling updates, placement constraints or secret manager. For HA /
# zero-downtime use a real orchestrator (out of scope here).
name: small-api

# Bounded, rotated logs for every service (extension field + YAML anchor).
x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # The only published port. Override with PROXY_PORT for local use.
      - "${PROXY_PORT:-80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    networks:
      - frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/healthz || exit 1"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s
    logging: *default-logging
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    pids_limit: 100

  api:
    build:
      context: .
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Values are interpolated from .env (never literals in this file).
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "postgres://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://default:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@cache:6379/0"
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    # No `ports:` on purpose: the API is reachable only through the proxy.
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request,sys; r=urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3); sys.exit(0 if r.status == 200 else 1)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    logging: *default-logging
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 0.5
    pids_limit: 200

  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Explicit list (not env_file) so only the vars Postgres actually needs are
    # injected — the Redis password and proxy port stay out of this container.
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: "${POSTGRES_USER}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}"
      POSTGRES_DB: "${POSTGRES_DB}"
    networks:
      - backend
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    # No `ports:` on purpose: never expose Postgres to the host.
    healthcheck:
      # $$ escapes Compose interpolation so the container's own env is used.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s
    logging: *default-logging
    mem_limit: 1g
    cpus: 1.0
    pids_limit: 200

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--requirepass", "${REDIS_PASSWORD}", "--appendonly", "yes", "--maxmemory", "200mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
    environment:
      # Lets `redis-cli` (and the healthcheck) authenticate without -a on the CLI.
      REDISCLI_AUTH: "${REDIS_PASSWORD}"
    networks:
      - backend
    volumes:
      - cache_data:/data
    # No `ports:` on purpose: never expose Redis to the host.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s
    logging: *default-logging
    mem_limit: 256m
    cpus: 0.5
    pids_limit: 100

volumes:
  pgdata:
  cache_data:

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true   # no gateway / no egress; db+cache are unreachable from outside

hy4/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim

# No bytecode, unbuffered logs, no pip cache: smaller image, predictable runtime.
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /app

# Install pinned dependencies before copying source so this layer is cached
# independently of application changes. Versions come only from requirements.txt.
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# .dockerignore keeps .env (secrets), docs and VCS data out of the image.
COPY . .

# Dedicated unprivileged user. Application code stays root-owned and read-only
# to the runtime user; gunicorn needs no write access to /app.
RUN groupadd --system app && \
    useradd --system --gid app --no-create-home --home-dir /app app
USER app

EXPOSE 5000

# Production WSGI server. Flask's built-in server is single-process and is not
# safe for production; FLASK_ENV=development also risks the Werkzeug debugger.
# The application must expose a Flask `app` object in app.py and GET /health.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "--workers", "2", "--threads", "2", "--timeout", "30", "--access-logfile", "-", "--error-logfile", "-", "app:app"]

hy4/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

worker_processes auto;

events {
    worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/json;
    charset       utf-8;

    # JSON lines in a tightly bounded format; no log injection surprises.
    log_format json_combined escape=json
        '{"time":"$time_iso8601","remote":"$remote_addr","method":"$request_method",'
        '"uri":"$uri","status":$status,"rt":$request_time,'
        '"upstream_rt":"$upstream_response_time","ua":"$http_user_agent"}';
    access_log /dev/stdout json_combined;
    error_log  /dev/stderr warn;

    sendfile        on;
    tcp_nopush      on;
    server_tokens   off;

    # Keep upstream sockets warm for repeated API calls.
    upstream api_backend {
        server api:5000;
        keepalive 16;
    }

    # Bound request/response sizes and slow clients. A JSON API has no uploads.
    client_max_body_size    1m;
    client_body_timeout     10s;
    client_header_timeout   10s;
    send_timeout            30s;
    keepalive_timeout       15s;
    proxy_connect_timeout   5s;
    proxy_send_timeout      30s;
    proxy_read_timeout      30s;

    server {
        listen 80;
        server_name _;

        # Cheap, dependency-free liveness endpoint for the proxy itself.
        location = /healthz {
            access_log off;
            return 200 "ok\n";
            add_header Content-Type text/plain;
        }

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://api_backend;

            # Required for HTTP/1.1 keepalive to the upstream.
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";

            # Preserve the real client information; overrides any spoofed values.
            proxy_set_header Host              $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host  $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Request-ID      $request_id;

            # The app needs to trust these; adjust the count behind extra proxies.
            # proxy_set_header Forwarded ...;  # optional RFC 7239

            # Don't silently retry non-idempotent API methods.
            proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
            proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;

            # Explicit JSON content type for proxied responses/errors.
            proxy_set_header Accept "application/json";
        }
    }
}

Short, correct baseline hardening: fail-fast secrets, internal backend, health gating, limits, .dockerignore excludes .env. Concise runbook with correct ALTER USER rotation; rollback is git-only.

Strengths

  • Concise runbook covering all five areas
  • Fail-fast :? secrets

Weaknesses

  • No Redis auth, no read-only/cap restrictions
  • Rollback via git stash/checkout and rebuild only

Evidence the grader checked

Objective checks

Files

muse/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Response — highest-risk original problems and verification

Highest-risk problems in the original configuration

  1. Hardcoded credentials in compose.yaml (admin:password, both in DATABASE_URL and the db environment). Committed secrets leak via git history and are readable by anyone with repo access. Fixed by sourcing all credentials from .env (required :? interpolation fails fast when unset) with only placeholders in .env.example.
  2. Database and cache ports published to the host (5432, 6379, plus the API's 5000). Postgres/Redis were reachable from the network with weak known credentials. Fixed by publishing only nginx:80; db/cache sit on an internal: true backend network and the API is expose-only.
  3. Postgres data not persisted (no volume). Any down, upgrade, or host restart silently destroyed all data. Fixed with a named pgdata volume plus backup/restore procedures in RUNBOOK.md.
  4. Development server running as root (flask run with FLASK_ENV=development on the full python:3.13 image). Debug-mode behavior, no process management, and a needless root user maximize blast radius. Fixed with a slim image, dedicated appuser, and gunicorn.
  5. Unreproducible, unpinned builds (:latest images; pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignoring the pinned requirements.txt). Every build could drift or pull a compromised release. Fixed with pinned image tags and pip install -r requirements.txt.
  6. No health checks or ordered startup (plain depends_on, COPY . . before install). The API raced the database on every boot and failures stayed silent. Fixed with per-service health checks and condition: service_healthy dependencies.
  7. Bare nginx proxy (no forwarded headers, no timeouts). The API saw wrong client IPs/scheme and a hung upstream could hold connections forever. Fixed with X-Forwarded-*/Host headers, connect/read/send timeouts, body limits, and a dedicated /nginx-health probe.
  8. Secrets baked into image layers (COPY . . before install, no .dockerignore). A local .env would have been copied into the image. Fixed with .dockerignore excluding .env and install-before-copy layer ordering.

What changed (summary)

  • Dockerfile: slim pinned-base image, non-root appuser, reproducible install from requirements.txt, gunicorn, image-level HEALTHCHECK.
  • compose.yaml: no hardcoded secrets, no public db/cache/api ports, pinned images, pgdata volume, frontend/backend networks (backend internal), health checks + health-gated startup, unless-stopped restarts, bounded logging, modest resource limits.
  • nginx.conf: proxy headers, timeouts, body limits, server_tokens off, upstream with fail thresholds, /nginx-health endpoint.
  • .env.example: documents every variable with placeholder secrets.
  • Added .dockerignore, RUNBOOK.md, RESPONSE.md.

Assumptions (no app source was supplied)

  • API entrypoint is app:app and it serves GET /healthz → 200.
  • Redis stays passwordless on the isolated backend network (documented opt-in for auth in .env.example).

Verification performed (no containers started, no network used)

  • docker compose config with dummy env vars: exit 0; rendered output confirms only proxy publishes a port, db mounts pgdata, backend network is internal, all four health checks and three service_healthy gates present.
  • docker compose config without secrets: fails fast naming the missing variable (Set POSTGRES_USER in .env), exit 1.
  • Secret scan over compose.yaml/Dockerfile/nginx.conf: no literal credentials — only ${POSTGRES_*} references and a .dockerignore comment mention them.
  • :latest and flask run/FLASK_ENV scans: no remaining hits.
  • Dockerfile contains USER appuser, pip install -r requirements.txt, and a gunicorn CMD.
  • nginx.conf: braces balanced (6/6); all required proxy headers, timeouts, client_max_body_size, server_tokens off, upstream, and health endpoint present.
  • Not run (per constraints): docker build, docker compose up, nginx -t (no nginx binary installed); image pulls would require network access.

muse/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook — small Python API behind nginx (Compose)

Stack: proxy (nginx) → api (gunicorn/Flask) → db (Postgres 16), cache (Redis 7, ephemeral). Single-host Compose deployment.

Assumptions

  • The API entrypoint is app.py exposing Flask object app, and it serves GET /healthz with HTTP 200 when ready (also after DB/Redis checks pass).
  • A .env file exists (see "Startup"). DATABASE_URL/REDIS_URL are built by Compose; only Postgres credentials and the nginx host port are set.

Startup

  1. cp .env.example .env, then set a strong POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env.
  2. docker compose up -d --build
  3. docker compose ps — every service should reach (healthy).
  4. curl -f http://localhost:<NGINX_HTTP_PORT>/healthz should return 200.

Stop: docker compose stop. Full teardown (containers + networks, data kept in the pgdata volume): docker compose down.

Health verification

  • docker compose ps shows per-service health status.
  • Proxy itself: curl -f http://localhost:<NGINX_HTTP_PORT>/nginx-health
  • End to end: curl -f http://localhost:<NGINX_HTTP_PORT>/healthz
  • Postgres: docker compose exec db pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" (load .env into the shell first, or substitute values literally).
  • Redis: docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping (expect PONG).
  • Logs: docker compose logs --tail=100 <service>.

Startup order is health-gated: api waits for db and cache to be healthy; proxy waits for api. A service stuck in (unhealthy) blocks its dependents — inspect its logs before restarting anything.

Backup / restore

Postgres data lives in the named volume pgdata and survives down and container recreation. It is deleted only by docker compose down -v.

  • Logical backup: docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" > backup-$(date +%F).sql
  • Restore to a running stack: cat backup.sql | docker compose exec -T db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"
  • Volume-level backup (stack stopped): docker run --rm -v <project>_pgdata:/data -v "$PWD:/out" alpine tar czf /out/pgdata-$(date +%F).tgz -C /data .
  • Verify a backup by restoring into a scratch database and running a smoke query; never treat an unrestored dump as a verified backup.

Redis is a cache with no volume: nothing to back up. It starts empty after recreation by design.

Secret handling

  • Secrets live only in .env (mode 600, never committed). No credentials are hardcoded in compose.yaml, Dockerfile, or nginx.conf.
  • .dockerignore excludes .env so secrets are never baked into image layers via COPY . ..
  • Rotate the Postgres password: update .env, then docker compose exec db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "ALTER USER \"$POSTGRES_USER\" WITH PASSWORD '<new>'" and docker compose up -d api to pick up the new DATABASE_URL. A restart of db is not needed for the password change itself.
  • Treat any credential once committed to git as compromised: rotate it.

Rollback

  1. Identify the last good state: docker compose config (current rendered config) and your git history for these files.
  2. Code/config rollback: git stash or git checkout -- <files> to the last good commit, then docker compose up -d --build.
  3. Data rollback: restore a pg_dump backup as above. Note restores lose writes made after the backup; there is no point-in-time recovery here.
  4. Verify with the health checks above before declaring the rollback done.

What Compose does not do

This is one host with local restart policies and log rotation — not a full orchestrator. There is no multi-host failover, rolling deploys, autoscaling, or secret store. deploy.resources.limits documents intent and caps local usage; reservations need Swarm/Kubernetes semantics. Plan a migration before those properties are required.

muse/03-infra-management/TASK.md

Task 03 — Infrastructure management: harden a small deployment

Review and improve the supplied Dockerfile, compose.yaml, and nginx.conf for a small Python API behind nginx with Postgres and Redis. Do not add Kubernetes or unrelated services.

Goals:

  • No embedded credentials or public database/cache ports.
  • The API runs as a non-root user with a production server and reproducible dependency installation.
  • Add meaningful health checks and startup dependencies based on health.
  • Persist Postgres data, make internal service communication explicit, and add sensible restart/logging/resource settings without pretending Compose is a full orchestrator.
  • Proxy headers and timeouts should be appropriate for a JSON API.
  • Keep local operation straightforward through .env.example.

Deliver corrected configuration and a concise RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling, and rollback. Write RESPONSE.md listing the highest-risk original problems and verification you performed. Work only in this directory; do not actually start containers.

#   cp .env.example .env
# Never commit .env (see RUNBOOK.md).

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-before-first-run
POSTGRES_DB=app

# Host port mapped to nginx:80. Container ports stay fixed.
NGINX_HTTP_PORT=80

# Redis has no password and is reachable only on the internal backend
# network. If you need auth, set REDIS_PASSWORD here AND update the
# cache command/healthcheck and the api REDIS_URL in compose.yaml.

muse/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Shared logging profile: bounded local log files so a chatty service
# cannot fill the host disk.
x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - frontend
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.25"
          memory: 128M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget --no-verbose --tries=1 --spider http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health || exit 1"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s

  api:
    build:
      context: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER in .env}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:?Set POSTGRES_DB in .env}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://cache:6379/0"
    expose:
      - "5000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M
    healthcheck:
      # Requires the API to serve GET /healthz with HTTP 200.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "python -c \"import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/healthz', timeout=4)\""]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s

  db:
    image: postgres:16-bookworm
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER in .env}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:?Set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - backend
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$${POSTGRES_USER}\" -d \"$${POSTGRES_DB}\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 15s

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - backend
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

volumes:
  pgdata:

networks:
  frontend:
  backend:
    internal: true

muse/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

FROM python:3.13-slim

# Minor-version pin balances reproducibility with security updates.
# For immutable builds, pin this image by digest as well.

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

WORKDIR /app

RUN groupadd -r appuser && useradd -r -g appuser appuser

# Install dependencies first for layer caching; requirements.txt is
# version-pinned so installs are reproducible.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .

USER appuser

EXPOSE 5000

# The API must expose GET /healthz returning 200 (see RUNBOOK.md).
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/healthz', timeout=4)"

# Production WSGI server. Assumes app.py exposes Flask object `app`;
# adjust the module if the real entrypoint differs.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", "--workers", "2", "--timeout", "30", "app:app"]

muse/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

worker_processes auto;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
  default_type application/octet-stream;

  access_log /var/log/nginx/access.log;
  error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log warn;

  server_tokens off;

  # Sensible limits for a JSON API: reject oversized bodies early,
  # don't hold slow clients forever.
  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_body_timeout 10s;
  client_header_timeout 10s;
  keepalive_timeout 65s;
  send_timeout 30s;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json;
  gzip_min_length 256;

  upstream api {
    server api:5000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
  }

  server {
    listen 80;
    server_name _;

    # Liveness probe for the proxy itself (used by Compose healthcheck).
    location = /nginx-health {
      access_log off;
      add_header Content-Type text/plain;
      return 200 'ok';
    }

    location / {
      proxy_pass http://api;
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";

      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

      proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
      proxy_read_timeout 30s;
      proxy_send_timeout 30s;

      proxy_next_upstream error timeout;
    }
  }
}

Simple correct configuration; correct rotation caveat; rollback via git. No Redis auth; minimal runtime hardening beyond non-root API and no-new-privileges.

Weaknesses

Evidence the grader checked

Objective checks

glm-5.3/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Response — Task 03: Infrastructure hardening

Highest-risk problems in the original configuration

  1. Credentials in version control — compose.yaml embedded admin / password twice (db environment and DATABASE_URL). Anyone with repo access has production DB credentials; anyone watching a CI log sees them too.
  2. Database and cache published to the host — 5432:5432 and 6379:6379 were bound on all host interfaces. Redis had no authentication, so on many networks it was remotely reachable and writable (a well-known RCE path via module loading). Postgres was reachable with the weak committed password.
  3. Flask development server as the production process — flask run + FLASK_ENV=development means the Werkzeug dev server (no concurrency tuning, debug-oriented behavior) handling real traffic.
  4. No readiness gating — depends_on only ordered container startup, so the API routinely booted before Postgres accepted connections and crashed or served 500s.
  5. No Postgres persistence — no volume on /var/lib/postgresql/data; docker compose down destroyed all application data.
  6. Unreproducible build — pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignored the pinned requirements.txt (floating versions, different image per build); all service images were :latest.
  7. Container ran as root with COPY . . — no .dockerignore, so a local .env (or any future secret file) would be baked into image layers, readable by anyone with image pull access, running as root.
  8. No restart policy, no log limits — a crash stayed down; json-file logs grew unbounded until the host disk filled.
  9. Unconfigured proxy — nginx forwarded nothing (Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto missing, so the API cannot see client IPs/protocol), used HTTP/1.0-style upstream connections, and had default 60s proxy timeouts with no body-size limit; version leaked via Server: header.

Changes made

  • compose.yaml: all secrets interpolated from .env with :? fail-fast errors; no published ports for db/cache/api (expose only documents internal ports); named db_data volume; health checks for all four services with depends_on: condition: service_healthy; split frontend / backend networks, backend marked internal: true (no egress, and the proxy cannot reach db/cache at all); restart: unless-stopped; rotated json-file logging; memory/CPU limits; no-new-privileges on every service; pinned image tags (nginx:1.27-alpine, postgres:17, redis:7-alpine).
  • Dockerfile: pinned base (python:3.13-slim-bookworm); installs the pinned requirements.txt (dependency layer cached separately); non-root app user; gunicorn production CMD (exec form, tuned workers); dev-server env removed.
  • nginx.conf: proxy headers, HTTP/1.1 + keepalive upstream, connect/send/read timeouts tuned for a JSON API, client_max_body_size 1m, server_tokens off, gzip for JSON, and a proxy-local /health endpoint for the compose healthcheck.
  • New files: .dockerignore (keeps .env, VCS files, caches out of the image), .gitignore (keeps .env out of git), expanded .env.example (all variables with generation guidance), RUNBOOK.md (startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret handling incl. password rotation, rollback).

Verification performed

Offline, without starting any containers:

  • docker compose config (Compose v5.5.0, client-side validation) renders the full stack cleanly with test values: only the proxy publishes a port, db/cache/api are expose-only, all health checks, resource limits, network attachments, and the db_data volume resolve as intended.
  • With .env absent, docker compose config exits non-zero with actionable "required variable ... is missing" errors — confirmed the fail-fast secret handling works.
  • A Python structural check over nginx.conf: balanced braces, every directive terminated, and all required proxy-header/timeout directives present. (No nginx binary is available here, so nginx -t could not be run — full syntax validation should be done at first up.)
  • Dockerfile checked programmatically: exec-form CMD parses as valid JSON, references gunicorn, and the file contains no dev-server remnants; non-root user and --no-cache-dir install confirmed.
  • No credential strings remain in Dockerfile/compose.yaml/nginx.conf; .env.example contains placeholders only. No container was started and no network was used.

Assumptions (adjust if wrong)

  • The Flask app is exposed as app in app.py (gunicorn app:app) and serves GET /health with 2xx. Both are one-line changes (Dockerfile CMD / api healthcheck) and are called out in RUNBOOK.md.
  • Versioned image tags were chosen as stable majors; pin to exact digests in a real release pipeline.

glm-5.3/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook — app stack (nginx / API / Postgres / Redis)

A single-host Docker Compose deployment. nginx is the only publicly reachable service; the API, Postgres, and Redis live on internal networks (backend is internal: true, so it has no internet egress either).

client -> proxy (nginx, :80) -> api (gunicorn :5000) -> db / cache
         frontend network            frontend + backend      backend

Prerequisites

  • Docker Engine + Docker Compose v2 (docker compose version)
  • A .env file in this directory (see below)

First-time startup

cp .env.example .env
$EDITOR .env          # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (openssl rand -hex 24)
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps     # all four services should report (healthy)

Compose interpolates credentials from .env and refuses to start with a clear error if any required variable is missing. The API waits for db and cache to pass their health checks before starting; the proxy waits for the API.

The application must expose GET /health returning 2xx — the compose healthcheck for api and the gunicorn entrypoint assume this. If your Flask module/object is not app:app, change the gunicorn argument in the Dockerfile.

Health verification

# Container-level (healthchecks from compose.yaml)
docker compose ps

# Proxy is serving (nginx answers this locally, no upstream involved)
curl -fsS http://localhost/health

# End-to-end through nginx to the API
curl -fsS http://localhost/<any-real-api-route>

# Component checks from inside the stack
docker compose exec db pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"
docker compose exec cache redis-cli ping
docker compose exec api python - <<'PY'
import os, urllib.request
urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:5000/health", timeout=3)
print("api healthy")
PY

# Logs (json-file driver, rotated at 10m x 3 files per container)
docker compose logs --tail=100 api
docker compose logs -f proxy

Backup / restore (Postgres)

Data persists in the named volume db_data, so it survives docker compose down.

First load your .env into the shell (the commands below expand $POSTGRES_USER / $POSTGRES_DB locally):

set -a; source .env; set +a

# Backup (custom-format dump; portable and compressible)
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -Fc "$POSTGRES_DB" > backup.dump

# Restore into an empty database, or clean existing objects first
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" --clean --if-exists \
  -d "$POSTGRES_DB" < backup.dump

# Physical fallback: snapshot the volume (stop writes first)
docker compose stop api
docker run --rm -v <project>_db_data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/db_data.tgz -C /data .
docker compose start api

Store dumps off-host. Restore order: stop api (so nothing writes during restore), restore, then docker compose up -d.

Secret handling

  • All credentials live in .env, which is git-ignored and excluded from the image build via .dockerignore. Nothing is hardcoded in compose.yaml / Dockerfile.
  • Generate the DB password with openssl rand -hex 24. Use only characters that are safe inside a URI (hex is), or URL-encode them — the password is interpolated into DATABASE_URL.
  • Password rotation: changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env does NOT affect an already-initialized volume. Rotate like this:
    docker compose exec db psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "ALTER USER \"$POSTGRES_USER\" WITH PASSWORD '<new>';"
# then update .env and restart the API
docker compose up -d api
  • For production, prefer a real secret store (Vault, cloud secret manager) or at least Docker secrets / an orchestrator; .env is a convenience for local/small deployments, not an access-control mechanism. Restrict file permissions (chmod 600 .env).

Rollback

The state that matters is db_data plus the deployed configuration.

# 1. Roll back the configuration to the previous version
git checkout <previous-tag-or-commit> -- Dockerfile compose.yaml nginx.conf

# 2. Rebuild and restart (data volume is untouched)
docker compose up -d --build

# 3. If the data schema also regressed, restore the matching dump
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" --clean --if-exists \
  -d "$POSTGRES_DB" < backup.dump

Useful operations:

docker compose down          # stop and remove containers; db_data survives
docker compose down --volumes   # DANGER: deletes Postgres data permanently
docker compose restart api   # bounce a single service

Take a fresh pg_dump before any rollback that touches the database.

Limits of this setup (Compose is not an orchestrator)

  • Single host only; if the machine dies, everything is down. restart: unless-stopped restarts crashed containers, but there is no rescheduling.
  • Resource limits are enforced by the kernel where supported (cgroups), but there is no autoscaling or cluster self-healing.
  • Log rotation is per-container (10 MB x 3); aggregate logs elsewhere if you need retention.
  • Backups are manual — schedule them via cron/host tooling if this stops being a dev deployment.

glm-5.3/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Docker Compose v2+ file. All credentials are interpolated from .env
# (see .env.example); services fail to start with a clear error if missing.
#
# Note: Compose is not an orchestrator. restart policies and resource limits
# are best-effort on a single host; there is no autoscaling, rescheduling,
# or cluster-level self-healing here.

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Only externally published port in the stack.
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - frontend
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 128M
          cpus: "0.50"
    healthcheck:
      # nginx serves /health itself (see nginx.conf), so this check
      # reflects the proxy, not the upstream API.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q --spider http://localhost/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s

  api:
    build: .
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Internal only: reached through the proxy, never published.
    expose:
      - "5000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - frontend
      - backend
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 512M
          cpus: "1.00"
    healthcheck:
      # App must expose GET /health returning 2xx (see RUNBOOK).
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health', timeout=3)"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 15s

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    restart: unless-stopped
    expose:
      - "5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?set POSTGRES_USER in .env}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:?set POSTGRES_DB in .env}
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - backend
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 512M
          cpus: "1.00"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    expose:
      - "6379"
    networks:
      - backend
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    logging: *default-logging
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 256M
          cpus: "0.50"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s

volumes:
  db_data:

networks:
  frontend:
  backend:
    # No default gateway: db/cache cannot reach the internet, and the proxy
    # cannot reach them at all (only api is attached to backend).
    internal: true

FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

WORKDIR /app

# Unprivileged user for running the application.
RUN groupadd --system app \
    && useradd --system --gid app --home-dir /app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

# Install pinned dependencies first so the layer is reused unless
# requirements.txt changes (fast, reproducible builds).
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code with correct ownership, then drop privileges.
COPY --chown=app:app . ./
USER app

EXPOSE 5000

# Production WSGI server. Assumes the Flask app object is exposed as `app`
# in `app.py` at the project root; adjust the module path if not.

     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:5000", \
     "--workers", "2", \
     "--threads", "4", \
     "--worker-tmp-dir", "/dev/shm", \
     "--timeout", "60", \
     "--graceful-timeout", "30", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "app:app"]

glm-5.3/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

worker_processes auto;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
  default_type application/json;

  sendfile on;
  tcp_nopush on;
  keepalive_timeout 30s;

  # Don't advertise the nginx version in headers or error pages.
  server_tokens off;

  # JSON API: payloads are small; reject oversized bodies early.
  client_max_body_size 1m;
  client_body_timeout 10s;
  client_header_timeout 10s;

  gzip on;
  gzip_min_length 256;
  gzip_types application/json;
  gzip_proxied any;

  # Keepalive connections to the upstream (works with proxy_set_header Connection "").
  proxy_http_version 1.1;

  server {
    listen 80;
    server_name _;

    # Timeouts tuned for a JSON API: fail fast when connecting,
    # but allow slow handlers up to 30s.
    proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
    proxy_send_timeout 30s;
    proxy_read_timeout 30s;

    # Proxy-local health endpoint. Used by the compose healthcheck and
    # by the operator; it deliberately does NOT hit the upstream.
    location = /health {
      access_log off;
      return 200 "ok\n";
    }

    location / {
      proxy_pass http://api:5000;
      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";
    }
  }
}

hy4-flash/03-infra-management/RESPONSE.md

Response — Infrastructure hardening

Files delivered

Corrected Dockerfile, compose.yaml, nginx.conf, completed .env.example; added .dockerignore and .gitignore; new RUNBOOK.md and this RESPONSE.md.

Highest-risk problems in the original configuration

  1. Hardcoded credentials everywhere (critical). compose.yaml embedded postgres://admin:password@db:5432/app, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password, and a Redis URL; .env.example had a different user (app vs admin), so the documented setup did not match the actual deployment and the database would not initialize consistently. Secrets were baked into a file likely to be committed. Fixed by sourcing everything from .env ${...} variables (git/docker ignored), building URLs at runtime, and enforcing Redis auth with --requirepass.

  2. Database and cache published to the host (critical). db exposed 5432 and cache exposed 6379 on all interfaces with no authentication on Redis (redis://cache:6379, no password) and a guessable Postgres password. Anyone able to reach the host could read/modify data or take over the cache. Fixed by removing all ports: from db and cache, placing them on an internal: true backend network reachable only by api, and only publishing nginx on a configurable, localhost-default HTTP_PORT.

  3. Development server in production (high). The Dockerfile used FLASK_ENV=development and flask run, which is slow, single-process, and not safe for production; . was copied before install (no layer caching); unpinned pip install flask psycopg2 redis ignored the pinned requirements.txt that was already present, so builds were not reproducible; the container ran as root. Fixed with a pinned base image, install from requirements.txt before copying code, non-root numeric UID/GID, and gunicorn with sensible worker/timeout/log settings.

  4. Startup order not based on readiness (high). Plain depends_on: [db, cache] only waits for container creation; the API could start before Postgres/Redis were accepting connections and crash-loop. Fixed with condition: service_healthy plus real health checks for db, cache, and api (and the proxy gated on the API).

  5. No data persistence or durability (high). Postgres had no volume — all data was lost on container recreation. Redis had no persistence/auth. Fixed with named volumes pgdata and redisdata, AOF on Redis, and a documented pg_dump/pg_restore backup/restore path.

  6. No resource/log/restart controls (medium). No restart policy, unbounded logs, no CPU/memory limits. Added restart: unless-stopped, JSON-file log rotation (10 MB × 3), advisory deploy.resources.limits, and explicit stop_grace_period. Documented clearly that these are not full orchestration.

  7. Bare nginx proxy (medium). No forwarded headers, no timeouts, no body size limit, no keepalive, no health endpoint. Fixed with X-Forwarded-* headers, HTTP/1.1 upstream keepalive, connect/send/read timeouts, client_max_body_size 2m, a lightweight /healthz, and denial of hidden files (/.), plus a read-only config mount.

  8. No operational documentation (medium). Added RUNBOOK.md covering startup, health verification, backup/restore, secret rotation, and rollback.

Verification performed (static only — no containers started)

  • docker compose -f compose.yaml config and config -q both succeeded after substituting sample values from .env.example; confirmed the merged render has: only proxy with a published port (127.0.0.1:80 by default), no ports on db/cache, internal: true on backend, named volumes, health checks, and service_healthy dependency conditions.
  • YAML parsed cleanly with PyYAML; confirmed every dependency in requirements.txt uses an exact == pin.
  • nginx.conf checked structurally: balanced braces (7/7 after stripping strings/comments) and presence of all required proxy/timeout/health directives. Full nginx -t was not possible: no nginx image or binary is available locally and network access is disabled.
  • Dockerfile checked: non-root USER, gunicorn CMD, no flask run, presence of HEALTHCHECK, dependency install from pinned requirements.txt, and no development-mode env var. Dependency install before COPY . . preserves layer caching.
  • Credential-leak scan of the tracked config files: no literal password remains (only ${VAR} references and the CHANGE_ME placeholders in .env.example).
  • Confirmed no containers were started at any point.

Known limitations / assumptions

  • The application source (app.py) was not provided; the Dockerfile assumes a Flask app object at app:app and that GET /healthz returns 200, as the task's health-check goal requires. If the route differs, set HEALTHCHECK_PATH / update the probes accordingly.
  • nginx -t and an actual image build could not be run in this offline environment; those are recommended as the next live checks before deployment.

hy4-flash/03-infra-management/RUNBOOK.md

Runbook — small API stack

Four services: proxy (nginx, the only public listener), api (Python/Flask behind gunicorn), db (Postgres), cache (Redis). Compose is used for local / small-scale operation only; it is not a full orchestrator. restart: unless-stopped restarts crashed containers but provides no rescheduling, rolling updates, or cross-host self-healing. The deploy.resources.limits keys are advisory CPU/memory caps honored by Docker, not a scheduler guarantee.

Prerequisites & first-time setup

  1. Docker Engine with the Compose v2 plugin (docker compose version).

  2. Create secrets and the local env file (never commit .env):

    cp .env.example .env
# Generate two independent secrets and paste them into .env:
openssl rand -hex 32   # POSTGRES_PASSWORD
openssl rand -hex 32   # REDIS_PASSWORD

  3. Fill in POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, REDIS_PASSWORD, and HTTP_PORT (use 127.0.0.1:80 for localhost-only, or 0.0.0.0:80 to bind all interfaces). .env is excluded by .gitignore and .dockerignore so it neither enters version control nor the image.

  4. Build and start:

    docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --build

Startup order is health-gated: db and cache must pass their health checks before api starts; api must pass its /healthz check before proxy starts. This replaces the original depends_on list, which only waited for container creation, not readiness.

Health verification

docker compose -f compose.yaml ps                 # all services Up (healthy)
docker compose -f compose.yaml logs -f --tail=100
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1/healthz                # nginx -> {"status":"ok"}
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1/<your-api-route>       # proxied JSON from gunicorn

What each check covers:

  • db: pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" (Postgres accepting connections).
  • cache: authenticated redis-cli ping via REDISCLI_AUTH (Redis accepting the password).
  • api: GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz must return 200 (gunicorn + app alive). The application must implement this route; the same probe is declared both in Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK and in compose.yaml.
  • proxy: nginx's own /healthz returns a static JSON 200, useful for uptime probes.

The dedicated edge and backend networks are explicit: only proxy and api share edge; only api, db, and cache share backend, which is internal: true (no outbound route). Postgres and Redis publish no host ports.

Backup / restore (Postgres)

Backups run from the db container so no host Postgres client is needed.

Backup (logical dump, gzipped, timestamped):

docker compose -f compose.yaml exec -T db \
  sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -Fc' \
  > backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).dump

Rotate and store dumps off-host (encrypted). Do not keep them in the build context. Restore into a fresh/empty database:

# Stop the API first to avoid writes during restore.
docker compose -f compose.yaml stop api
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec -T db \
  sh -c 'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists' \
  < backup_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.dump
docker compose -f compose.yaml start api

Volume-level (physical) backup alternative must be done while the DB is stopped for consistency, e.g. docker run --rm -v <pgdata-volume>:/data -v $PWD:/backup busybox tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data . — use the logical pg_dump method above for routine backups.

Redis has --appendonly yes with data in the redisdata volume; it is a cache, so treat its contents as disposable on restore.

Secret handling

  • All credentials live only in .env (git/docker ignored) and are injected at runtime. No password is baked into compose.yaml, the image, or nginx config.
  • DATABASE_URL / REDIS_URL are assembled in Compose from ${...} vars. Redis uses --requirepass "$REDIS_PASSWORD"; its healthcheck authenticates via REDISCLI_AUTH. Postgres uses SCRAM (scram-sha-256).
  • Rotate a secret: update .env, then recreate consumers: docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate api cache db. Rotating the Postgres password also requires updating any existing roles/ connections; test before rotating in production.
  • Never paste real secrets into docker inspect output, logs, tickets, or chat. For production, replace .env with a real secret manager / Docker secrets and pin the base image by digest (FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm@sha256:...).

Updates, rollback, and teardown

# Rebuild after code/dependency changes:
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --build api
# Roll back to a previously tagged image:
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --no-build --force-recreate api \
  # after setting `image:` to the last known-good tag in compose.yaml

Rollback procedure:

  1. Stop writes: docker compose -f compose.yaml stop api proxy.
  2. Restore the last good pg_dump (see above) if the release migrated schema.
  3. Re-point image: (or git checkout the previous commit and rebuild) to the last known-good version, then docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --build.
  4. Re-run the health verification steps above.

Teardown (removes containers/networks; named volumes are preserved unless --volumes is added — do not add it unless you intend to delete data):

docker compose -f compose.yaml down

Notes: nginx.conf is mounted read-only (:ro). Logs are JSON-file with a 10 MB × 3 rotation per service to avoid unbounded disk use. Gunicorn uses 3 workers / 2 threads, 30 s timeouts, and recycles workers after 1000 requests.

hy4-flash/03-infra-management/compose.yaml

# Compose spec (no `version:` key needed for Compose v2).
# All secrets come from the environment / .env file -- none are embedded here.
# Copy .env.example to .env and fill in real values before starting.

services:
  proxy:
    container_name: small-api-proxy
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: &default-logging
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "10m"
        max-file: "3"
        tag: "{{.Name}}"
    ports:
      # The ONLY public entry point. Bind to loopback via HTTP_PORT in .env.
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-127.0.0.1:80}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - edge
    # Advisory limits. Compose restart policies are not orchestration: no
    # rescheduling, rolling updates, or self-healing beyond a plain restart.
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 128M

  api:
    container_name: small-api
    build: .
    image: small-api:local
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    environment:
      # Credentials injected from .env; nothing sensitive is baked into the image.
      DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/${POSTGRES_DB}"
      REDIS_URL: "redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@cache:6379/0"
      FLASK_APP: "app:app"
      # No service ports published: the API is reachable only inside `edge`.
    expose:
      - "8000"
    # Requires the app to expose GET /healthz (200 when ready). Same probe is
    # baked into the image via Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK; declared here explicitly.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import sys,urllib.request; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=4).status==200 else 1)"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 20s
      retries: 3
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - edge
      - backend
    stop_grace_period: 40s  # let gunicorn finish in-flight requests (30s timeout)
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M

  db:
    container_name: small-api-db
    image: postgres:17-bookworm
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: "${POSTGRES_USER}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}"
      POSTGRES_DB: "${POSTGRES_DB}"
      POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD: "scram-sha-256"
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    # No `ports:`: Postgres is private to the `backend` network.
    expose:
      - "5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$${POSTGRES_USER}\" -d \"$${POSTGRES_DB}\""]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 20s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.00"
          memory: 512M

  cache:
    container_name: small-api-cache
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *default-logging
    # Enforce a password at runtime; the literal never appears in this file.
    command: ["sh", "-c", "exec redis-server --requirepass \"$$REDIS_PASSWORD\" --appendonly yes"]
    environment:
      REDIS_PASSWORD: "${REDIS_PASSWORD}"
    # No `ports:`: Redis is private to the `backend` network.
    expose:
      - "6379"
    volumes:
      - redisdata:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "REDISCLI_AUTH=\"$${REDIS_PASSWORD}\" redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 10s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M

volumes:
  pgdata:
  redisdata:

networks:
  edge:
    # Proxy <-> API; this is the only network with a published host port.
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    # API <-> db/cache only, with no route out (`internal: true`).
    driver: bridge
    internal: true

hy4-flash/03-infra-management/Dockerfile

# Pin the base image by digest for fully reproducible builds, e.g.
#   FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm@sha256:<digest>
# A fixed variant tag is used here so the image stays buildable without a
# network lookup of a digest. See RUNBOOK.md.
FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm

# Don't write bytecode or buffer stdout/stderr: Python output goes straight to
# Docker's log driver so `docker logs` shows the application in real time.
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies from the pinned manifest *before* copying application
# code so the dependency layer is cached and rebuilds are reproducible. Every
# version in requirements.txt is pinned with == (use `pip freeze`/a lock file
# or --require-hashes with a hash manifest for supply-chain-grade pinning).
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip==25.2 \
    && python -m pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

# Run as an unprivileged, fixed UID/GID given numerically so the build does
# not depend on useradd/groupadd being present in the slim base image.
# Binding to 8000 (>1024) needs no NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
RUN chown -R 10001:10001 /app
USER 10001:10001

EXPOSE 8000

# Liveness probe: the application must expose GET /healthz (override via
# HEALTHCHECK_PATH). A 200 response is required; urllib is in the stdlib so no
# extra packages or shell tools are needed in the slim image.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=15s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import os,sys,urllib.request; \
p=os.environ.get('HEALTHCHECK_PATH','/healthz'); \
r=urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000'+p, timeout=4); \
sys.exit(0 if r.status==200 else 1)" || exit 1

# Production WSGI server instead of the Flask development server. Gunicorn's
# access/error logs are written to stdout/stderr for the container log driver.
CMD ["gunicorn", "app:app", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "3", \
     "--threads", "2", \
     "--timeout", "30", \
     "--graceful-timeout", "30", \
     "--keep-alive", "5", \
     "--max-requests", "1000", \
     "--max-requests-jitter", "100", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-"]

hy4-flash/03-infra-management/nginx.conf

user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;

error_log  /var/log/nginx/error.log warn;
pid        /var/run/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections  1024;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/octet-stream;

    log_format  main  '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" '
                      '$status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" '
                      '"$http_user_agent" rt=$request_time urt=$upstream_response_time';
    access_log  /var/log/nginx/access.log  main;

    sendfile        on;
    keepalive_timeout  65;

    # Upstream group with keepalive to the API. The static name `api` is
    # resolved at startup via Docker's embedded DNS; depends_on ensures the
    # API is already up and healthy by then.
    upstream api_upstream {
        server api:8000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
        keepalive 32;
    }

    server {
        listen       80;
        server_name  _;

        # JSON request bodies: cap size instead of accepting arbitrarily large payloads.
        client_max_body_size 2m;
        client_body_timeout 15s;
        client_header_timeout 15s;

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://api_upstream;

            # Forward client information to the app (X-Forwarded-*).
            proxy_set_header Host              $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host  $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port  $server_port;

            # HTTP/1.1 + empty Connection are required for upstream keepalive.
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";

            # Timeouts tuned for a JSON API: don't hang clients on slow backends.
            proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
            proxy_send_timeout    30s;
            proxy_read_timeout    30s;

            # Don't buffer JSON responses; stream them and ignore upstream
            # Cache-Control for the proxy's own caching (none configured).
            proxy_buffering off;
            proxy_request_buffering on;
        }

        # Lightweight proxy health endpoint for liveness/uptime checks.
        location = /healthz {
            access_log off;
            add_header Content-Type application/json;
            return 200 '{"status":"ok"}';
        }

        # Never serve hidden files (e.g. leaked .env, .git) if a static root
        # is ever added.
        location ~ /\. {
            deny all;
        }
    }
}
